    Language & API reference

    SIPL, in full.

    The language, its standard modules, and the tools around them. Explore syntax and types, then move into web services, data, interfaces, AI, reproducible projects, testing, and debugging.

    fn start()Cross-platformAutomatic JITChecked bytecode
    Start with the language →Create a project →Write a test →

    SIPL Language Reference#

    This is the complete language on one page. An AI model can use it as a system prompt.

    1. The syntax decision: braces for structure, line breaks for statements#

    The brace-versus-indentation argument comes down to two concerns:

    • Brace programmers want structure that stays correct after copy-paste, reformatting, or token-by-token generation. Whitespace must never change meaning.

    • Indentation programmers want clean code without semicolons and clutter, and they want indentation to always match the structure.

    SIPL meets both needs:

    RuleWho it satisfies
    Blocks use { }, and whitespace never changes meaningBrace programmers, AI models, copy-paste
    No semicolons. A line break ends a statement (; is optional to put two statements on one line).Indentation programmers
    No parentheses around conditions: if x > 0 {Indentation programmers
    and, or, not instead of &&, \|\|, !Readability
    One official style (4 spaces, { on the same line), enforced by sipl fmtEveryone: indentation always matches structure

    The line-break rule follows Go: a line break ends a statement only when the line ends with a name, literal, ), ], }, return, break, or continue. So expressions can continue across lines after an operator, comma, or opening bracket. A line that starts with . continues the previous line:

    2. Program structure#

    Top-level functions can be declared in any order. Named test "description" { ... } blocks are available to sipl test in test sources; production run and build commands reject them. See Testing and API documentation.

    3. Variables and types#

    let fixes the name. Lists and Maps that the name points to can still be changed with their mutating methods.

    Annotations are enforced by sipl check whenever the source type is known. This includes initializers, assignments, function and method arguments, constructor fields, and return values. A function with a non-None return annotation must return on every structural path. Any is an explicit dynamic boundary: values flowing out of it retain the same runtime checks, including the permitted Int-to-Float conversion.

    TypeLiteralNotes
    Nonenonethe absence of a value
    Booltrue, false
    Int42, 1_000_00064-bit; overflow is an error
    Float3.14, 1e-964-bit; always prints with a .
    String"text {expr}"immutable; \n \t \" \\ \{ \}
    List[T][1, 2, 3]T is the item type; trailing comma allowed
    Map[K, V]{"key": value}, {:}K is the key type, V the value type; keeps insertion order
    Range0..10includes 0, excludes 10
    Functionfn(x) => x * 2
    Result[T]result.ok(value), result.err(fail)a successful value of type T, or a Fail

    Annotation types: Any None Bool Int Float Number String List Map Range Function Type Fail Result Ai Bytes Regex Prng Instant Monotonic Duration Date LocalDateTime TimeZone Interval Cron Locale Translator, parameterized List[T], Map[K, V], Result[T], or the name of any user type. Generic types may nest, for example List[Map[String, Int]]. An Int is accepted where a scalar Float is expected and is converted automatically.

    Generic collections and results#

    • List[T], Map[K, V], and Result[T] are invariant. List[Int] is not a List[Float]; this prevents mutation through an alias from violating the element type.

    • Plain List, Map, and Result remain valid and mean that their contained values are dynamic.

    • Literal contents, indexing, loops, keys(), values(), and unwrap() propagate their known types.

    • Map keys may be None, Bool, Int, Float, Number, String, Bytes, or Any. Numeric map literals infer Number keys because 1 and 1.0 are the same key in SIPL.

    • When a value crosses from Any into a generic type, the VM validates its contents. A validated collection remembers its descriptor, so later checks are O(1) and every mutation through any alias must preserve the type.

    4. Operators (highest to lowest precedence)#

    OperatorsMeaning
    x.y x(...) x[i]member, call, index (negative index counts from the end)
    -xnegate
    * / %/ always returns Float; % follows the sign of the left operand
    + -+ also joins String+String and List+List
    ..range
    == != < <= > >=comparisons do not chain; 1 == 1.0 is true
    notBool only
    andBool only, short-circuit
    orBool only, short-circuit

    "Total: " + 5 is an error. Use interpolation instead: "Total: {5}".

    5. Control flow#

    Conditions must be Bool. Write if not list.isEmpty, not if list.

    A for loop over a Map may change the values of existing keys, but adding or removing keys during the loop is an error. To do that, loop over map.keys() instead.

    5b. Closed enums and exhaustive match#

    An enum declares a closed set of nominal variants. Payload fields are named and typed:

    • A variant without a payload is a value: State.Loading. Do not call it.

    • A payload variant is a constructor. It accepts positional or named arguments: State.Failed(7, "bad") or State.Failed(reason: "bad", code: 7).

    • Enums are nominal. Two enums with identical variants are still different types, and enums in different modules are distinct.

    • match evaluates its subject once and is an expression. The subject must have a statically known enum type.

    • Every variant must appear exactly once. Missing, duplicate, unknown, incorrectly qualified, or incorrectly bound patterns are compile errors. There is deliberately no wildcard pattern.

    • Payload bindings are immutable typed locals in declaration order.

    • A pattern may be unqualified (Ready(value)), enum-qualified (State.Ready(value)), or module-qualified (network.State.Ready(value)).

    • Expression arms must produce one compatible type. Int, Float, and Number arms merge to Number; incompatible results are compile errors. A block arm produces None unless it exits with return or fail.

    • Because { ... } immediately after => is a block arm, parenthesize a Map literal result: Ready(value) => ({"value": value}).

    • Enum values compare structurally, print with their variant and named payloads, expose their enum through .type, and retain runtime validation when crossing an Any boundary.

    6. Functions#

    Functions are values. Closures capture variables by reference, and each loop iteration gets a fresh variable. Parameters cannot be reassigned; copy one into a var if you need to change it.

    Core native operations with shared contracts also accept named arguments; sipl api symbol --json lists their exact labels/types. Labels may reorder supplied arguments, but cannot skip earlier optional parameters or name a variadic parameter. APIs not yet in that inventory require positional calls. See API discovery for precise properties and inferred awaited types.

    6b. Failures (try, fail, next)#

    • try needs a fail block, a next block, or both, in that order.

    • Inside the handler, fail is an immutable local Fail value. Its read-only properties are why (the message), kind ("fail", "runtime", "file", or "system"), and line (the originating source line).

    • fail("reason") raises a failure. fail(fail) re-raises the same value, preserving its message and line.

    • Runtime failures propagate through function calls and built-in callbacks to the nearest active handler. Syntax and compilation errors are not catchable.

    • next runs after success or failure, including when return, break, or continue leaves the protected block or handler. Nested cleanup runs from inner to outer.

    • A failure raised in a handler still runs its next block before propagating. A failure or return in next replaces the pending failure or return.

    • Without a handler, an uncaught failure stops the program with a diagnostic and stack trace. There are no catch or finally keywords, and try is not an expression.

    7. Types#

    • Declared only at the top level. Names are PascalCase. Every field needs a type; there are no default values.

    • The constructor takes every field and checks its type (an Int is accepted for a Float field).

    • Inside methods, self is the instance. Fields are properties (p.x), and methods are called with ().

    • Every type inherits the base Object. It may override toString() (used by print and interpolation) and equals(other) (used by ==, contains, indexOf). type, hash and copy are fixed.

    • Default == compares the fields of two values of the same type. Values of different types are never equal.

    • Instances cannot be Map keys (they are not hashable).

    7b. Modules (use)#

    • One file is one module. Its name is the file name, and its members are always written module.name.

    • use goes at the top level of a file. Paths are relative to the file that contains the use.

    • Names starting with _ are private to their file.

    • A module's vars can only be changed by that module's own code. Give it a function for outside changes.

    • Each module is loaded once and initialized before the files that use it. Modules that use each other in a circle are an error; move the shared part into a third module.

    • Types in different modules are different types even with the same name. p.type shows geometry.Point.

    • Module members are resolved when compiling: no lookup cost at run time, and wrong names or argument counts are reported before the program runs.

    Data and I/O modules#

    • json.parse(text), json.isValid(text), and json.stringify(value, pretty?) convert between JSON and SIPL values. JSON objects become String-keyed Maps; null becomes none.

    • result.ok(value) and result.err(fail) construct a Result. Results expose .isOk, .isErr, .value, and .error, plus unwrap(), unwrapOr(default), map(fn), andThen(fn), and mapError(fn).

    • path provides join, normalize, isAbsolute, basename, dirname, and extension. fs provides text/binary-safe readText/writeText, exclusive empty-file createFile, exists, isFile, isDirectory, list, recursive sorted walk (relative files, no symlink traversal), size, makeDirectory, remove, and copy.

    • http.request(method, url, options?), http.get(url, options?), and http.post(url, body, options?) return NetTask. Poll with net.poll() or block explicitly with .wait() to obtain a typed HttpResponse with .status, .headers, .body, and .url. Portable TLS, streaming Bytes, cancellation, redirect policy, proxies, pooling, certificates, and connect/read/total deadlines are covered in HTTP.

    • tcp, udp, websocket, and framing share the NetTask/CancelToken model. See networking for bounded streams, socket services, and WebSocket client/server APIs.

    • The web module provides routes, middleware, static files, and secure server-side sessions with OS-generated opaque IDs, bounded expiry, rotation, and destruction; see docs/WEB.md.

    • auth, identity, and optional ldap provide password hashes, PKCE/OIDC/JWT validation, immutable Identity values, and native directory access. OidcClient and LdapDirectory network methods return NetTask. See identity and authentication for supported protocols, trust boundaries and optional SDKs. These module names follow the existing top-level reserved-name rule.

    • The generic graphics module provides typed applications, retained scenes, transforms, cameras, input, and depth-tested drawing without exposing backend-specific names; see docs/GRAPHICS.md.

    Logging and media#

    log.open(options?) creates an explicit Logger; audio.open(options?) creates an AudioApp that owns AudioSound handles; audio.stream(path, options?) creates an AudioStream with native chunked playback for long music files; image creates owned Image values. Their contracts, limits and examples are discoverable through sipl api. See logging, audio, and images. The new built-in names log, audio, and image follow the existing top-level reserved-name rule; use a distinct name for a top-level variable or module member.

    8. Formatting#

    sipl fmt file.sipl rewrites a file in the one official style. sipl fmt --check only reports. The formatter keeps every comment and refuses to write anything that would change the program.

    9. User interface (ui)#

    The interface is redrawn from your variables on every frame. Widgets return the new value, so there are no callbacks and nothing to keep in sync. Positions are in logical pixels from the top-left corner. Colors are Strings: "#RGB", "#RRGGBB" or "#RRGGBBAA".

    KindNames
    Windowui.open(title, width, height) · ui.openFixed(title, width, height) (fixed client size) · ui.frame() · ui.close() · ui.redraw() (request the next frame for animation) · ui.setTitle(text) · ui.setBackground(color) · ui.platform ("windows", "linux", or "headless")
    Text and entryui.heading(value, options?) · ui.text(value, options?) · ui.textInput(label, text, style?) → String · ui.textArea(label, text, rows, style?) → String
    Actions and choicesui.button(labelOrItem, options?) → Bool · ui.contextMenu(id, x, y, open, items, options?) → Map · ui.checkbox(label, checked, style?) → Bool · ui.toggle(label, enabled, style?) → Bool · ui.radio(label, selected, style?) → Bool · ui.slider(label, value, min, max, style?) → number · ui.select(label, selected, options, style?) → selected option · ui.colorPicker(label, color, style?) → color String
    Navigationui.tabs(id, selected, options, style?) → selected option · ui.collapsible(label, open, style?) → Bool
    Feedbackui.progress(label, value, min, max, style?) · ui.spinner(label, style?) · ui.badge(value, style?) · ui.tooltip(text, style?) immediately after its target widget
    LayoutWidgets stack top to bottom · ui.row(fn() { ... }) places widgets side by side · ui.box(width, height, fn() { ... }, options?) creates a clipped surface · ui.panel(x, y, width, height, options?) → geometry Map · ui.scrollView(height, offset, fn() { ... }) → new offset · ui.scrollbar(id, x, y, length, offset, viewport, content, options?) → new offset · ui.separator(style?) · ui.space(size)
    Drawingui.drawRect(x, y, width, height, color, radius?) · ui.drawCircle(x, y, radius, color) · ui.drawLine(x1, y1, x2, y2, color, thickness?) · ui.drawText(x, y, value, color?, options?)
    Inputui.mouseX · ui.mouseY · ui.isMouseDown · ui.isMousePressed / ui.isMouseReleased (this frame) · ui.isRightMouseDown · ui.isRightMousePressed / ui.isRightMouseReleased · ui.hasFocus · ui.wheel · ui.keys (e.g. ["left", "ctrl+s"]) · ui.typedText · ui.width · ui.height · ui.isOpen
    Fontui.setFont(path?, pixelSize?) · ui.usePixelFont() · ui.fontRenderer · ui.fontSize; see UI fonts
    Text and clippingui.charWidth · ui.lineHeight · ui.textWidth(text) · ui.clip(x, y, width, height) · ui.unclip()
    Clipboardui.clipboard (text) · ui.setClipboard(text)

    For continuous game movement, ui.keyDown(key) returns whether a key is held while the window has focus. It accepts letters (case-insensitive), digits, "left", "right", "up", "down", "shift", "ctrl", "alt", "space", "enter", "escape", and "tab". Use ui.keys for per-frame key events and shortcuts; use the native gamepad module for controllers. Tests can enqueue held-key changes with ui.setKeyDown(key, down) on an open window. On macOS, Command also maps to ctrl. Ctrl shortcut events additionally support digits, plus/equal and minus. ui.moveMouse(x, y) queues pointer movement for UI automation without pressing a button.

    ui.tooltip(text, style?) attaches to the preceding widget. A one-second monotonic hover delay precedes display; clicks, dragging, leaving the widget, focus loss and popup capture suppress stale hints. Tooltips are painted in a final overlay above panels and later drawing, independent of their parent's clip. Long hints wrap and stay inside the window. Idle native windows wake once at the hover deadline rather than continuously animating.

    ui.titleBar(height, dragWidth, interactive?) optionally replaces the native Windows caption with a client-drawn region and returns whether the platform supports it. Height is 0..128 (0 restores the native caption), drag width is 0..16384 logical pixels. interactive is a list of up to 64 rectangles {x,y,width,height} that retain normal client input. All remaining space in the top region is a native caption hit target: dragging moves the window and double-clicking maximizes it. The OS continues to own frame resizing. ui.windowAction("minimize"|"maximize"|"close") requests a native window action; maximize toggles restore. Both APIs return false on unsupported backends; ordinary windows retain their existing behavior unless explicitly opted in. Applications using client chrome must draw their own caption controls.

    Buttons and styled entry/choice widgets accept paired integer x and y options for absolute positioning. For example, ui.textInput("Name", name, {"x": 220, "y": 100, "width": 240}) places the input at that location without advancing the normal layout cursor.

    Text drawn with ui.text, ui.heading, or ui.drawText is selectable by default: drag across it, then use Ctrl+C. Multiline text is one selection block, so a drag can span lines and the copied String preserves newline characters. For decorative labels that should not accept selection, pass the explicit option {"unselectable": true} (ui.drawText takes it as the fifth argument). ui.textInput and ui.textArea support click/drag selection, Shift+arrow selection, and the usual Ctrl+A/C/X/V shortcuts. Multiline text areas scroll with the wheel, keep the caret visible, and show a thin scrollbar only when their content exceeds the visible rows. Inside a frame, ui.textAreaWrap(text, before, after) wraps the last drawn text area's selection with two strings and returns the updated text. With no selection, it inserts both strings at the caret and leaves the caret between them; formatting buttons can call it even when the text area was drawn in the previous frame.

    Native pickersui.filePicker(title?) · ui.folderPicker(title?) · ui.saveBox(defaultName?) → selected path or none when cancelled
    Automationui.click(x, y) · ui.rightClick(x, y) · ui.drag(x1, y1, x2, y2) · ui.typeText(text) · ui.pressKey(name) · ui.scroll(notches) · ui.screenshot(path) (PNG)

    Shared widget styles#

    ui.setStyle(source) replaces the shared style with a validated snapshot of a Map. The source can be exported by a SIPL module or loaded with json.parse(fs.readText("theme.json")). Updating the original Map has no effect until setStyle is called again. An empty Map or ui.resetStyle() restores built-in defaults. Styles can be installed before opening a window and persist across window reopenings.

    Every flow widget accepts an optional trailing style Map, including text, headings, choices, status widgets, text entry, scroll views, tooltips, and separators. Buttons, boxes, panels, scrollbars, context menus, and video controls accept style fields in their existing options Map. A reusable Map can be supplied as the style option. Resolution order is built-in defaults, common source fields, the source's widgets[widgetName], reusable style, then direct options. ui.withStyle(source, fn) temporarily overlays the common and widget source fields; nested scopes restore both after completion or an error. Widget-specific fields still override common fields within a scope. A box's local style affects its frame; use withStyle to style its children as well.

    ui.getStyle() returns a detached Map of resolved common values; ui.getStyle("button") returns resolved defaults for one widget. These are useful for custom drawing and style editors. They exclude per-call overrides; use the original source Map to save or reload the entire theme. Unknown source fields and widget names, malformed colors, and invalid types or ranges raise an error before replacing the active source. Existing non-style behavior options remain valid.

    FieldsMeaning
    background, text, border, mutedWidget surface, foreground, outline, secondary text
    accent, hover, pressed, onAccentActive controls, hovered/pressed controls, check marks and contrasting text
    selected, selectedText, selectionSelected surfaces, selected tab text, text-selection fill
    track, thumb, focus, placeholderSlider/scroll track, knob/scrollbar thumb, focused outline/caret, empty input hint
    disabledBackground, disabledText, enabledDisabled appearance and interaction; enabled is a Bool
    shadow, windowBackgroundContext-menu shadow and window clear color
    fontScaleInteger text scale from 1 to 8; default 2, headings 3; relative to the active setFont face
    width, heightFlow-widget dimensions, 0 for automatic or 1–16384 logical pixels; slider width sets its rail width
    radius, borderWidthCorner radius 0–8192 and outline thickness 0–64 logical pixels
    padding, spacing, windowPaddingContent/label inset, gap after a flow widget, and outer layout inset; 0–1024 logical pixels

    Colors accept #RGB, #RRGGBB, and #RRGGBBAA, including transparent fills. Fields apply where a widget draws that part: for example, shadow belongs to context menus, and thumb to sliders, toggles, radios, and scrollbars. Explicit panel, box, scrollbar, and video geometry stays in their existing arguments; container padding controls child layout. Larger text can be paired with an explicit control height. Disabled containers disable their own resizing or scrolling; child controls resolve their own enabled values. Color-picker swatches, HSV gradients, and contrast samples retain their actual color values.

    Widget names for widgets and getStyle are text, heading, button, checkbox, toggle, radio, slider, select, tabs, collapsible, progress, spinner, badge, colorPicker, tooltip, textInput, textArea, box, panel, scrollbar, contextMenu, scrollView, separator, and drawVideo.

    Action backgrounds follow accent and action text follows onAccent unless explicitly supplied. Focus and selected text follow accent; tracks follow border; placeholders and disabled text follow muted. Hover and pressed colors remain separately configurable. See examples/ui_styles.sipl for a live theme whose accent can be changed with a color picker.

    Toolbar buttons and context menus share a C menu-item parser. Define actions in SIPL as {"id": "createFile", "label": "Create file", "shortcut": "Ctrl+N", "enabled": true}. Only label is required; id defaults to the label, shortcut to empty, and enabled to true. IDs and labels contain 1–512 bytes; shortcut hints at most 128. A String item uses that String as both ID and label. SIPL dispatches the selected ID and implements keyboard shortcuts; C draws shortcut hints without installing global key bindings. Disabled items cannot activate from mouse or keyboard.

    ui.button(item, options?) returns whether it was clicked. Its default placement still follows flow layout. Options x and y together select absolute placement; width and height override its measured size. Options also accept enabled, background, hover, pressed, text, and muted colors. Coordinates are 0–16384 and dimensions 1–16384. Button identity follows the item's ID rather than its display label.

    ui.contextMenu accepts 1–64 items and returns {open, selected, x, y, width, height}. Assign open back to application state; selected is the chosen item's ID or empty when nothing was selected. Mouse clicks or Enter activate an enabled item; Up/Down skip disabled items. Escape, an outside click, or window focus loss closes the menu. It fits within the window and scrolls longer lists with the wheel or keyboard. Options are minWidth and background, text, border, hover, muted colors. Only one popup is active at a time. The optional openingPress: true ignores the press used to open a popup in that frame; pass false afterward so outside clicks dismiss normally.

    Call the menu before processing underlying inputs. While open, it consumes mouse presses, typed text, keys, and wheel input. C paints it above later widgets at presentation and screenshot time, independent of the enclosing clip. The same event path handles right clicks and focus changes on Windows and Linux; ui.rightClick injects matching headless events.

    Panels and boxes share optional resize handles. Pass a stable id and a resize List containing any of "left", "right", "top", "bottom"; the default is no handles. Each handle occupies six pixels inside its edge, highlights on hover, shows a centered grip, and captures a drag until release, including outside the panel. Windows and Linux show the corresponding resize cursor. Reserve these edge pixels when drawing custom children. enabled: false disables resizing. Options also accept minWidth, maxWidth, minHeight, maxHeight, and background, border, accent colors. Default minimum dimensions are 32 pixels (or the window size if smaller); default maxima are the window size. Limits must satisfy 1 <= min <= max <= 16384. Panels are additionally constrained to their enclosing clip.

    ui.panel draws an absolute surface and returns {x, y, width, height, resizing}. Keep the returned geometry in application state; derive adjacent rectangles from it each frame. Left/top drags move the origin while keeping the opposite edge fixed. A box with options returns the same geometry and automatically moves subsequent flow widgets when its size changes. Flow boxes keep their layout origin for all handle sides. A three-argument box retains its None return. Three-argument boxes require dimensions of at least 32 pixels; boxes with options accept dimensions from 1 to 16384. Call resizable controls before custom child input: captured presses are removed from ui.isMousePressed, and native widgets drawn afterwards cannot also activate from that press.

    ui.scrollbar uses application-defined units for offset, viewport, and content, so a code editor can scroll in rows or columns. It clamps to 0..max(0, content - viewport), supports dragging the thumb and clicking the track, and returns the updated offset. Options are horizontal (default false), thickness (4–32, default 12), enabled, and background, thumb, accent colors. Length and viewport must be positive; content may be zero. A bar with no overflow draws a full thumb and does not capture input. Stable IDs preserve capture across frames. ui.drag queues a press, movement, and release on successive input frames for deterministic desktop/headless tests.

    select and tabs take a non-empty List and return one of its values. Radio buttons are composable: set the shared choice when a radio returns true. A scroll view keeps no hidden application state, so assign its returned offset each frame:

    colorPicker starts as a compact current-color display and 16-swatch palette. Its Expand control opens the full editor inline in the same SIPL window: saturation/value field, hue and opacity strips, current and previous colors, RGB/HSL/HSV values, tint and shade suggestions, color harmonies, and white/black WCAG contrast ratios. Compact returns to the small state. The widget returns the selected #RRGGBB or #RRGGBBAA String every frame.

    When hosted in an openFixed window, the picker automatically switches the client area between its fixed 420×150 compact size and 740×450 expanded size. The fixed window has a close button but no minimize, maximize, or resize controls.

    The three picker functions use native Windows dialogs or built-in canvas dialogs on Linux. Linux dialogs let you browse folders, type or paste a path (Ctrl+L), choose with Enter, and cancel with Escape. Saving an existing file requires an explicit replacement confirmation. They return none on cancellation and in headless test mode.

    Linux windows use X11/XWayland and the same canvas and fonts as Windows. Desktop window decorations follow the host theme. make SIPL_UI_X11=0 builds a runtime for headless use without X11 development packages. The macOS implementation hosts the same widgets in a Cocoa window, including Retina scaling, clipboard and file panels. Command shortcuts use the existing ctrl+ key names. See Mac build and acceptance for its deployment target and pending native qualification.

    Key names: backspace delete enter tab escape left right up down home end pageUp pageDown, the same with shift+ in front (shift+left), and ctrl+a … ctrl+z, ctrl+space, and ctrl+enter. Ctrl combinations also preserve Shift, for example ctrl+shift+g. Input arrives in the order it happened: a frame never mixes a click with keyboard input, and holds typed text followed by at most one key.

    Files and the system#

    ModuleNames
    filefile.read(path) → String · file.write(path, text) · file.exists(path) · file.isFolder(path) · file.list(folder) → sorted names
    workspaceProject-confined list(root, relative) · read(root, relative) · write(root, relative, text) · replace(root, relative, old, new) · makeDirectory(root, relative); see AGENT.md
    pathpath.absolute(path) resolves against the process working directory and normalizes lexically; the target need not exist. join, normalize, basename, dirname, extension, isAbsolute provide path operations.
    systemsystem.exec(arguments) → {"output": String, "exitCode": Int, "outputTruncated": Bool} runs a literal argument list without a shell · system.run(command) is the legacy shell API · system.args · system.executable · system.program · system.platform · system.securityRevision

    sipl run program.sipl a b makes system.args == ["a", "b"].

    system.securityRevision is a read-only Int reporting the runtime's security patch level (currently 2). Toolkit's runtime compatibility check requires at least that revision; rebuild old runtimes and packaged applications to update them. SIPL programs run with the current user's OS permissions. File/process APIs and Toolkit Run commands are not a sandbox for untrusted code.

    Set SIPL_UI=headless to run without a window: tests, CI and servers. In headless mode ui.frame() returns false once there is no input left to process.

    10. Built-in names (the complete list)#

    Every value (base Object)#

    .type · .toString() · .equals(x) · .hash() · .copy()

    Int / Float#

    .toInt() (truncates) · .toFloat()

    String#

    Properties: .length · .isEmpty

    .toUpper() · .toLower() · .trim() · .trimStart() · .trimEnd() · .split(sep) / .split() (splits on whitespace) · .contains(s) · .startsWith(s) · .endsWith(s) · .indexOf(s) (-1 if missing) · .replace(old, new) (replaces all) · .replaceFirst(old, new) · .repeat(n) · .slice(start, end?) · .chars() · .reverse() · .toInt() / .toFloat() (none if invalid) · .padStart(width, fill?) · .padEnd(width, fill?)

    List[T]#

    Properties: .length · .isEmpty · .first · .last (none if empty)

    Mutating: .push(x, ...) · .pop() · .insert(i, x) · .removeAt(i) · .remove(x) (→ Bool) · .clear()

    Non-mutating: .contains(x) · .indexOf(x) · .slice(start, end?) · .chunk(size) · .flatMap(fn) · .groupBy(fn) · .join(sep) · .reverse() · .sort() · .sortBy(fn) · .map(fn) · .filter(fn) · .reduce(fn, initial) · .find(fn) · .any(fn) · .all(fn) · .sum() · .min() · .max()

    Batching, flattening, and grouping#
    MethodResultRules
    chunk(size: Int)List[List[T]]Positive size; consecutive shallow copies of at most that many items. Empty input returns []; a size larger than the input gives one batch.
    flatMap(transform: Function)List[Any]Invoke once per input item and concatenate the returned Lists, flattening exactly one level. A non-List result fails. Output is limited to 1,000,000 items.
    groupBy(key: Function)Map[Any, List[T]]Invoke once per input item. The result must be a supported Map key: None, Bool, Number, String or Bytes. Groups follow first-key appearance, and items retain input order.

    These methods allocate new containers and leave the source structure unchanged. Copies are shallow: mutable objects inside them retain their identity. chunk and groupBy preserve validated input item types in their batches, including through Any aliases. flatMap results are dynamic because a callback can return different item types; an explicit List[T] annotation validates them.

    flatMap and groupBy iterate a shallow snapshot taken before the first callback. A callback may clear, extend, or reorder the original list without changing which items are visited. Callback failures propagate normally; callback side effects are not rolled back. chunk takes O(n) time and space; groupBy takes expected O(n) time and O(n) space; flatMap takes O(n + m) time and space plus callback work, where m is the output count. Named arguments are available: numbers.chunk(size: 2) and numbers.groupBy(key: fn(n) => n % 2).

    Map[K, V]#

    Properties: .length · .isEmpty

    .get(key, default?) · .set(key, value) · .contains(key) · .remove(key) (→ Bool) · .keys() · .values() · .clear() · indexing map[key] (error if missing) and map[key] = value

    Result[T]#

    Properties: .isOk · .isErr · .value (none on failure) · .error (none on success)

    .unwrap() · .unwrapOr(default) · .map(fn) · .andThen(fn) · .mapError(fn)

    Range#

    Properties: .length · .isEmpty · .start · .end

    .contains(n) · .toList()

    Function#

    Read-only properties: .name, .callCount (successful calls), .loopCount (loop backedges executed), .jitStatus, and .nativeCallCount.

    Type (a type itself) and instances#

    Type property: .name. Instances: every field as a property, the type's methods, and the base Object members.

    Global functions#

    print(...) · input(prompt?) · assert(cond, message?) · abs(x) · sqrt(x) · pow(a, b) · floor(x) · ceil(x) · round(x) (these three return Int) · min(a, b, ...) · max(a, b, ...) · random() · randomInt(min, max) (max excluded) · exit(code?)

    Standard-library types and modules#

    Bytes, Regex, Prng, Instant, Monotonic, Duration, Date, LocalDateTime, TimeZone, Interval, Cron, Locale, and Translator support type annotations. The native bytes, unicode, regex, url, encoding, math, time, i18n, env, and config modules are available globally. String stores UTF-8 bytes; its core length, indexing, and slicing use bytes. Unicode scalar/grapheme operations are explicit. HTTP bodies use Bytes. The callable time() has been removed; use time.now() for UTC timestamps and time.monotonic() for elapsed measurements. See the standard-library API contracts for limits and examples.

    The explicit secrets.load(path) / secrets.save(path, map) APIs encrypt local JSON settings with Windows DPAPI. secrets.userPath() locates the current user store; project stores live under the project's .sipl-toolkit. Toolkit remembers OpenAI/Google keys with these APIs; see encrypted settings.

    12. AI cheat sheet#

    API discovery and the coding loop#

    Native contracts for the language core and modules including networking, time, HTTP/HTTPS serving, logging, audio, images, gamepads, PDF, document collections, and linear algebra share one inventory: src/native_api.def. Compiler/editor inference, native named arguments, option-key/type validation, and discovery consume that inventory. Operation-specific native checks still enforce ranges, nested data, security, resource bounds, and ownership. APIs outside that inventory, including many UI, graphics, worker, and AI operations, retain their module references and require positional arguments. Use sipl api to check which contracts are available in the runtime you are using.

    Find a contract or complete program#

    Select an exact symbol, a module, or a native type. No selector lists the inventory. JSON output has schemaVersion: 1, runtimeVersion, entries, shapes, matched, returned, truncated, and ok. Each entry includes its kind, named parameters, signature, return/awaited type, effects, option schema, limits, failure guidance, availability, example, and reference path. Parameters are structured objects with name, type, optional, and variadic. Property entries include mutable: native sound controls have checked setters, while image dimensions and other read-only metadata cannot be assigned. Options and named Map shapes use semicolon-separated field:Type contracts; option keys are optional unless the operation's reference explicitly requires them. | means alternatives, not new SIPL union-annotation syntax. Generic placeholders T, K, V, and Self refer to the receiver's type. Dynamic JSON, unions, and callback-dependent results remain conservative Any in the compiler.

    --limit accepts 1–1024 and explicitly reports truncation. Unknown symbols return ok: false and exit 1. Usage errors exit 2. --verify compares required core/module/type operations and arities against the actual runtime tables; the regression suite also executes self-contained contract examples and checks their result types. Discovery does not execute example code or contact a server.

    --task returns an exact, complete recipe embedded from examples/recipes/: files, json, http, cli, service, gui, scheduling, clock_tests, library, logging, audio, or image. JSON includes task, description, command, path, and source. command is the driver (run, test, or doc), not a shell command. Read the recipe's explicit argument assertions before running it. Recipe tests compare embedded bytes with source and exercise file outputs, loopback HTTP/service behavior, scheduling, headless GUI, documentation, and normal/GC-stress execution. After changing a recipe, regenerate its embedding:

    Names and awaited types#

    Known native operations accept the same argument-label syntax as user functions:

    Evaluation stays in source order; native dispatch reorders the resulting values. Labels may reorder supplied parameters but cannot skip an earlier optional parameter or name a variadic parameter. Unknown/duplicate labels fail. Native operations without metadata continue to require positional arguments.

    Awaited types come from the same contracts: await http.get(...) produces an inferred HttpResponse; awaiting Interval.next() produces Monotonic. Annotated async user functions preserve their declared return type through their task and await. Task[T]/NetTask[T] describe inferred editor facts; they are not additional user annotation syntax. Input/domain failures remain catchable native errors, including inside negative tests.

    Generate, check, repair, prove#

    1. Retrieve the relevant symbol or task, then make a small change.

    2. Run sipl fmt --check file.sipl and sipl check --json file.sipl.

    3. Apply only a verified suggested fix, or use its code/range/help to repair.

    4. Run sipl test tests --filter "relevant case" --json build/tests.json.

    5. Keep a full make test / run_tests.ps1 verification gate.

    The editor service caches compiler facts, invalidates changed files and known dependents, and runs cancellable background analysis. Ordinary CLI checks are fresh, compile-only checks; they do not use a persistent cache or execute SIPL. Test selection is an explicit filter, not inferred affected-test selection. See LSP.md, TESTING.md, and DEBUGGING.md for structured diagnostics, reports, and crash data.

    Reproducible measurements#

    On Windows use python and build/sipl.exe. The suite pins its version, runtime version/binary hash, and canonical recipe source hashes, then measures median discovery/check latency with a monotonic clock. Baseline comparisons require matching task source. This is a tooling baseline, not a claim of measured model success or token savings. Semantic recipe tests are a separate gate.

    Optional --agent-results imports actual measurements without calling a model, spending tokens, or executing generated code. Input is an object with pinned model, promptVersion, and a nonempty tasks list. Each task has task, Boolean firstCheckPassed/success, and nonnegative finite repairs, inputTokens, outputTokens, toolCalls, and codingMilliseconds. The report aggregates success rates and repair/token/tool/time totals. Real agent runs must pin prompts, environment, and task inputs themselves; never substitute canonical recipe checks for first-generation success.

    Everyday standard library#

    Native processes and completed files#

    system.exec(arguments: List[String]) -> Map launches an executable with a literal argument list. The first item names the executable; remaining items are its arguments. It inherits the current directory and environment, supplies closed input, waits for completion, and captures combined standard output/error. Use it inside a SIPL worker for long jobs in a desktop application.

    The result contains exitCode, output, and outputTruncated. Capture retains up to 8 MiB while continuing to drain the child. Limits are 1..4096 arguments and 1 MiB of UTF-8 argument bytes; Windows additionally limits its encoded command line to 32,766 characters. NUL bytes and an empty executable are rejected. Executable lookup uses PATH. Missing executables report exit code 127. Arguments are passed directly to the process, with Windows CRT quoting where required. Descendants retain their SIPL worker's process group or Job Object, so worker cancellation terminates the encoder as well as its SIPL parent.

    fs.move(source, destination, replace?: Bool) publishes a completed regular file on the same volume. By default an existing destination causes failure and is preserved. Explicit replace: true performs an atomic replacement, useful for progress snapshots. Stage temporary files beside their destination. On POSIX, exclusive publication uses a hard link followed by source removal; if removing the source fails, both names remain and the call reports failure.

    The native modules bytes, unicode, regex, url, encoding, math, time, i18n, env, and config are available in every program. No import or package download is required. New annotation names are Bytes, Regex, Prng, Instant, Monotonic, Duration, Date, LocalDateTime, TimeZone, Interval, Cron, Locale, and Translator.

    The native auth, identity, and optional ldap libraries provide password hashes, secure random tokens, OAuth/OIDC, JWT validation, typed identities and directory access. Their APIs, LDAP SDK requirements, ui.passwordInput and security boundaries are documented in the identity guide, with working examples. LDAP availability is explicit through ldap.available; other standard libraries remain usable without a directory SDK.

    The optional native webview module hosts the installed Windows WebView2 engine. webview.available reports availability; webview.run(url, options?) opens a same-origin window without a SIPL/JavaScript authority bridge. The reusable meeting library supplies one-call meeting server/desktop setup, WebRTC signaling, admission, chat and file/PDF sharing. It builds on web.serve with its optional literal IPv4 host and server-owned window.

    Invalid arguments and resource limits raise catchable Fail values. APIs do not silently replace malformed text, discard unknown regex flags, or read unrequested environment variables. Tables below state parameters, returns, failures, and a canonical example; each section states effects and complexity.

    This prerelease changes HTTP request/response bodies to Bytes and removes the callable global time(). Use time.monotonic() for measurements and time.now() for UTC timestamps. Examples and Toolkit use these APIs directly.

    Bytes and binary I/O#

    Bytes is immutable binary storage, limited to 16 MiB per value. Indexing returns an Int from 0 to 255; negative indices count from the end. Out-of-range indices fail. Iteration yields bytes, or index/byte pairs with two loop names. Equality compares contents. Bytes can be Map keys. .length is an Int and .isEmpty is a Bool; assignments to bytes or their properties fail.

    API and parametersReturnFailuresCanonical example
    Bytes(values?): List of Int, Bytes, or omittedBytes; existing Bytes is returned unchangedNon-Int entries, values outside 0..255, size limitBytes([0, 128, 255])
    bytes.fromList(values)BytesSame constructor validationbytes.fromList([65, 66])
    bytes.fromHex(text)BytesMalformed hex or size limitbytes.fromHex("00ff")
    bytes.fromBase64(text)BytesMalformed/noncanonical padded base64 or size limitbytes.fromBase64("AP8=")
    bytes.encodeUtf8(text)BytesInvalid UTF-8 or size limitbytes.encodeUtf8("é")
    value.slice(start: Int, end?: Int)New BytesNon-Int boundsBytes([1, 2, 3]).slice(1, 3)
    value.toList()List[Int]Allocation failureBytes([1, 2]).toList()
    value.secureEquals(other: Bytes)BoolNon-Bytes argumentBytes([1]).secureEquals(Bytes([1]))
    value.toHex()String, lowercase hexAllocation failureBytes([255]).toHex()
    value.toBase64()String, standard padded base64Allocation failureBytes([255]).toBase64()
    value.decodeUtf8()StringInvalid UTF-8Bytes([195, 169]).decodeUtf8()
    fs.readBytes(path: String, maxBytes?: Int) / file.readBytes(...)BytesI/O error, invalid path, byte limitfs.readBytes("assets/image.png", 1048576)
    fs.writeBytes(path: String, data: Bytes) / file.writeBytes(...)NoneI/O error, invalid path, non-Bytes inputfs.writeBytes("output.bin", Bytes([0, 255]))
    path.absolute(path: String)Absolute normalized String; target need not existInvalid path, unavailable working directorypath.absolute("music/song.mp3")
    fs.createFile(path: String)NoneExisting file/folder, missing parent, invalid path, I/O errorfs.createFile("new.txt")

    Slices use an exclusive end, clamp bounds, and return empty Bytes when the end precedes the start. File read limits default to 16 MiB and must be between zero and 16 MiB. Text APIs fs.readText/file.read and fs.writeText/file.write validate UTF-8; use binary APIs for arbitrary data.

    Constructors, slices, conversions, content equality, and hashing take O(n) time; new values use O(n) space. Length, indexing, and emptiness take O(1). secureEquals visits every byte for equal-length inputs without data-dependent early exit; different lengths return false immediately. It is intended for comparing secrets of a known, fixed length. Binary reads and writes perform filesystem I/O and take O(n) time and O(n) read space; writes can create or truncate files. Other Bytes APIs only allocate values.

    fs.createFile creates an empty file exclusively and never replaces an existing entry, including a symlink. Its parent must already exist. It performs one filesystem create/close operation with O(path length) conversion space on Windows. Explorer uses it after inline filename confirmation, so concurrent changes cannot cause an existing file to be truncated.

    HTTP options body and http.post bodies require Bytes. Response body is Bytes. Web handler request bodies are Bytes; responses accept String text or Bytes binary data. See HTTP and Web.

    ZIP archives#

    zip uses the bundled MiniZip and zlib sources. zip.open(path) opens an existing ZIP or creates an empty one and returns a ZipArchive. Call zip.close(archive) when done; later calls with that handle fail. All methods perform blocking filesystem I/O.

    API and parametersReturnEffect
    zip.open(path: String)ZipArchiveOpen or create a ZIP file
    zip.close(archive: ZipArchive)NoneClose the handle
    zip.add(archive: ZipArchive, source: String, entryName?: String)NoneAdd a disk file, replacing an entry with the same name; default name is the source basename
    zip.remove(archive: ZipArchive, entryName: String)BoolRemove matching entries; returns whether any existed
    zip.list(archive: ZipArchive)List[String]List entry names in archive order
    zip.read(archive: ZipArchive, entryName: String)BytesRead a stored or deflated entry, up to 16 MiB
    zip.extract(archive: ZipArchive, entryName: String, destination: String)NoneStream a stored or deflated entry to disk without the Bytes limit, replacing the destination only after a successful extraction

    Added entry names must be relative paths using /, without .. segments. zip.add and zip.remove rewrite the archive through a temporary file in the same folder and replace the original only after a successful write. Writers and streaming extraction retain their file and directory handles inside a private staging directory; they do not close and reopen a shared temporary filename. The final commit stays anchored to the opened destination parent and replaces the destination entry rather than following a destination symlink. Rewriting copies existing stored and deflated entries without expanding them. Encrypted entries and other compression methods fail without changing the original. ZIP metadata other than entry names, timestamps, attributes, comments, and archive comment is not retained when rewriting. zip.read returns Bytes, so use .decodeUtf8() for text. The 16 MiB limit applies to one in-memory Bytes value, not to the archive or files added to it. Use zip.extract for larger entries.

    Unicode text model#

    String stores UTF-8 bytes. Its core .length, indexing, .chars(), .slice(), and .reverse() operate on bytes, without implicit normalization. A byte slice can cut a multibyte character; Unicode APIs reject invalid results. Use Bytes for binary storage and the explicit Unicode APIs for text units. String .toUpper()/.toLower() map ASCII only, independently of machine locale. Unicode casing is available through the unicode module.

    unicode.version reports the supported Unicode data version as a String. Scalar values exclude surrogates and are between zero and U+10FFFF; embedded U+0000 is preserved. Graphemes are extended grapheme clusters, including combining sequences, emoji ZWJ sequences, and regional-indicator pairs. All defaults are locale-free.

    API and parametersReturnFailuresCanonical example
    unicode.isValid(value: String or Bytes)BoolWrong input typeunicode.isValid(Bytes([128]))
    unicode.codePoints(text: String)List[Int]Invalid UTF-8 or size limitunicode.codePoints("é😀")
    unicode.fromCodePoints(values: List[Int])StringInvalid scalar/type or size limitunicode.fromCodePoints([233, 128512])
    unicode.graphemes(text: String)List[String]Invalid UTF-8 or size limitunicode.graphemes("á🇺🇸")
    unicode.sliceCodePoints(text, start: Int, end?: Int)StringInvalid UTF-8/type or size limitunicode.sliceCodePoints("aé😀z", 1, 3)
    unicode.normalize(text, form?: String)StringInvalid UTF-8, unknown form, output size limitunicode.normalize("é", "NFC")
    unicode.caseFold(text)StringInvalid UTF-8 or size limitunicode.caseFold("Straße")
    unicode.toUpper(text)StringInvalid UTF-8 or size limitunicode.toUpper("é")
    unicode.toLower(text)StringInvalid UTF-8 or size limitunicode.toLower("É")

    Normalization accepts NFC (default), NFD, NFKC, and NFKD. Case folding uses full Unicode mappings, including expansions such as ß to ss; it does not implicitly normalize. Unicode upper/lower use simple scalar mappings, which differ from full string casing where a character expands. Code-point slicing uses exclusive/clamped/negative bounds like Bytes slicing.

    Effects are allocation only. Validation and conversions take O(n) time and O(n) output space; validation alone uses O(1) additional space. Code-point slicing scans the input even for a small slice. Normalization is normally linear but canonical ordering can take O(n²) for a long combining sequence. Inputs and resulting text are limited to 16 MiB.

    Encodings and CSV#

    Binary encoders take Bytes. Their inverse returns Bytes; text conversion is a separate decision. JSON remains the existing json module. Configuration loading uses that same parser. There is no second JSON or general TOML API.

    API and parametersReturnFailuresCanonical example
    encoding.utf8Encode(text: String)BytesInvalid UTF-8 or size limitencoding.utf8Encode("hello")
    encoding.utf8Decode(data: Bytes)StringInvalid UTF-8/typeencoding.utf8Decode(Bytes([104, 105]))
    encoding.hexEncode(data: Bytes)StringWrong input typeencoding.hexEncode(Bytes([255]))
    encoding.hexDecode(text: String)BytesOdd length, nonhex digit, size limitencoding.hexDecode("ff")
    encoding.base64Encode(data: Bytes)StringWrong input typeencoding.base64Encode(Bytes([102]))
    encoding.base64Decode(text: String)BytesInvalid alphabet/padding/pad bits, size limitencoding.base64Decode("Zg==")
    encoding.percentEncode(data: Bytes)StringWrong input typeencoding.percentEncode(Bytes([32, 255]))
    encoding.percentDecode(text: String)BytesInvalid percent escape or size limitencoding.percentDecode("%20%FF")
    encoding.csvParse(text: String, delimiter?: String)List[List[String]]Invalid UTF-8, quoting, delimiter, or limitsencoding.csvParse("name,age\r\nAda,37\r\n")
    encoding.csvWrite(rows: List[List[String]], delimiter?: String)StringWrong cell/row types, empty row, invalid UTF-8/delimiter, size limitencoding.csvWrite([["name", "age"], ["Ada", "37"]])

    Hex decoding accepts either case. Base64 is the standard alphabet with required padding, no whitespace, and canonical unused bits. Percent encoding preserves ASCII letters, digits, and -._~; other bytes become uppercase %HH. Decoding leaves + literal; it is not form-urlencoded decoding.

    CSV uses a one-byte delimiter, default comma, excluding quote, newline, carriage return, NUL, and non-ASCII bytes. Quoted fields may contain newlines and doubled quotes. Parsing accepts CRLF, LF, and CR row endings, preserves empty fields, performs no numeric conversion, and limits input to 16 MiB and 100000 fields. Empty input has zero rows. Writing emits CRLF and quotes fields as needed, including a sole empty cell; output is limited to 16 MiB.

    Effects are allocation only. Each API takes O(n) time and O(n) output space. Encoded strings may be larger than the 16 MiB binary input limit; decoded Bytes remain bounded. CSV also allocates a List for each row and a String for each field. CSV writing does not enforce the parser's 100000-field limit.

    Compiled regular expressions#

    regex.compile(pattern: String, flags?: String, limits?: Map) -> Regex compiles a regular-expression pattern in Unicode mode. Flags are i (case-insensitive), m (multiline anchors), s (dot matches newline), and x (extended syntax). Unknown or repeated flags fail. Syntax errors report the pattern offset and compiler message. Named captures use (?<name>...). Pattern size is at most 4096 bytes, nesting at most 128, and capture count at most 64.

    Canonical compile example: regex.compile("(?<word>\\w+)", "i").

    Limit Map keyDefaultAllowed Int range
    maxInputBytes10485761..16777216
    maxMatches10001..10000
    maxWork10000001..10000000

    Unknown limit keys fail. Every matching call checks the input limit and shares one work budget across candidate starting positions and all global matches. Automatic callouts and engine match limits stop excessive backtracking; engine depth is capped at 128 and engine heap at 4 MiB. Matching does not use JIT. Returned captures/replacement output have a 16 MiB budget. Hitting any budget raises Fail rather than returning a partial result. maxWork counts engine work checks, not milliseconds or an exact cross-version instruction count.

    Regex API and parametersReturnFailuresCanonical example
    .isMatch(text: String)BoolInvalid UTF-8 or resource limitregex.compile("^a").isMatch("abc")
    .find(text: String)Match Map or NoneInvalid UTF-8 or resource limitregex.compile("\\d+").find("item42")
    .findAll(text: String)List[Map]Invalid UTF-8 or any match/output/work limitregex.compile("\\d+").findAll("1 and 2")
    .replace(text: String, replacement: String)StringInvalid UTF-8, bad replacement capture, resource limitregex.compile("\\d+").replace("item42", "[$0]")

    .pattern and .flags are read-only Strings. Match Maps contain text, start, end, groups, and named. Start/end are UTF-8 byte offsets, with exclusive end; groups include the whole match at index zero, and unmatched optional captures are None. Named is a String-keyed Map. Global operations support empty matches, retry a nonempty alternative at the same position, then advance by a whole Unicode scalar when necessary.

    Replacement templates accept $0, numbered captures such as $1, ${name}, and $$ for a literal dollar. SIPL string interpolation requires escaping the braces in a named template: "$\{name\}". Unknown capture references fail. Replace processes all nonoverlapping matches.

    Effects are allocation only; compiled values are GC-managed. Compilation cost depends on pattern expansion. Matching is bounded backtracking, not a linear-time guarantee: work may grow rapidly but is stopped by the configured budget. Result construction takes O(total returned bytes + captures) time and space. Programs should choose smaller limits for smaller workloads.

    URLs#

    URL helpers handle absolute URLs and relative references. Inputs/outputs are limited to 65536 bytes, ports to 0..65535, and query Lists to 1000 pairs. Unescaped controls, spaces, backslashes, malformed escapes, invalid schemes, and invalid bracketed IP literals fail. Hosts use ASCII DNS names or IP literals; supply international DNS names in ASCII IDNA form. No implicit DNS lookup, filesystem access, or network request occurs.

    API and parametersReturnFailuresCanonical example
    url.parse(text: String)Map of componentsInvalid URL text/type or limitsurl.parse("https://example.com/a?q=one#top")
    url.build(parts: Map)StringInvalid component types/host/port, ambiguous path, or limitsurl.build({"scheme": "https", "host": "example.com", "path": "/a b"})
    url.encode(text: String)Encoded String componentInvalid UTF-8 or size limiturl.encode("a&b é")
    url.decode(component: String)StringBad escapes or decoded invalid UTF-8url.decode("a%26b%20%C3%A9")
    url.parseQuery(query: String)List of [String, String] pairsBad escapes/UTF-8 or query/pair limitsurl.parseQuery("q=one&q=two")
    url.buildQuery(pairs: List)StringInvalid pair types or query/pair limitsurl.buildQuery([["q", "a&b"], ["q", "two"]])

    Parsed fields are scheme, authority (Bool), userinfo, host, port, path, query, fragment, encoded (true), and ipLiteral (Bool). Missing optional components are None; path is always String. Host excludes IP brackets. Encoded components retain their percent escapes.

    Builders accept raw component Strings by default, encode their UTF-8 bytes, and lowercase the ASCII scheme/host. An explicit host introduces authority; its nonempty path gets a leading slash when needed. Port/userinfo require a host. A path beginning // without a host fails to avoid changing its meaning. The encoded: true marker returned by parse preserves existing escapes when rebuilding; use raw values without that marker when composing new URLs. ipLiteral: true preserves brackets for IPvFuture literals.

    Prefer query pairs over a query String when composing values. Duplicate keys and their order are preserved. Plus signs are literal, missing = means an empty value, and a trailing & adds no extra pair. Helpers do not resolve dot segments, infer default ports, or apply browser-specific URL rewriting. Effects are allocation only; time and output space are O(n).

    Math and deterministic random objects#

    math.pi, math.tau, and math.e are read-only Float constants. Angles use radians and scalar inputs accept Int or Float. math.clamp preserves Int precision when all three arguments are Int; otherwise it returns Float.

    API and parametersReturnFailuresCanonical example
    math.sin(x: Number)FloatNonfinite angle/typemath.sin(math.pi / 2)
    math.cos(x: Number)FloatNonfinite angle/typemath.cos(0)
    math.tan(x: Number)FloatNonfinite angle/typemath.tan(0)
    math.asin(x: Number)Floatx outside [-1, 1] or wrong typemath.asin(0)
    math.acos(x: Number)Floatx outside [-1, 1] or wrong typemath.acos(0)
    math.atan(x)FloatNaN/typemath.atan(1)
    math.atan2(y, x)FloatNaN/typemath.atan2(1, 0)
    math.sinh(x: Number)FloatNaN/typemath.sinh(0)
    math.cosh(x: Number)FloatNaN/typemath.cosh(0)
    math.tanh(x: Number)FloatNaN/typemath.tanh(0)
    math.log(x: Number)Floatx <= 0, NaN, or wrong typemath.log(math.e)
    math.log2(x: Number)Floatx <= 0, NaN, or wrong typemath.log2(8)
    math.log10(x: Number)Floatx <= 0, NaN, or wrong typemath.log10(100)
    math.exp(x)FloatNaN/typemath.exp(1)
    math.sqrt(x)FloatNegative value, NaN, or wrong typemath.sqrt(9)
    math.clamp(value, min, max)Int or FloatReversed bounds, NaN/typemath.clamp(20, 0, 10)
    math.isFinite(x: Number)BoolWrong typemath.isFinite(math.pi)
    math.isNaN(x: Number)BoolWrong typemath.isNaN(math.pi)
    math.prng(seed: Int)PrngWrong seed typemath.prng(42)
    rng.nextFloat()Float in [0, 1)Allocation failuremath.prng(42).nextFloat()
    rng.nextInt(min: Int, max: Int)Int in [min, max)min >= max or wrong typemath.prng(42).nextInt(0, 10)
    rng.bytes(length: Int)BytesLength outside 0..16 MiB or wrong typemath.prng(42).bytes(16)

    Scalar functions take O(1) time/space and perform no I/O. Floating-point overflow may yield infinity; these are Float operations, not exact decimal arithmetic. Libm rounding can differ slightly across platforms.

    Prng uses xoshiro256** with SplitMix64 seeding and 53-bit Float draws. Equal seeds and equal call sequences produce equal outputs across supported platforms. .seed is a read-only Int. Draws mutate that object's state only; objects share no hidden random state. Integer draws use rejection sampling to avoid modulo bias (expected O(1)); Float draws are O(1), and byte generation is O(n) time/space. This generator is for simulation/tests, not cryptographic keys or secrets. Decimal and arbitrary-precision integer types remain future work.

    Instants, monotonic points, and durations#

    These immutable types keep wall-clock timestamps separate from elapsed time. Instant is signed Int64 nanoseconds since the Unix epoch in UTC. Monotonic is a point on the system monotonic clock with an unspecified origin; it is suitable for measurements within the running environment, not persistent timestamps. Duration is a signed Int64 count of nanoseconds. Precision of the actual clocks depends on the platform.

    API and parametersReturnFailuresCanonical example
    time.now()InstantClock unavailable/out of rangetime.now().unixSeconds
    time.monotonic()MonotonicClock unavailable/out of rangetime.monotonic()
    time.duration(nanoseconds: Int)DurationWrong typetime.duration(1000000)
    time.seconds(value: Number)Duration, truncated to whole nanosecondsNonfinite/out of range/typetime.seconds(0.25)
    time.elapsed(start: Monotonic)DurationWrong clock kind or subtraction overflowtime.elapsed(time.monotonic())
    time.sleep(duration: Duration)NoneWrong type, negative duration, >24 hours, OS failure, called from async codetime.sleep(time.seconds(0.01))
    point.since(earlier: same clock kind)DurationMixed clocks or overflowtime.now().since(time.now())
    value.add(offset: Duration)Same type as receiverNon-Duration offset or overflowtime.duration(1).add(time.duration(2))

    Read-only properties: Instant .unixNanoseconds: Int, .unixSeconds: Float; Monotonic .nanoseconds: Int; Duration .totalNanoseconds: Int, .totalSeconds: Float, and .totalMilliseconds: Float. Wall-clock differences can be negative when the clock changes. Arithmetic checks Int64 overflow. Use monotonic points for elapsed measurements. Instant differences compare stored timestamps and may reflect wall-clock corrections.

    All operations take O(1) time/space apart from sleep's elapsed wait. Clock reads observe the OS; sleep blocks the calling thread (rounded up to a millisecond on Windows). Constructors/arithmetic only allocate values.

    Calendar values and explicit timezones#

    Date and LocalDateTime are immutable proleptic Gregorian values, years 1..9999. A local datetime has nanosecond precision and carries no timezone. Converting it to an Instant requires an explicit TimeZone; the narrower Instant range is 1677-09-21T00:12:43.145224192Z through 2262-04-11T23:47:16.854775807Z. A timezone is an exact, case-sensitive IANA identifier. Neither TZ, the machine timezone, nor the process locale supplies an implicit default.

    SIPL bundles public-domain IANA tzdata 2026c, including historical offsets, compatibility aliases, and future recurring DST rules expanded across the entire Instant range. The executable and packaged programs contain this data on every platform. zone.version identifies the snapshot; future political rule changes require updating the bundle. Regenerate it with scripts/embed_tzdata.py from a leap-free TZif tree compiled by zic. The generator validates every transition against Python's independent TZif reader and does not run during ordinary builds.

    API and parametersReturnFailuresCanonical example
    Date(year: Int, month: Int, day: Int)DateInvalid date/type/rangeDate(2024, 2, 29)
    LocalDateTime(year, month, day, hour, minute, second?: Int, nanosecond?: Int)LocalDateTimeInvalid date, hour 0..23, minute/second 0..59, nanosecond 0..999999999LocalDateTime(2026, 10, 14, 9, 30)
    TimeZone(id: String)TimeZoneUnknown IANA name, NUL, invalid UTF-8, >255 bytesTimeZone("America/New_York")
    time.fromUnixNanoseconds(value: Int)InstantWrong typetime.fromUnixNanoseconds(0)
    time.parseDate(text: String)DateRequires exactly YYYY-MM-DD and a valid datetime.parseDate("2024-02-29")
    time.parseLocal(text: String)LocalDateTimeRequires YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SS[.fraction] without an offsettime.parseLocal("2026-10-14T09:30:00")
    time.parse(text: String, zone?: TimeZone, disambiguation?: String)InstantMalformed/range; no offset and no zone; supplied offset disagrees with zone; DST gap/overlaptime.parse("2026-10-14T09:30:00-04:00")
    time.format(instant: Instant, zone: TimeZone)StringWrong types; historical offset not a whole minutetime.format(time.now(), TimeZone("UTC"))
    calendar.toIso()String—Date(2024, 2, 29).toIso()
    calendar.addDays(days: Int)Same calendar typeWrong type or resulting year outside 1..9999Date(2024, 2, 29).addDays(1)
    date.daysSince(earlier: Date)Int calendar-day countWrong typeDate(2024, 3, 1).daysSince(Date(2024, 2, 28))
    local.add(offset: Duration)LocalDateTimeWrong type/calendar rangeLocalDateTime(2026, 1, 1, 0, 0).add(time.seconds(-1))
    local.toInstant(zone: TimeZone, disambiguation?: String)InstantDST gap, unresolved overlap, invalid policy, Instant rangelocal.toInstant(TimeZone("UTC"))
    instant.toLocal(zone: TimeZone)LocalDateTimeWrong typetime.now().toLocal(TimeZone("Asia/Tokyo"))
    zone.offsetAt(instant: Instant)Duration, local minus UTCWrong typeTimeZone("America/New_York").offsetAt(time.now())

    Date/local read-only properties are .year, .month, .day, and .weekday (ISO Monday=1 through Sunday=7). Local datetimes also expose .hour, .minute, .second, .nanosecond, and .date. Zones expose .id and .version. Calendar equality compares fields; timezone equality compares the supplied identifier. Aliases have the same rules but retain their own identifiers.

    ISO output is locale-invariant ASCII. Parsing follows the Gregorian extended ISO-8601 / RFC 3339 profile above: seconds are required, fractions have 1..9 digits, offsets use Z or ±HH:MM, and lowercase t/z are accepted. -00:00 identifies a UTC instant but its unknown-local-offset metadata is not retained. Leap seconds, 24:00, week and ordinal dates, whitespace separators, and excess precision fail. Output uses uppercase T/Z and trims trailing fractional zeros without losing precision. Offsets containing historical seconds cannot be emitted in RFC 3339; format the Instant in UTC instead.

    For overlapping local times, the default "reject" policy fails; "earlier" and "later" select the chronological occurrence. Nonexistent local times always fail. Calendar-day and local arithmetic operate on calendar fields; an elapsed 24-hour Duration added to an Instant may land at a different local hour after a DST change.

    Calendar arithmetic is O(1). Zone lookup is O(log Z); offset lookup is O(log T) for a zone's T transitions. Local conversion tests its fixed set of distinct offsets, each with a binary search. No conversion mutates OS timezone settings.

    Timers, intervals, and cron#

    Schedules create cancellable NetTask waits on the existing async event loop. They inherit lexical task ownership, admission bounds, failure propagation, and scope-exit cancellation described in ASYNC.md. The caller supplies the work in an async function; native scheduling never invokes user callbacks.

    API and parametersAwaited result / returnFailuresCanonical example
    time.timer(delay: Duration)NetTask yielding NoneNegative duration or monotonic overflowawait time.timer(time.seconds(0.25))
    time.at(instant: Instant)NetTask yielding the target InstantWrong type/operation admission limitawait time.at(time.now().add(time.seconds(10)))
    time.interval(period: Duration)IntervalPeriod <1 ms or monotonic overflowtime.interval(time.seconds(1))
    interval.next()NetTask yielding the scheduled Monotonic tickA wait is already pending; deadline overflowlet tick = await interval.next()
    time.cron(expression: String, zone: TimeZone)CronInvalid syntax/type; expression >256 bytestime.cron("30 9 * * 1-5", TimeZone("America/New_York"))
    cron.nextAfter(after: Instant)First matching Instant strictly after afterNo occurrence within eight years or Instant's rangecron.nextAfter(time.now())
    cron.next()NetTask yielding the scheduled InstantA wait is already pending; no next occurrenceawait cron.next()

    Duration timers and interval phases use only the monotonic clock. Interval ticks retain their original phase and skip missed ticks; one pending wait per schedule prevents overlapping consumers and unbounded queues. Native timers have no hidden network timeout, so long waits survive until completion or owner cancellation. Resolution depends on the OS and event loop (approximately one millisecond); nanosecond values do not promise nanosecond wakeups.

    Calendar alarms and cron use UTC wall time to decide when a civil deadline is due and follow wall-clock corrections. A past time.at target completes on the next event-loop turn. This is calendar scheduling, not elapsed measurement.

    Cron has five numeric fields: minute 0..59, hour 0..23, day-of-month 1..31, month 1..12, weekday 0..7 (0 and 7 mean Sunday). Fields support *, comma lists, inclusive ranges, and positive /step values on wildcards, ranges, or a numeric start (e.g. 5/15 selects 5, 20, 35, 50 in the minute field). Names, seconds, and extended operators are unsupported. When either day field begins with *, both day masks must match, including stepped wildcards. Otherwise day-of-month and weekday combine with OR. DST gaps are skipped and both occurrences of an overlapping local minute are eligible. Computation scans at most eight years of calendar days and the selected hours/minutes, testing offsets without touching the wall clock in nextAfter. next() chooses from the current wall time and skips past runs.

    Explicit locale formatting and translations#

    i18n never reads or sets the process-wide locale. Locale objects identify an explicit supported profile: en-US, en-GB, de-DE, fr-FR, ja-JP, or es-ES. Other names fail instead of falling back to a machine default. These are deliberately bounded formatting profiles, not a full CLDR/ICU implementation.

    API and parametersReturnFailuresCanonical example
    i18n.locale(id: String)LocaleUnsupported name/type, NUL, invalid UTF-8, >64 bytesi18n.locale("de-DE")
    i18n.number(value: Number, locale: Locale, fractionDigits?: Int)String, grouped ASCII digits and localized separatorsNonfinite/type; fraction digits outside 0..9i18n.number(1234.5, i18n.locale("de-DE"), 2)
    i18n.formatDate(value: Date/LocalDateTime/Instant, locale: Locale, zone: TimeZone, style?: String)StringWrong type; style other than "short"/"long"i18n.formatDate(time.now(), i18n.locale("en-US"), TimeZone("UTC"))
    i18n.translator(locale: Locale, catalog: Map)Translator with an immutable snapshot of messagesNon-String keys/values; >1000 messages or >1 MiB totali18n.translator(i18n.locale("en-US"), {"hello": "Hello"})
    translator.translate(key: String, parameters?: Map)StringMissing key or String parameter; malformed braces; >1 MiB outputtranslator.translate("hello")

    Number formatting defaults to two fractional digits; Int values keep their full 64-bit precision. Float rounding follows fixed-decimal C formatting in an explicit C numeric locale scoped to the operation. French grouping uses U+202F. Date formatting defaults to "short"; "long" uses localized month names. An Instant is converted using the supplied zone. Date/local values retain their calendar fields, and local/converted values append a 24-hour clock time.

    Locale .id and Translator .locale are read-only. Locale equality compares the profile ID. Catalog keys are at most 128 UTF-8 bytes and messages at most 16 KiB; messages and supplied String parameters must be valid UTF-8. Templates substitute {name} literally; {{ and }} escape braces. Values requiring number/date formatting should be formatted explicitly before substitution. Missing translations raise Fail; there is no implicit fallback language or global translation catalog. Number/date formatting is O(output length), and translation is O(template plus output length) with Map lookups for parameters.

    Explicit environment and configuration#

    Allowlist arguments are required. Environment names must be portable ASCII identifiers, 1..128 characters; allowlists hold at most 256 entries. Missing variables produce None, and values must be valid UTF-8 of at most 1 MiB. The APIs use platform environment-name matching; use consistent spelling, especially on case-insensitive Windows.

    API and parametersReturnFailuresCanonical example
    env.read(names: List[String])Map[String, String or None] containing requested names onlyInvalid name/type/list/value limitsenv.read(["APP_PORT"])
    env.get(name: String, allowed: List[String], default?: String or None)String or None/defaultName absent from allowlist, invalid names/types/value limitsenv.get("APP_PORT", ["APP_PORT"], "8080")
    config.load(path: String, allowedPaths: List[String], maxBytes?: Int)JSON object MapPath not allowlisted, I/O, invalid UTF-8/JSON, nonobject root, byte limitconfig.load("app.json", ["app.json"])
    config.merge(base: Map, overrides: Map)New shallow Map; overrides winWrong argument typesconfig.merge({"port": 8080}, {"port": 9000})

    Configuration allowlists hold at most 256 paths and compare exact path spelling, without searching directories or expanding environment variables. Read limits default to 1 MiB and accept 1..16 MiB. Allowlisting selects the requested file; it is not a filesystem sandbox or a symlink restriction. Loading uses the existing JSON parser and its nesting/node limits. Merge copies entries, leaves its arguments unchanged, and shares nested values. There is no automatic global configuration, implicit dotenv load, or hidden precedence chain.

    Environment reads observe process state and allocate O(total returned bytes) space; allowlist scanning and value copying take O(names + bytes) time plus platform lookup cost. Configuration loading reads the filesystem in O(file bytes) time/space plus JSON parsing costs. Merge only allocates a new Map, using expected O(base entries + override entries) time and space.

    Structured logging#

    Logging is explicit: create a Logger, pass it to code that needs it, and derive child contexts. There is no global logger configuration. Console output defaults to stderr, leaving stdout free for program results and CLI protocols.

    Use sipl api log --json and sipl api Logger --json for the same named arguments, options, return types, and limits used by editor discovery.

    Sinks and levels#

    log.open(options?: Map[String, Any]) -> Logger accepts:

    OptionDefaultMeaning
    sink"console""console" for readable stderr, "json" for JSON stderr, or "file"
    formatsink-specific"text" or "json"; file defaults to JSON
    pathnoneRequired nonempty UTF-8 path for a file sink; rejected on other sinks
    level"info"Minimum "debug", "info", "warn", or "error"
    context{}Structured context snapshot shared by records from this logger
    bufferBytes0Explicit native buffer limit, 0..1 MiB; zero writes and flushes each record
    history0Optional in-memory ring, 0..1024 JSON records, at most 16 MiB capacity
    maxRecordBytes16384Record limit, 256 bytes..1 MiB, including timestamp/keys/newline
    maxBytes10485760File size before rotation, 256 bytes..1 GiB
    maxFiles3Retained archives, 0..16; zero truncates the current file at rotation

    File maxRecordBytes must not exceed maxBytes. Options, context types, and limits are validated before opening or creating a file. Unknown options fail. Maps require String keys; structured serialization is bounded to depth 16 and 4096 visited values. Cycles, excessive nesting, and oversized records fail before that record reaches a sink. Non-JSON objects are represented as a type marker without invoking user callbacks; nonfinite numbers are strings.

    logger.write(level, message, attributes?), debug, info, warn, and error return None. Sink I/O is synchronous, including from async tasks; buffering reduces write frequency but is not an async/nonblocking transport. Messages are String and attributes are Map[String, Any]. JSON records have timestamp, level, message, context, and attributes. Timestamps use the temporal wall-clock provider and UTC RFC-3339 with nanoseconds; they never use the machine timezone. Elapsed measurements remain the caller's explicit monotonic-clock responsibility. test.clock controls timestamps in tests.

    logger.with(context) returns a Logger with a redacted context snapshot; child keys override parent keys without changing the parent. Trace/request IDs are ordinary explicit structured context fields, not ambient task globals. Child loggers share a sink, minimum level, buffer, rotation, and history.

    Read-only properties are closed: Bool, level: String, and bufferedBytes: Int. history() -> List[String] returns redacted JSON records oldest-first; filtered levels never enter history. A buffered record enters history when accepted, not when committed to disk.

    Lifecycle, buffering, and rotation#

    flush() synchronously checks pending writes and fflush; it is not an fsync or durable-storage guarantee. close() flushes and closes the shared sink for all children, is idempotent, and does not close process stderr. Writes, flushes, and deriving new children after close fail. History remains readable after close.

    On normal process exit, pending sinks receive a best-effort checked flush. The last garbage-collected child also performs a best-effort flush. Abrupt termination or a power failure can lose buffered records: explicitly flush or close when correctness depends on observing a write error. Sink I/O failures raise a file failure and invalidate the sink, rather than repeatedly retrying a potentially partially written record.

    File sinks append to existing files. Before a record would exceed maxBytes, the old file moves to path.1, previous archives advance to path.2 and beyond, and a fresh current file opens. The oldest configured archive is removed. Each physical file is bounded by the configured maximum after new writes; an existing oversized file is rotated before the next record. The logger owns the current path and path.1 through path.maxFiles; do not use these names for unrelated data.
