Concurrent writers to the same path and cross-process rotation are not supported in this beta. Large media/metrics/tracing exports are not part of this module.

    Default privacy#

    Console, JSON, file, and history outputs all apply default redaction. Sensitive attribute/context key names (case and separators ignored) cover passwords, tokens, authorization/cookies, secrets/API/private/signing keys, credentials, email/phone/address/birth-date/card/social-security fields. Nested maps/lists are processed; sensitive-key values are replaced completely. Obvious email addresses, Bearer credentials, and password=.../token: ... forms in strings are also redacted. There is no switch to disable this in the beta.

    Crash reports and structured test failure reports apply the same default rules to sensitive local/captured variable names, map keys, instance/enum field names, and textual values. Explicit interactive debugger inspection retains its normal raw-value semantics; treat an interactive debug session as privileged access.

    This is best-effort detection, not a guarantee that arbitrary prose, opaque strings, source paths, user-defined secret field names, or every locale's PII are safe. Do not log secrets, raw HTTP bodies, or personal data; pass safe identifiers and structured allowlisted attributes. Terminal/source diagnostics and explicit print output are not automatically sanitized by the logger.

    Phase-2 metrics, tracing spans, health/profiling/GC statistics, asynchronous export sinks, and OpenTelemetry remain optional follow-up packages.

    Authentication, LDAP, and identity#

    SIPL provides directory integration through ldap, password and OAuth/OIDC helpers through auth, and an immutable, annotatable Identity type. These are libraries, without new language syntax. Networking uses NetTask and the existing event loop. Cryptography uses the runtime's existing OpenSSL-compatible library; LDAP uses a maintained platform SDK.

    This is an initial implementation with a deliberately bounded feature set. Windows and Linux builds and controlled-provider tests are included. A real AD domain, Entra tenant, or Google application needs deployment-specific testing; mock tests do not establish compatibility with every organization policy.

    Identity and authorization#

    identity.create(values) accepts trusted application data. It does not authenticate arbitrary claims, validate a password, or turn browser-supplied roles into trusted permissions. Verify credentials/tokens first, then obtain roles and permissions from an application-controlled policy or allowed-user table. OIDC identities start with no roles or permissions. CRM-ERP performs this mapping using its own users and role tables.

    Properties are id, provider, name, email, groups, roles, permissions, claims, expiresAt (integer Unix seconds), and isAuthenticated. Missing optional strings/lists/claims default to empty; expiry defaults to one hour. id must be a nonempty string. Lists allow 1,024 entries; strings and copied JSON have bounded sizes. Lists and claims returned by properties, and toMap(), are defensive copies.

    Methods: hasRole(name), hasGroup(name), hasPermission(name), requirePermission(name), and toMap(). The first four also have module forms: identity.hasRole(user, name), etc. Expired identities never grant permissions. Matching is exact and case-sensitive. A role named admin has no universal meaning in the runtime: the application defines that policy. CRM-ERP defines admin as all present and future application permissions.

    Passwords and random values#

    APIBehavior
    auth.randomToken(bytes = 32)CSPRNG bytes encoded as unpadded base64url; 16–64 bytes
    auth.pkce(verifier?)Map with verifier, challenge, and method: "S256"; generates a verifier when absent
    auth.passwordHash(password)PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256, 600,000 iterations, 16-byte random salt, 32-byte key
    auth.bcryptHash(password, cost = 12)Openwall bcrypt, $2b$ output, 16-byte random salt; cost 4–16
    auth.passwordVerify(password, hash)Verifies PBKDF2 and bcrypt $2a$/$2b$/$2y$; constant-time comparison; malformed bounded hashes return false

    PBKDF2 password strings accept 1–1,024 UTF-8 bytes; applications set their own password policy. CRM-ERP requires at least 12 bytes. Hashes are self-describing sipl-pbkdf2-sha256$iterations$salt$key values. Verification accepts 600,000 to 2,000,000 iterations, bounding resource use. Password hashing is synchronous CPU work; directory and HTTP I/O run asynchronously. Rate-limit login attempts and use a dummy hash for unknown usernames, as CRM-ERP does.

    Bcrypt is bundled in every build using pinned Openwall crypt_blowfish 1.3, the implementation family used by PHP. The upstream reentrant implementation and per-hash self-test are retained; salts use the existing OpenSSL/LibreSSL CSPRNG. There is no optional SDK, host crypt() dependency, or bcrypt DLL. system.buildFeatures["bcrypt"] records this required support.

    New bcrypt passwords must contain 1–72 UTF-8 bytes, without NUL; oversized passwords raise an error rather than being silently truncated. The limit counts encoded bytes, not characters. Verification retains bcrypt's historical 72-byte truncation for compatibility with existing PHP/Apache hashes, with the existing 1,024-byte input bound. Empty passwords can be verified against legacy bcrypt hashes but cannot be generated by bcryptHash.

    Bcrypt generation and verification accept costs 4–16; the default for new hashes is 12. Hashes requesting a larger cost, unsupported prefixes such as $2x$, or noncanonical salt/digest encodings return false before derivation. The cost ceiling bounds CPU work. .htpasswd retains its existing cost ceiling of 14. passwordHash() continues generating PBKDF2, and passwordVerify() recognizes both formats, so existing accounts remain usable. Password generation/verification are synchronous CPU work and do not log passwords.

    Implementation provenance: Openwall crypt_blowfish, pinned source and checksum.

    ui.passwordInput(label, value, style?) reuses native text-input editing, draws one mask character per Unicode code point, and disables copy/cut. It returns the actual password string. Passwords and tokens are ordinary SIPL values and can be exposed by explicit logging or serialization: do not log them. The language does not yet have a redacting Secret value or guaranteed erasure of all GC-managed string copies.

    OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect#

    In the callback, obtain code and state from the query and retrieve that browser's stored transaction:

    Configuration fields are issuer, clientId, optional clientSecret, caFile, timeout (100–30,000 ms, default 10,000), and allowLoopbackHttp (false). Unknown fields fail. Production endpoints require HTTPS with chain and hostname validation, no URL credentials or fragments, and no automatic redirects. The explicit test option permits HTTP only for literal loopback hosts. Callback URLs may use HTTP on loopback for local apps.

    discover() returns NetTask[Map], reads issuer/.well-known/openid-configuration, verifies exact issuer equality, and checks the authorization, token, and JWKS endpoints. It snapshots metadata internally; editing the returned Map cannot redirect credential requests.

    Authorization requests always use S256 PKCE, without plain or non-PKCE fallback. When discovery lists PKCE methods, it must include S256 to begin a sign-in. Providers such as Microsoft Entra omit this discovery extension despite supporting S256; an absent field is accepted and S256 is still required in every request. Configure a provider with documented S256 support. Machine client-credentials grants do not depend on that authorization-flow capability. See Microsoft's PKCE flow.

    begin(redirectUri, scopes = "openid profile email") returns a transaction with authorization URL, random state/nonce/verifier, redirect URI, and expiry. Keep the whole transaction server-side. It expires after ten minutes; at most 128 pending transactions are retained per client. Scopes must begin with openid. Redirect URIs must also be registered exactly with the provider.

    exchange(transaction, code, returnedState) returns a NetTask. It compares state against the session transaction and the client's private transaction store, consumes the transaction once, sends the PKCE verifier, exchanges the code, fetches the provider's JWKS over validated HTTPS, verifies the ID token, and returns:

    • accessToken, tokenType: "Bearer", integer expiresAt;

    • optional refreshToken and scope;

    • a verified identity with issuer and subject, name/email, claims, and expiry.

    Returned tokens are intended for server-side use. Client secrets use the client_secret_post token-endpoint method; public PKCE clients omit the secret. The implementation does not use password or implicit grants.

    refresh(refreshToken, originalIdentity?) returns a NetTask. When an ID token is returned, the original Identity is required; its issuer, subject, and original nonce must match. OAuth-only refreshes may return access tokens without an identity. Refresh-token rotation is returned to the application; persist the replacement securely when using durable tokens.

    clientCredentials(scopes = "") requires a client secret and returns a NetTask with a machine token, never a fabricated user Identity. These helpers share SIPL's bounded HTTP connection pool and cancellation behavior. Buffered provider JSON is capped at 256 KiB. Client configuration stays private inside the native object; it has no public secret property.

    Microsoft Entra ID and Google#

    Both return the same OidcClient API. Microsoft requires the explicit tenant GUID and uses its v2.0 issuer; shared tenant aliases and domain aliases are not accepted. Google pins https://accounts.google.com. Other clouds, specialized policies, and standards-compliant providers use auth.oidc with their exact issuer. Register your application, scopes, redirect URL, and appropriate public/confidential client type in the provider's administration interface. No cloud credentials or example tenant IDs are shipped.

    JWT verification boundary#

    auth.verifyJWT(token, jwks, options) returns verified claims. Required options are issuer and audience; optional values are nonce, clockSkew (0–120 seconds, default 30), accessToken, and code. It accepts only RS256 with 2048–4096-bit RSA keys or ES256 with P-256 keys. It verifies signatures before trusting claims, then checks subject, exact issuer, audience and authorized party, integer expiration/issued-at/not-before dates, expected nonce, and at_hash/c_hash when present. Multiple audiences require matching azp.

    The verifier rejects unsigned/HMAC tokens, ambiguous keys, duplicate JSON keys, unsupported critical headers and remote key URLs. JWT size is at most 64 KiB, with at most 64 JWKs. It never fetches a key URL supplied by a token. Standalone callers must obtain JWKS from a trusted issuer, and must not use this ID-token helper as a generic authorization policy for arbitrary access tokens.

    LDAP and Active Directory#

    ldap.connect(options) configures a directory without network I/O. Options:

    FieldDefault / behavior
    hostRequired hostname or IP literal, without a URL scheme
    port636; set 389 explicitly when using StartTLS
    startTLSfalse: LDAPS; true: StartTLS is required before credentials
    timeout5,000 ms; 100–30,000 ms per native SDK operation
    baseDNBase for findUser/findGroup helpers
    userAttributesAMAccountName; use uid or userPrincipalName as appropriate
    bindDN, passwordOptional nonempty service credentials for directory searches
    caFileOpenLDAP CA bundle; Windows uses the Windows certificate trust store
    integratedfalse; Windows-only process-account SSPI negotiate bind

    All connections require validated TLS. StartTLS never falls back to plaintext. Windows also rejects negotiated protocols below TLS 1.2 and ciphers below 128 bits. OpenLDAP requires a valid chain and matching subject alternative name, with TLS 1.2 minimum. Referral chasing is disabled so credentials are not forwarded to another server. Windows caFile is rejected explicitly: install the directory's issuing CA through Windows trust management.

    authenticate(username, password) validates credentials on a separate connection, returning NetTask[Bool]: invalid credentials return false; transport/TLS/policy errors raise a failure. Empty usernames/passwords are rejected before I/O. It does not replace the service identity used for search. bind(username, password) validates and replaces that directory's service credentials only after success.

    findUser(name) and findGroup(name) return NetTask[Map|None]; an ambiguous lookup fails. Returned entries contain dn and attributes, a Map of attribute names to lists of values. Valid non-NUL UTF-8 values become strings; binary values become Bytes. Helpers return common user attributes and memberOf, objectGUID, and objectSid when supplied by the directory.

    isMember(userDN, groupDN, options?) searches the group entry's member attribute. Set attribute for uniqueMember or a directory-specific schema. Set nestedAD: true for AD's transitive matching rule 1.2.840.113556.1.4.1941. This is an explicit AD feature, not a generic recursive group walker. POSIX primary groups, AD tokenGroups expansion, ranged member attributes and forest-wide authorization need application-specific handling.

    search(baseDN, filter, options?) returns NetTask[Map] containing entries, a Bytes cookie, and estimatedTotal. Options are scope (base, one, sub; default sub), attributes (1–64 names), pageSize (1–500; default 100), and a returned cookie (at most 4 KiB). An empty cookie finishes the paged search. Reuse the same directory and query for subsequent pages; the native connection stays open for server paging state. Each extracted page is bounded to 1 MiB. Size-limit errors fail rather than silently returning partial search results. Paged searches require server support.

    ldap.escapeFilter implements RFC 4515 value escaping; ldap.escapeDN escapes DN components under RFC 4514. Helpers validate attribute names and escape lookup values automatically. A raw search filter is deliberately an advanced, trusted application input, not a safe place to concatenate browser input.

    LDAP jobs use native worker threads, capped at eight jobs and 64 directories. SIPL values remain on the VM thread. Await a directory operation before reusing that same directory; independent directories can run concurrently. Cancelling a NetTask ends the await, while an already executing SDK operation finishes under its configured deadline before native resources are reclaimed. close() releases the connection once no directory operation is running.

    Windows integration and build support#

    On Windows, ldap.available and ldap.integratedAvailable are true. The Windows SDK's WLDAP32/SSPI implementation performs directory authentication; integrated: true uses the current process account with negotiate semantics. OS/domain policy controls Kerberos versus permitted fallback. This does not add HTTP Negotiate/NTLM middleware, impersonation, delegation, or a full PrincipalContext replacement. Validate your domain's channel-binding and signing requirements in the intended deployment.

    On POSIX desktop builds, OpenLDAP headers and libraries are required; Ubuntu's SDK package is libldap-dev. Make fails if they are absent, and rejects SIPL_LDAP=0. Windows uses its system SDK. Runtime directory configuration and a reachable directory server are only needed when an application uses LDAP.

    Web sessions and secret storage#

    Use web.sessions, rotate with web.sessionRotate after authentication, and store only a local user identifier, authorization version and expiry in the server-side session. Resolve current permissions from trusted storage on every protected operation. Sessions should be Secure and HttpOnly in production. OIDC redirect callbacks require SameSite=Lax rather than Strict, with state and nonce validation; keep ordinary API writes protected against foreign origins. CRM-ERP includes these integration patterns for its local, LDAP and OIDC logins.

    Windows has secrets.load/save backed by current-account DPAPI. The existing API deliberately fails on unsupported platforms instead of storing plaintext. For portable deployments, use explicitly allowlisted environment variables provided by a deployment secret manager. Tokens default to process memory; the runtime does not automatically write them to a configuration file or add them to logs. A general POSIX keychain and redacting Secret type remain roadmap work, rather than an insecure file fallback.

    Verification and references#

    The HTTPS fixture signs its own RS256/ES256 tokens and tests PKCE, state replay, nonce and claim mismatches, invalid signatures, ambiguous keys, duplicate JSON, refresh, client credentials, issuer mismatch and certificate rejection. The OpenLDAP fixture tests real LDAPS/StartTLS, bind validation, searches, membership, binary attributes, filter injection and pagination. Fixtures run normally and with GC stress, using temporary data without cloud accounts or installed services. Both drivers also launch an isolated CRM-ERP copy to verify allowed-user mapping, additive roles, denial of unauthorized operations, and session revocation through its real HTTP handlers. The OIDC driver exercises the browser callback, state/replay checks and session rotation. The LDAP driver verifies that choosing LDAP cannot fall back to a local password. Both standalone examples run against these fixtures as well.

    Protocol references: OAuth security BCP / RFC 9700, OIDC Core, PKCE / RFC 7636, OpenLDAP TLS, Microsoft LDAP SSL.

    Images#

    The first-party image module provides typed, owned Image values on Windows, Linux and headless runtimes. It does not require graphics hardware. PNG/JPEG are built in; WebP is included by default and can be disabled at build time. PDF generation is available through the pdf module; video and animated images have separate APIs. Office documents are separate future work.

    Use sipl api image --json and sipl api Image --json for the exact signatures, effects and option contracts. See the runnable recipe.

    Ownership and formats#

    image.open(path, options?) reads a bounded regular file. image.decode(bytes, options?) decodes existing Bytes. The default pixel format is RGBA: row-major, tightly packed, unsigned 8-bit channels, straight (unpremultiplied) alpha. Explicit "format": "RGB" requests three channels. Unknown formats fail; there is no automatic byte-order guessing or reinterpretation.

    image.create(width, height, options?) creates zeroed pixels (transparent black for RGBA, black for RGB). Options include format and a color List containing exactly three or four Ints from 0 to 255. image.fromPixels(width, height, format, bytes) requires an exact byte count and copies the source buffer.

    Read-only properties are width, height, format and closed. pixels() returns a detached copy as Bytes; pixel(x, y) returns a List of channels. Neither exposes a dangling view of native memory. crop, resize and convert return independent Images. convert("RGB") explicitly drops alpha; convert("RGBA") adds opaque alpha to RGB pixels. All pixel operations fail after close(). Close is idempotent; dimensions/format remain inspectable. Garbage collection is a fallback, not a substitute for closing large images.

    Geometry, drawing and compositing#

    crop(x, y, width, height) requires a positive rectangle entirely inside the image. resize(width, height, filter?) supports "nearest" and the default "bilinear". Bilinear interpolation uses premultiplied colors internally to avoid transparent-edge halos, then returns straight-alpha bytes. It interpolates encoded channel values; linear-light/HDR resizing is not promised.

    setPixel(x, y, color), fill(color), rect(x, y, width, height, color) and line(x1, y1, x2, y2, color) mutate pixels. Drawing replaces channels; it does not implicitly alpha blend. Coordinates and rectangles must be inside the image; line drawing is deterministic, one-pixel-wide and not antialiased.

    clone() makes an independent pixel copy for edit history. stroke(x1, y1, x2, y2, size, color, mode) paints circular brush stamps along a line, clipped to the image; mode is "paint" (source-over alpha) or "erase" (reduces alpha). Size is 1..256. floodFill(x, y, color, tolerance) replaces the contiguous region matching the starting pixel within 0..255 per channel and returns the number of changed pixels. shape(kind, x1, y1, x2, y2, thickness, color, filled) draws a line, rectangle, or ellipse. adjust(kind, amount?) changes RGB channels in place while preserving alpha; kinds are invert, grayscale, sepia, brightness, and contrast, with amount -100..100 for the last two. flip("horizontal"|"vertical") changes pixels in place. rotate90(clockwise) returns an independent image with swapped dimensions.

    composite(source, x, y, opacity?) performs source-over alpha blending with finite opacity in 0..1. It clips to the destination bounds, supports RGB and RGBA sources/targets, and safely snapshots self-compositing before mutation. Positions must be within -16384..16384. No source pixels are changed.

    Drawing in the UI and Toolkit#

    ui.setIcon(picture) sets an open window's native icon on Windows and Linux/XWayland. Use an RGBA Image no larger than 256 x 256 pixels. The platform copies the pixels, so the Image can be closed immediately after the call.

    Call ui.drawImage(x, y, width, height, picture) inside a UI frame to draw an open Image into a rectangle in logical pixels. It supports RGB and RGBA, respects ui.clip(), applies the display scale, and blends transparency over the existing canvas. Scaling uses bilinear interpolation with premultiplied colors to avoid transparent-edge halos. Coordinates must be finite and sizes nonnegative; zero-sized and offscreen rectangles draw nothing. The operation borrows pixels only for the call and neither changes nor closes the image. Closed images fail clearly.

    Toolkit opens .png, .jpg, .jpeg, and .webp files from the Explorer or Open dialog in read-only image tabs. Images fit the available area while preserving aspect ratio; small images retain their native size. A checkerboard shows transparency, and the footer reports dimensions and scale. The tab's Reload button reads changes from disk. Unsupported, corrupt, or oversized images show a preview error instead of opening their binary data as text. Closing an image tab releases its pixel storage. Preview behavior is written in toolkit/image_preview.sipl; the canvas primitive works without Vulkan.

    Encoding and metadata#

    encode(format, options?) returns Bytes; save(path, format, options?) writes those bytes using an explicit "png", "jpeg" or "webp" codec. Extensions do not silently choose an encoder. PNG is lossless and does not accept quality. JPEG uses quality 1..100, default 90; it cannot encode alpha and rejects nonopaque RGBA unless the caller explicitly converts or composites onto a background. JPEG cannot be made lossless with a flag.

    WebP defaults to lossless encoding, preserving alpha and transparent pixels' hidden RGB values. {"lossless": false, "quality": 90} selects lossy WebP. The available backends are always inspectable with image.codecs(), which returns {"png": true, "jpeg": true, "webp": Bool}. An absent backend fails clearly; it does not encode a different format. WebP is required in desktop builds; feature-off switches are rejected. Vendor-backed builds do not download anything.

    EXIF orientations 1..8 in PNG, JPEG and WebP are applied by default, including mirroring and width/height exchange. Decode option applyOrientation: false preserves source coordinates. Orientation parsing only reads bounded TIFF IFD0 fields; malformed EXIF, invalid tag types/counts and invalid orientations fail even when orientation application is disabled. Encoding emits fresh pixel data without EXIF, GPS, comments, ICC profiles or other source metadata. ICC color management is not implemented; channels are used as supplied. High-bit-depth PNG and HDR are explicitly unsupported instead of silently reducing precision. Animated PNG/WebP are rejected instead of silently returning one frame.

    Native editing operations#

    Image.effect(kind, options?) stages its output before committing pixels. Validation or scratch-allocation failure leaves the original unchanged. Kinds are saturation, hue, gamma, exposure, threshold, posterize, solarize, temperature, tint, vibrance, levels, autoLevels, gaussianBlur, sharpen, unsharpMask, findEdges, emboss, pixelate, noise, vignette, motionBlur, highPass and colorBalance.

    Options are numeric amount (-100..100; default 25), integer radius (1..32; default 3), levels (2..256; default 6), seed (0..2147483647; default 1), angle (-180..180 degrees), gamma (0.1..10; default 1), black (0..254), white (1..255; black must be below white), and red, green, blue (-100..100 offsets). Unknown keys and kinds fail explicitly. Hue amount spans -180..180 degrees; exposure amount 25 is one stop; threshold/solarize map -100..100 onto 0..255. Hue is an RGB matrix rotation; these are 8-bit RGB adjustments, without ICC/HSL color management.

    Gaussian/motion blur and mosaic use premultiplied alpha to avoid hidden-color halos. Other effects retain original alpha. Gaussian uses separable sampling, edge clamping and at most 64 MiB of float scratch plus 16 MiB of staged output at the image pixel ceiling. Run large operations in a worker to keep UI input responsive. Noise uses a local deterministic seed.

    composite(source,x,y,opacity?,blend?) adds optional normal, multiply, screen, overlay, darken, lighten, difference, exclusion, hardLight, softLight, colorDodge and colorBurn blending. Existing four-argument Normal compositing keeps its previous behavior. Blend colors use source-over alpha; RGB/RGBA formats can be mixed explicitly as before. mix(source, amount) interpolates premultiplied pixels including alpha, requires matching dimensions/formats and accepts amount 0..1.

    gradient(x1,y1,x2,y2,from,to,kind) paints a linear or radial color gradient; colors match the image's channel count, and a zero-length vector does nothing. text(text,x,y,color,size?) rasterizes up to 4096 UTF-8 bytes using the shared UI font renderer, with size 8..256 (default 24), preserving surrounding transparency. Text is a raster operation, not an editable text object.

    Untrusted-media limits#

    image.limits() exposes the hard ceilings. Each image is limited to 16384 per dimension, 4,194,304 pixels and 16 MiB of pixel bytes. Encoded input and output are each limited to 16 MiB. Decode options maxInputBytes, maxWidth, maxHeight and maxPixels can lower these limits but cannot raise them. Create supports the same dimension/pixel limits. Encode option maxOutputBytes lowers the output limit. All limits are positive Ints; unknown option keys fail.

    PNG chunk lengths, CRCs, zlib checksum and exact decoded scanline sizes, JPEG segment/frame/scan boundaries, and WebP RIFF chunks/features are validated before pixel decoding. Dimensions and checked pixel counts are validated before allocating destination pixels. stb PNG/JPEG decoding/encoding uses a 64 MiB temporary-allocation budget. WebP uses checked upstream allocation and bounded dimensions, single-threaded encoding and a bounded output callback; its internal scratch allocations are not governed by the stb budget. Operations are synchronous and bounded by these resource limits, not cancellable background tasks or hostile-code sandboxing. Applications should use smaller limits for thumbnails and other untrusted uploads and close resources promptly.

    Image errors use SIPL's normal runtime failure handling; file failures retain the file kind. Native codec buffers never contain SIPL references. Tests cover all EXIF transforms/endian variants, exact PNG/lossless WebP, JPEG tolerances, draw/resize/composite behavior, truncated input, malformed metadata, oversized headers, decompression budgets, forged JPEG termination markers and packaged programs in normal/GC-stress modes.

    Dependencies are pinned in stb's image pin and libwebp's pin, with upstream license and patent notices kept alongside the sources.

    UI fonts#

    SIPL uses a smooth embedded monospace font by default. Labels, controls, drawn text, and the Toolkit editor share the same measured character grid. Packaged applications include the default font, so users do not need to install a font or place a font file beside the executable.

    Glyphs are cached by Unicode scalar and display size, with at most 512 entries and 8 MiB of cached mask data. Changing fonts clears that cache.

    Toolkit font choice#

    Choose View → Font → Smooth for scalable text or View → Font → Pixel (5x7) for SIPL's compact pixel style. The selection applies to the current Toolkit session. Smooth text is selected when Toolkit starts.

    Font APIs#

    ui.setFont(path?: String or None, pixelSize?: Int) -> None selects a monospace TrueType/OpenType font. Omit the path, or pass none, to use the embedded font. Omit the size to use 16 logical pixels; accepted sizes are 8..32. Font files must be nonempty and at most 16 MiB. Paths must be nonempty Strings without NUL bytes and at most 4096 bytes. The font must have a Unicode character map and a fixed character width. Proportional fonts fail because the editor, text-entry controls, and selection calculations share a monospace grid.

    A failed font change leaves the current font and metrics unchanged. A successful change clears text caches and entry scroll offsets and requests a redraw. Select a font before opening or drawing the UI.

    ui.usePixelFont() -> None selects the built-in 5x7 renderer. It clears text caches and entry scroll offsets and requests a redraw. Normal text uses 12-pixel cells and 18-pixel lines. Call ui.setFont() to switch back to the embedded smooth font and default size.

    Metrics and Unicode#

    Read-only property or APIReturn and meaningCanonical example
    ui.fontRendererString identifying the active rendererprint(ui.fontRenderer)
    ui.fontSizeInt logical size for the active fontprint(ui.fontSize)
    ui.charWidthInt measured logical cell widthprint(ui.charWidth)
    ui.lineHeightInt logical spacing between text linesprint(ui.lineHeight)
    ui.textWidth(text)Int width on the current character gridui.textWidth("Hello")

    Use these metrics for custom layouts, caret positions, and selections instead of assuming a fixed character width.

    UTF-8 code points supported by the selected font render directly. Missing glyphs use the replacement glyph or ?. The fixed grid advances once per scalar, including combining characters. Complex-script shaping, bidirectional layout, grapheme-aware editing, automatic font fallback, and color emoji are not currently supported.

    Web Server#

    Server-rendered .sipl.html pages compile to restricted SIPL bytecode and use context-aware output rules. See SIPL Pages for the <^ ... ^> syntax, safe data boundary, compilation model, and traffic plan.

    Start#

    Defaults: the html folder relative to the working directory, port 8080, and the loopback address 127.0.0.1. The root must already exist.

    serve blocks until stopped or interrupted. Port 0 selects an available ephemeral port. web.port reports the bound port; web.isOpen reports whether the server is running. A handler can call web.stop() to stop accepting requests and drain queued responses. Ctrl+C terminates the process.

    Registered routes run before the static fallback. Therefore a web.get("/", home) route can render pages/index.sipl.html even though the static server still uses html/index.html when no / route returns a response. The page filename is not discovered by the static server; web.render selects it.

    Try the bundled example from the repository root:

    The bundled example listens at http://127.0.0.1:8082/.

    Listener address and optional native window#

    The default listener remains loopback. To select another IPv4 interface, pass {"host": "0.0.0.0"} (all interfaces) or a specific literal IPv4 address in the fourth argument. Hostnames and IPv6 listeners are not accepted. Opening an interface changes network exposure; configure HTTPS and application access as appropriate. TLS itself does not change the selected address.

    A Windows WebView2 build can own a desktop window with {"window": {"title": "My app", "width": 1280, "height": 850}}. SIPL opens the window after binding the listener, serves requests on the VM thread, and stops the listener when the window closes. web.stop() also closes an owned window. No window work occurs unless this option is supplied. Window options also include profile (engine data path), url (override the default actual loopback listener URL), and closeAfterMs (0 by default, up to 120000). HTTPS or loopback HTTP is required for a web window, and navigation is confined to its initial origin. Unsupported builds fail and close the listener. See the meeting guide for the native API and one-call meeting library.

    HTTPS#

    web.serve(root?, port?, handler?, options?) accepts certFile and keyFile in its fourth argument. Supply both to serve HTTPS directly on Windows and Linux:

    Open https://127.0.0.1:8443/. The existing html directory is the public static root; the certs directory is separate. Certificate/key paths are relative to the process working directory, or may be absolute. certFile is a PEM certificate chain with the server certificate first, followed by any intermediate certificates. keyFile is its matching, unencrypted PEM private key. Use a certificate valid for the hostname or IP clients connect to, and keep private keys outside the public static root with restricted file access. Encrypted key files are rejected without an interactive password prompt.

    TLS 1.2 and TLS 1.3 are supported. Older protocols, TLS compression, and renegotiation are disabled. The listener defaults to 127.0.0.1; HTTPS does not change the address selected by host. It accepts encrypted traffic only. TLS handshake and encrypted read/write/shutdown operations are nonblocking; a stalled handshake expires after 10 seconds and does not hold up other connections. The HTTP routes, Pages, static fallback, sessions, keep-alive and request limits work over either transport. web.isSecure is true while an HTTPS listener is active and false after it stops. The startup message prints the correct http:// or https:// URL, including the actual port when using port 0.

    Omit both options (or pass an empty Map / none) to retain HTTP. Supplying only one, an invalid path, an unreadable certificate, a malformed/encrypted key, or a key that does not match the certificate fails startup and leaves no listener open. Unknown options are errors. There is no automatic downgrade to HTTP. Certificates are loaded at startup; stop and restart the server to renew them. Certificate issuance, browser trust installation, ACME renewal, mutual TLS, and HTTPS redirects are not managed by this API.

    For a temporary local development certificate, use an installed OpenSSL CLI:

    The generated certificate is self-signed; browsers will warn until you explicitly trust your development certificate. Public deployments should use a certificate issued by a trusted authority. Production session cookies should keep their default secure: true setting when using direct HTTPS or a TLS reverse proxy. The runtime uses its existing OpenSSL-compatible TLS dependency: static LibreSSL on MSVC Windows builds and the system TLS libraries on Linux.

    Optional .htaccess compatibility#

    Apache 2.4 .htaccess compatibility is separately opt-in through {"htaccess": true}. It applies to native SIPL routes and .sipl.html Pages, static files, and optional FastCGI applications. It can be selected per named host using virtualHosts. PHP is not required. With compatibility enabled, directory indexes default to index.sipl.html, index.html, then the optional FastCGI index. Native Page indexes can resolve through exact registered routes while their template source remains private. See Apache compatibility and migration for supported directives, security behavior, limits, and a native SIPL example.

    FastCGI applications#

    SIPL includes a native C FastCGI client with no additional libraries. Enable it through web.serve to send requests to an independently running PHP-FPM, php-cgi, or another FastCGI responder:

    For a local PHP example, start php-cgi -d cgi.fix_pathinfo=0 -b 127.0.0.1:9000 in a separate terminal, then run sipl run examples/web_fastcgi.sipl and visit http://127.0.0.1:8080/. SIPL connects to the application; it does not launch or manage its processes. The backend must see the same absolute script paths as SIPL and have permission to read them.

    The fastcgi Map accepts these options. Unknown names and invalid values fail before the listener opens.

    OptionDefaultMeaning
    host"127.0.0.1"Numeric IPv4/IPv6 address, or "localhost" (IPv4); no DNS lookup
    port9000TCP port, from 1 to 65535
    socketomittedAbsolute Unix socket path; Unix only; excludes host and port
    extension".php"Case-insensitive script suffix, dot plus 1–30 letters/digits
    index"index" + extensionPlain filename used for URLs ending in /
    timeout30000Total backend connection/request deadline in milliseconds, from 1 to 300000

    For PHP-FPM over a Unix socket, use {"fastcgi": {"socket": "/run/php/php-fpm.sock"}}, substituting the configured pool socket path. Other languages can select their own suffix and index, such as {"fastcgi": {"port": 9001, "extension": ".py", "index": "app.py"}}. certFile and keyFile can be supplied alongside fastcgi for direct HTTPS.

    Middleware, routes, and the optional SIPL handler run first. When they return none, a matching script runs through FastCGI. With htaccess disabled, a directory URL tries the configured script index first, then falls back to static index.html if that script does not exist. A missing or inaccessible matching script returns 404 and never falls through to serving its source. Only exact script filenames are supported: /index.php/extra does not invoke PHP or infer PATH_INFO. Omitting fastcgi on a later web.serve call disables it.

    CGI parameters include the canonical SCRIPT_FILENAME and DOCUMENT_ROOT, SCRIPT_NAME, raw REQUEST_URI and QUERY_STRING, REQUEST_METHOD, CONTENT_TYPE, CONTENT_LENGTH, server/peer addresses and ports, SERVER_PROTOCOL, HTTPS, REQUEST_SCHEME, PHP's REDIRECT_STATUS=200, and request headers as HTTP_*. PATH_INFO is empty. Repeated request headers are joined with commas (cookies with semicolons). Hop-by-hop headers, Proxy, and header names containing underscores are excluded to avoid CGI variable aliases and HTTP_PROXY injection. The server uses its bound address for SERVER_NAME; the supplied Host header remains available as HTTP_HOST.

    Scripts use the static server's confined file-opening checks. Traversal and hidden paths are rejected; Unix refuses symlinks, and Windows checks the final opened path against the canonical root. Keep the script tree writable only by trusted administrators: a separate FastCGI process reopens the checked filename, so SIPL cannot make that second open atomic with its own file check.

    The client uses FastCGI v1, the responder role, and one request per connection. It implements 8-byte records, 1-byte/4-byte parameter lengths, 65535-byte stream chunks, padding, explicit stream terminators, interleaved stdout/stderr, and END_REQUEST. For PHP compatibility, END_REQUEST also closes output streams when the backend omits their empty terminator records. Data after an explicit stream terminator is rejected. Multiplexing, pooling, authorizer/filter roles, and application process management are outside this implementation. See the FastCGI specification and PHP's FastCGI implementation.

    Backend sockets use the server's nonblocking poll loop, allowing other clients to progress during an upload or slow response. Request and response bodies are limited to 1 MiB, CGI response headers to 16 KiB and 128 fields. Responses are buffered until completion. Status, Location, binary bodies, repeated Set-Cookie, HEAD, and bodyless 204/304 responses are handled; SIPL computes HTTP framing and removes hop-by-hop response headers. Backend connection, protocol, size, and malformed-header failures return 502; overload returns 503; the deadline returns 504. Backend stderr is logged with escaped controls and a 16 KiB capture limit, never inserted into the HTTP body. Nonzero application exit status is logged while preserving a valid application response.

    SIPL Pages#

    Keep executable pages in a private folder separate from the static root:

    web.pages(root, options?) validates and compiles every .sipl.html file. reload defaults to false; enable it during development to atomically load valid edits while retaining the last valid compiled page after an error. web.render(literalPath, model) returns a standard response Map containing status 200, an HTML content type, and the rendered body. The model must be an acyclic tree of page-safe scalar, List, and Map values. Render paths are literal, relative paths below the configured root.

    Page source is never a static asset: the server returns 403 for any static request ending in .sipl.html, even if the static root is misconfigured to contain one. Use sipl page-check pages or Toolkit Scan to validate pages.

    SIPL Backend#

    The optional third argument is a fallback function called when no registered route matches:

    Request map fields:

    FieldValue
    methodHTTP method, such as GET or POST
    pathPercent-decoded path without its query string
    queryRaw query string without ?
    headersMap of lowercase header names to values; repeated ordinary headers retain the last value
    bodyImmutable Bytes, including arbitrary binary data

    A handler returns a String for a 200 text response, a Map with a String or Bytes body and optional integer status and Map headers, or none to use built-in static-file serving. Decode request text explicitly with request["body"].decodeUtf8() when expecting UTF-8. A Bytes response defaults to application/octet-stream unless headers specify another content type. The server owns Content-Length, Transfer-Encoding, and Connection; supplying them in a response produces 500.

    Uncaught handler failures become generic 500 responses; details are written to stderr, not exposed to clients. The server remains available. Startup errors are catchable with SIPL's try/fail blocks.

    Routes And Middleware#

    Register routes before calling web.serve(). web.route(method, pattern, handler) accepts GET, HEAD, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE, or OPTIONS; web.get(pattern, handler) and web.post(pattern, handler) are shortcuts. Patterns match the decoded path exactly, and :name captures one path segment in request["params"]:

    Use web.use(fn(request, continueRequest) { ... }) to register middleware. Calling continueRequest() runs the remaining middleware and then the matching route (or fallback handler). Middleware may return a response early, or modify the downstream response after continueRequest() returns. It may call the continuation at most once. A middleware that returns none without calling the continuation passes the request onward.

    Secure User Sessions#

    Call web.sessions() before web.serve() to enable server-side sessions:

    The cookie contains only a cryptographically random 256-bit opaque ID. Session values stay in server memory and may be any SIPL value. IDs come from the operating system's secure random source, are replaced by sessionRotate, and are invalidated immediately by sessionDestroy.

    Available operations, all of which require the current handler request:

    OperationResult
    web.sessionGet(request, key, default?)Stored value, default, or none
    web.sessionSet(request, key, value)Stores a value, creating the session lazily
    web.sessionHas(request, key)Whether the key exists
    web.sessionRemove(request, key)Whether a value was removed
    web.sessionRotate(request)Replaces the ID while preserving session values
    web.sessionDestroy(request)Deletes the session and expires its cookie
    web.sessionCountNumber of unexpired sessions currently stored

    web.sessions(options?) accepts:

    OptionDefaultMeaning
    cookie"sipl_session"Cookie name
    idleTimeout1800Maximum inactive seconds
    absoluteTimeout86400Maximum total session lifetime in seconds
    sameSite"Lax""Strict", "Lax", or "None"
    securetrueAdd the cookie Secure attribute
    maxSessions4096Bounded in-memory session capacity

    Cookies are host-only and always use Path=/ and HttpOnly. Secure is on by default, SameSite=None requires it, and the __Secure- and __Host- cookie prefixes cannot be used with secure: false. Duplicate, malformed, unknown, rotated, expired, and destroyed session IDs are rejected and cleared. Access refreshes idle expiry but never extends the absolute lifetime. When capacity is full, the least recently seen session is evicted.

    For plain-HTTP local development only, use a non-prefixed cookie with {"secure": false}. Production should retain secure: true over direct HTTPS or behind a TLS reverse proxy. Rotate the session immediately after successful authentication, use POST for logout, and add CSRF tokens to sensitive cookie-authenticated forms; SameSite is useful defense in depth, not a complete CSRF strategy.

    Sessions survive web.stop() followed by another web.serve() in the same process. They are intentionally in-memory: they do not survive process exit and are not shared across server processes. Persistent or distributed session stores remain application infrastructure rather than part of this embedded server.

    Scope And Limits#

    • HTTP/1.0 and HTTP/1.1, with HTTP/1.1 keep-alive and ordered pipelining.

    • Static GET and HEAD; trailing-slash paths use index.html. No directory listings.

    • 128 simultaneous connections; at most 100 requests per connection.

    • 16 KiB request headers, 64 headers, 1 MiB request and dynamic-response bodies.

    • 10-second request deadline and 30-second response deadline; slow clients do not block socket I/O for others.

    • Close-marked responses use a bounded one-second nonblocking input drain, avoiding TCP resets when rejected requests have unread bytes.

    • Static files stream in 64 KiB chunks instead of being loaded into VM Strings.

    • Percent-decoding is validated. Hidden and traversal path components, Windows separators/device-path syntax, and static .sipl files are rejected.

    • Windows checks the final opened file handle's path against the canonical root before reading. Unix opens path components relative to the root directory descriptor without following symlinks.

    • Chunked request bodies and Expect are deliberately unsupported and rejected with closed connections. Clients must provide Content-Length for bodies.

    • Optional direct HTTPS with PEM certificate/key files, TLS 1.2 or newer, and a 10-second handshake deadline.

    • No HTTP/2, HTTP/3, compression, ranges, cache validators, persistent/distributed session store, or database layer.

    This is a bounded embedded HTTP/HTTPS engine. For public deployment, an established reverse proxy can provide rate limiting, certificate renewal, and additional request policy. Review authentication, logging, process isolation, and workload limits for your application. SIPL handlers and disk reads execute synchronously: blocking backend work or cold or slow storage can delay other requests. Handlers run in request order.

    Toolkit workflow#

    Toolkit recognizes .sipl.html files as SIPL Pages and highlights HTML and SIPL tags together. Use Scan to validate a page. Run the .sipl controller that calls web.pages() and web.render() to view it through the server.

    Gather and the meeting library#

    Gather is a standalone SIPL meeting application with a browser frontend and a Windows desktop frontend. It includes camera/audio calls, screen/window/tab sharing, chat, raised hands, invitations, a host-controlled waiting room, participant removal, file downloads and synchronized PDF presentation controls. It does not connect to Microsoft Teams.

    The reusable library lives in libraries/meeting. Applications activate the complete service with one call:

    This example is for an entry file in the repository root. Adjust the relative import for another directory, or copy libraries/meeting beside your app and use meeting/meeting. No registry, Node, Python, browser automation or launcher script is used by the application. The browser source and styles are embedded in an imported SIPL module and included in packaged executables.

    meeting.serve({"port": 8083}) starts the same service for browsers without opening a desktop window. meeting.app({"url": "https://meet.example.com"}) opens a desktop client for an existing service. Remote mode accepts only url and the window options below; it does not start another server.

    The serving call blocks until the server stops. In local desktop mode SIPL starts the listener before opening the window, runs the engine on its own native GUI thread, and stops the listener when the window closes. Application authors do not implement a signaling protocol or manage a second process. One server/window can be owned by a VM at a time.

    Configuration#

    Gather reads examples/projects/Gather/config.json from beside its entry file or executable. A packaged executable can run without this file using the defaults. Certificate paths in that file are resolved relative to the file, independently of the working directory. Library callers pass paths directly.

    SettingDefaultMeaning
    port8083IPv4 listener port, 0–65535; zero chooses a free port
    host127.0.0.1Literal IPv4 address; use 0.0.0.0 to accept LAN traffic
    publicOrigin""Exact HTTPS origin, such as https://meet.example.com; adds the trusted host/origin and supplies invitation links
    certFile, keyFile""Paired PEM certificate chain/private key; existing SIPL TLS 1.2+ server
    createKey""Key required to create meetings; invitations/passcodes still govern joining
    maxParticipants6Approved participants per room, 2–8; eight additional waiting places
    iceServers[]Browser WebRTC ICE server configurations; at most eight entries

    Unknown settings fail. Non-loopback listeners require TLS and a createKey of at least 16 characters. An explicit public origin also requires that key, including behind a reverse proxy. A public origin has no trailing slash, path, query, fragment or user information. Enter the actual origin clients use; the library rejects unrelated HTTP Host and Origin headers.

    SIPL_GATHER_CREATE_KEY overrides the create key. The explicitly allowlisted SIPL_GATHER_TURN_USERNAME and SIPL_GATHER_TURN_PASSWORD override the respective fields in each configured ICE entry. These are read only when the service starts. Keep real credentials out of version control and use short-lived TURN credentials where your relay supports them. Approved and waiting clients receive the configured ICE settings after a valid invitation; keep those credentials limited to relay use.

    Desktop app also accepts title, profile, width (640–3840), height (480–2160), and closeAfterMs (0–120000, zero disables automatic close). The example stores the system engine profile in data/browser beside the entry file. That profile holds browser permissions/cookies; meeting rooms, messages and shared files remain in the serving process's memory.

    HTTPS and other computers#

    Local testing works at http://127.0.0.1:8083. Browser media APIs require a secure context: use HTTPS for another machine. Browsers must trust the certificate; SIPL never bypasses certificate warnings or media permission prompts. A certificate for a public hostname must match that hostname.

    For a direct HTTPS listener, edit the JSON configuration:

    Supply the certificate/key, point DNS at the server, and allow the selected TCP port through the firewall. The hostname must resolve and be reachable from the hosting desktop too. When publicOrigin is set, a locally hosted native window uses it, allowing its certificate to match. Certificate renewal is a deployment responsibility; restart the listener after replacing its files.

    Alternatively, put an existing HTTPS reverse proxy in front of SIPL's loopback HTTP listener. Set publicOrigin to its exact public HTTPS origin and set createKey; keep host at 127.0.0.1. Forward the original Host header and the /, /api and /api/file/... paths. Signaling uses short HTTP requests, so WebSocket upgrade configuration is unnecessary. Increase proxy body limits only enough for 256 KiB chunks. Do not expose the plaintext upstream publicly.

    Signaling, mediation and relays#

    SIPL owns the room/session broker: invitations, admission, member authentication, private offer/answer/ICE delivery, roster updates, chat, presentation state and file transfer. The bundled frontend owns WebRTC negotiation and reconnects. Neither part requires application-specific protocol code.

    Media uses browser WebRTC with DTLS-SRTP between participants. This first version uses a small-room peer mesh, not an SFU/mixing server: each participant sends to the other participants. The server is trusted with room metadata, chat and files; those travel over the application's HTTPS connection. This does not provide application-level end-to-end encryption for chat or files.

    The signaling server cannot by itself make media cross every firewall/NAT. For internet meetings configure reachable STUN/TURN services. For example:

    The client automatically uses the configured relay when ICE needs it. SIPL does not install or run coturn, provide a TURN server, allocate public relay addresses, configure firewalls, or provide an SFU. Use an existing managed or self-hosted relay. An empty ICE list can work on the same computer/LAN, but is not a guarantee of internet connectivity. The example performs no third-party STUN requests by default.

    Meeting behavior and boundaries#

    • Devices start off. Enabling a camera/microphone requests browser/OS permission. Disabling them stops the capture track. Speakers can be selected when the browser supports setSinkId. A click can be necessary to unlock audio playback.

    • Screen sharing uses the browser/OS picker, including its visible stop controls. System/tab audio is shared only if the selected source/browser supplies it. Mobile browsers may not support screen capture. SIPL does not capture silently.

    • A new meeting uses a waiting room by default. The host can admit/deny people, remove members, change admission for new arrivals or end the meeting. Turning off the waiting room does not automatically admit people already waiting. If the host leaves, the first remaining approved participant becomes host.

    • Invitations are random capabilities in the URL fragment, outside HTTP request targets. Anyone with an invitation and any required passcode can request entry. Keep both private. There is no persistent directory/account integration in Gather yet; its meeting roles are separate from CRM-ERP roles.

    • Browser HttpOnly/SameSite sessions and a per-tab bearer ticket jointly bind requests. Refreshing the same tab restores its session and renegotiates media. Reconnect media retries a failed connection. Expired/removed members must rejoin.

    • Only admitted members receive chat, other approved member details or file data. Signaling is recipient-specific and cannot cross rooms. The waiting list is visible only to the host. The frontend renders participant/chat/file text as text, not HTML.

    • PDFs use the system/browser PDF viewer, not an external document service. Use Gather's page controls for synchronized presentation. Scrolling or controls inside the native PDF viewer are local; PDF page counts are not extracted, and page controls accept 1–1000. A %PDF- prefix and .pdf extension identify a presentation candidate, not a comprehensive document validation/sanitization. Other files are download-only. The viewer can fall back to downloading.

    • Uploaded files are at most 8 MiB each, 16 per room, and 32 MiB across the server. Chunks are exactly 256 KiB except the final chunk. Uploads are ordered, private to the meeting, and never interpreted as server paths. The owner or host can remove a file. Abandoned incomplete uploads expire after two minutes.

    • At most 16 rooms exist. A room lasts six hours. Members expire after 45 seconds without requests; empty rooms expire after two minutes. Cleanup runs on API activity. Chat retains the latest 150 messages. Restarting/closing the hosting server removes every room, message and shared file. There is no recording, durable archive, calendar integration, telephony or large-conference SFU.

    Native runtime API and builds#

    The runtime adds optional webview.available and blocking webview.run(url, options?). web.serve accepts optional host and window options; window takes the same window settings plus optional url. The default is the actual loopback listener URL, including an automatically assigned port. The window may navigate only within its initial origin; popups and the SIPL/JavaScript native message bridge are disabled. No application authority is injected into pages. Media permissions remain browser/OS controlled.

    MSVC Windows builds use the pinned Microsoft WebView2 SDK header/static loader and the installed Edge WebView2 Evergreen Runtime. No Chromium distribution or WebRTC stack is bundled with SIPL. SIPL_WEBVIEW=0 omits the native backend. webview.available is false without a supported backend/installed engine. Linux/macOS builds currently serve the web frontend; a native web window backend for those platforms is not implemented. Existing native SIPL ui is unchanged. Existing HTTP servers keep their loopback default and do no window work unless window is supplied.

    Build the example's desktop and browser server executables with the current runtime. The desktop uses the Windows subsystem to avoid a console window:

    Copy config.json beside an executable to customize it. No source/assets or launcher scripts are needed there. Run Gather.exe --url=https://meet.example.com to open an existing service. Port overrides are accepted with --port=8084.

    Developer verification#

    The browser/native tests run on Windows with Node and installed Chrome/WebView2. They use separate profiles and synthetic capture devices; those test flags are never set by the application. The browser test checks actual inbound audio bytes and decoded video frames in both directions, screen capture, admission, safe chat, file/PDF transfer, refresh, host transfer and cleanup. The native test opens the actual Win32 window, captures media, and checks server shutdown on close. Physical devices, public NAT/TURN connectivity, external reverse proxies and other browsers still need deployment/device testing. Backend/model tests run on Windows and Linux; model tests also run with GC stress and Linux sanitizer builds.

    Edit the canonical frontend in libraries/meeting/web, then run python scripts/embed_meeting_assets.py. This generates assets.sipl; it is developer tooling only. The checked-in generated module keeps builds offline.

    SIPL Pages#

    Keep .sipl.html files outside the static html root. As defense in depth, the static server rejects requests for .sipl.html source with 403.

    SIPL Pages add server-rendered HTML without turning an HTML file into an unrestricted program. A route loads data, passes one explicit model to a page, and the page renders it with a single tag pair:

    <^ opens a SIPL Page tag and ^> closes it. There is no second output tag, raw-output shorthand, or alternate delimiter. Values are escaped by default. Tags contain one expression or page keyword and do not end with a semicolon. The pair is visually distinct, uncommon in HTML, and easy to identify without the EJS-style choice between silent, escaped, and raw tag variants. Page source is compiled away, so the delimiters never reach the browser.

    The source extension is .sipl.html. This keeps HTML tooling useful while making executable page sources easy for people, AI tools, the server, and security scanners to identify.

    Why this shape#

    PHP-style file execution is convenient, but it mixes routing, database access, business logic, and rendering. It also encourages work to be repeated on every request and makes authority difficult to see.

    SIPL Pages instead use an explicit controller/view boundary:

    The route is ordinary SIPL and owns side effects. The page owns presentation. This gives an AI a small, regular target: one model name, one delimiter pair, one escaping rule, and a short list of page constructs.

    Pages are compiled, not reparsed and interpreted for every request. Production startup compiles the page tree and fails early on malformed pages. Rendering then executes cached bytecode and appends into a bounded response buffer.

    API#

    Quick start and Toolkit workflow#

    The page is a view, not a standalone program. It needs a controller to provide its model and register an HTTP route. The bundled pair is:

    • examples/web.sipl — executable controller

    • pages/index.sipl.html — private compiled page

    From a terminal:

    Then open http://127.0.0.1:8082/.

    In the Toolkit, open pages/index.sipl.html and choose Scan to validate the page. To view it in a browser, open examples/web.sipl and choose Run. The Toolkit deliberately does not execute a page by itself because doing so would invent missing database/model values. Pressing Run while a page is selected now explains this in the Output panel.

    After rebuilding SIPL, restart the Toolkit so its background worker uses the new executable. Windows cannot replace build\sipl.exe while the Toolkit is running, so close it before running build.bat.

    Configure a private page root before starting the server:

    pages and html are deliberately different roots. Files in html are public static assets. Files in pages are executable source and are never served as files.

    A route queries data and renders a named page:

    web.render(path, model) returns the normal web response Map with status 200, Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8, and the rendered body. The controller can return it directly or change its status and application-owned headers.

    The first web.render argument must be a string literal and is resolved beneath the configured page root. Absolute paths, traversal, symlinks or junctions escaping the root, and a path derived from an HTTP request are rejected. Page files cannot be uploaded and executed at runtime. A controller that needs to choose a view uses ordinary branching with a literal render call in each branch.

    Only page-safe values may cross the model boundary: None, Bool, Int, Float, String, and acyclic List and Map trees containing those values. Database handles, collections, functions, native objects, and request objects are rejected. Model values are read-only while rendering; mutating collection methods are unavailable. This makes the page's authority visible in the model.

    Page syntax#

    A page is HTML plus the following constructs. All constructs use <^ and ^>.

    Escaped expressions#

    An expression writes its value:

    none writes nothing. Booleans and numbers use their canonical SIPL text. Strings are never treated as markup.

    Immutable local names#

    let gives a repeated expression a short name and writes nothing:

    Conditions#

    else if is supported. Every block ends with <^ end ^> so mixed HTML and SIPL never depends on matching braces across languages.

    Loops#

    Indexed iteration uses normal SIPL order:

    The v1 page language intentionally has no var, assignment, while, function declaration, import, file access, database access, networking, or session access. That work belongs in a route or an ordinary SIPL function. Page expressions can read and transform page-safe values with their safe built-in operations.

    HTML-aware output safety#

    Escaping must happen where a value is rendered because HTML text, attributes, URLs, CSS, and JavaScript are different parsing contexts. A global string replacement is not sufficient.

    The page compiler tokenizes the surrounding HTML and permits expressions only in supported contexts:

    Contextv1 behavior
    Element textHTML-escape &, <, >, ", and '
    Quoted ordinary attributeAttribute-escape; unquoted attributes are rejected
    href, src, action, and other URL attributesRequire html.url(...), validate the scheme, then attribute-escape
    Element name, attribute name, HTML commentReject dynamic output
    on*, style, and srcdoc attributesReject dynamic output
    Executable <script> or <style> contentReject dynamic output

    For example:

    html.url(value) accepts relative application URLs and explicit http or https URLs. Dangerous schemes such as javascript: are rejected. A later API may offer narrower helpers for route paths and query components.

    There is no raw-string tag in v1. html.include(...) is accepted only as a complete output expression and renders another compiled page directly; a database String cannot be cast to trusted markup. Rich user-authored markup requires a separately designed and maintained sanitizer; calling an escape hatch is not sanitization.

    Client data may be embedded only as non-executable JSON:

    html.json is accepted only in that exact context. It uses the SIPL JSON encoder and also protects the enclosing HTML script element, including <, >, &, and closing-script sequences. Inline JavaScript interpolation is not supported. Client code can read the element's text and call JSON.parse.

    To write the literal opening delimiter in visible text, use &lt;^.

    These rules follow OWASP's guidance that output encoding must match the final browser context and that dangerous contexts should not accept dynamic values: Cross Site Scripting Prevention Cheat Sheet.

    Partials#

    html.include renders another page beneath the same private root:

    The include path must be a string literal so dependencies are known at compile time. It is relative to the current page, cannot escape the page root, and is compiled once. Include cycles and excessive nesting are compile errors.

    Layouts and components can be added after the core renderer is measured. They should build on literal html.include dependencies and the same model boundary rather than add more delimiter forms.

    Compilation, caching, and errors#

    web.pages(root, options?) owns page compilation and caching.

    • The default production mode scans and compiles every .sipl.html file once before web.serve. A failure reports the page path, line, and column and prevents startup.

    • {"reload": true} is development-only. A changed page is compiled atomically; requests never observe a half-compiled page. The last good page may continue serving while the error is reported locally.

    • Literal HTML is stored as immutable chunks. Dynamic values are escaped directly into one geometrically grown, bounded output buffer; the renderer does not build a chain of temporary concatenated Strings.

    • The generated bytecode keeps source mappings back to the page. Runtime failures log the page location on the server and return the existing generic 500 response without source, model data, or stack details.

    • Page source is limited to 4 MiB and a root to 1,024 page files. Rendering is bounded to 1 MiB of output, 1,000,000 work units, 2 seconds, and 32 nested includes. Models allow at most 100,000 values, 64 levels, and 1 MiB of String data; cycles and non-finite Floats are rejected.

    The JIT may accelerate hot generated loops and expressions. HTML escaping, buffer growth, output limits, database latency, and request concurrency remain consistent regardless of the selected execution path.

    AI-facing tools#

    The CLI provides machine-readable validation rather than relying on a browser to reveal mistakes:

    page-check validates every page and returns a nonzero exit code on an error. Diagnostics include the source path, line and column when available, the rejected construct, and a focused repair message.

    page-explain reports static byte count, dynamic slots, loops, conditions, include dependencies, and the checked execution model.

    The Toolkit recognizes .sipl.html as SIPL Page, highlights HTML and SIPL tags in the same file, and uses the same page-check command for Scan. Page formatting is intentionally not automatic yet, so an HTML formatter cannot silently damage embedded SIPL tags.

    Security invariants#

    SIPL Pages enforce these rules:

    • Request or database text is data; it is never reparsed as a page or SIPL.

    • Every expression is context-escaped or rejected.

    • Page source is never returned by static serving or an error response.

    • Routes choose page paths; clients do not.

    • Pages cannot acquire file, network, database, session, process, or other capabilities through globals or model values.

    • Production requests perform no page parsing, compilation, or page-file I/O.

    • Output, work, nesting, and time are bounded.

    • Development reload cannot replace a valid cached page with a failed compile.

    Treat any feature that weakens one of these invariants as a separate security design, not a convenient template option. User-controlled template source can become server-side template injection and must never reach this compiler; see the OWASP server-side template injection guidance.

    Portable HTTP and TLS client#

    SIPL includes an HTTP and HTTPS client on Windows and Linux. Requests return NetTask; they do not perform a blocking transfer at the call site. Drive tasks with net.pollBlocking() in your event loop, or call .waitBlocking() to block explicitly. No separate networking program is required.

    This prerelease replaces the old response Map and synchronous request return value. Use http.get(url).waitBlocking().body, rather than http.get(url)["body"]. There is no await syntax requirement. See shared networking for cancellation, streams, TCP/UDP, and WebSockets.

    Requests and responses#

    API and parametersReturnsCanonical example
    http.client(options?: Map)HttpClient with a reusable connection poolhttp.client({"maxConnections": 4})
    http.request(method: String, url: String, options?: Map)NetTaskhttp.request("PUT", address, {"body": payload})
    http.get(url: String, options?: Map)NetTaskhttp.get(address).waitBlocking()
    http.post(url: String, body: Bytes or NetStream, options?: Map)NetTaskhttp.post(address, Bytes([0, 255])).waitBlocking()
    client.request(...), client.get(...), client.post(...)Same task APIs, using that client's poolclient.get(address).waitBlocking()
    client.close()None; cancels pending requests and closes idle connectionsclient.close()

    Module-level requests share a bounded default pool. Explicit clients isolate pools and provide deterministic cleanup. Client options are maxConnections (Int 1..64, default 8) and idleTimeout (Int milliseconds 1..600000, default 60000). At most 64 pools may exist. Idle pools are pruned when networking is polled; connection age/lifetime limits also prevent reuse of stale connections.

    HttpResponse is a native, annotatable type with read-only properties:

    PropertyType and meaning
    statusInt HTTP status code; zero before headers arrive
    headersMap of lowercase String names to UTF-8 String values; last value for duplicate names
    bodyBytes for buffered requests; NetStream when stream: true
    urlString final URL after permitted redirects
    readyBool: final response headers have arrived
    isOkBool: status is in 200..299

    Non-2xx status codes are ordinary responses. task.response exposes live headers/body for streaming; buffered body bytes are published on completion. task.result is none while pending. Inspect task.error when polling manually; task.waitBlocking() raises a catchable system Fail for network, policy, timeout, cancellation, certificate, or resource-limit failure. Invalid API arguments raise a runtime Fail before scheduling. Closed clients reject new requests.

    Scheduling copies native options and retains request data: O(header and option bytes), without waiting for I/O. Transfers take O(transferred/decoded bytes), plus DNS/TLS work. Buffered requests use O(body limit + headers) space; streaming requests use bounded queues and headers. Closing a client takes O(pending requests + cached connections). Effects include DNS, network I/O, cryptography, native allocations, and reading explicitly named certificate files.

    Request options#

    Unknown HTTP option names are rejected.

    OptionType, default, limits
    headersString-to-String Map; up to 128 entries and 64 KiB total; names up to 256 bytes, values up to 8192
    bodyBytes or upload NetStream; request body capped at 16 MiB
    connectTimeoutInt milliseconds 1..120000, default 10000; includes DNS and TLS connection setup
    readTimeoutInt milliseconds 1..120000, default 10000; maximum period without I/O progress after connection
    totalTimeoutInt milliseconds 1..120000, default 10000; includes redirects and backpressure pauses
    timeoutOptional shorthand supplying the default for all three timeouts; specific fields override it
    cancelCancelToken; checked by the shared scheduler and transfer progress callback
    streamBool, default false; exposes a response NetStream
    maxBodyInt bytes, default 16 MiB; buffered maximum 16 MiB, streaming maximum 64 MiB
    redirects"none" (default), "same-origin", or "cross-origin"
    maxRedirectsInt 0..10, default 5; applies only when following is enabled
    allowDowngradeBool, default false; explicitly permits HTTPS-to-HTTP redirects with cross-origin policy
    redirectWithBodyBool, default false; explicitly permits resending a body across origins
    proxyString proxy URL, or empty String to disable; unset means direct connection, without hidden environment-proxy lookup
    proxyUsername, proxyPasswordOptional String proxy credentials
    caFileOptional String path to a trusted PEM CA bundle
    clientCert, clientKeyOptional String client certificate/key input; see platform formats below
    clientCertTypeOptional certificate format such as "PEM" or "P12"
    clientKeyPasswordOptional String private-key/PKCS#12 password
    pinnedPublicKeyOptional SHA-256 public-key pin, e.g. "sha256//..."
    decompressBool, default false; enables gzip/deflate decoding
    maxExpansionRatioInt 1..1000, default 100; decoded bytes capped relative to encoded bytes, with 1 KiB allowance for small inputs
    idleTimeoutInt milliseconds 1..600000, default 60000; maximum age for reusable idle connections
    connectionLifetimeInt milliseconds 1..3600000, default 300000; maximum reusable connection lifetime

    Response headers are capped at 64 KiB across the transfer, including redirects, with at most 128 fields per response and 8192 bytes per value. Header names and values are validated; invalid UTF-8 values fail rather than becoming invalid SIPL Strings. The client owns Host, Connection, Content-Length, and Transfer-Encoding; application overrides are rejected. Proxy credentials use the dedicated options, rather than an injected Proxy-Authorization header.

    Read timeout pauses while a stream is deliberately backpressured. Total timeout continues, so a producer or consumer that never resumes cannot hold a task forever. Cancellation is cooperative: call net.pollBlocking() to observe token changes and move pending operations forward.

    Redirect policy#

    No redirects are followed by default. same-origin requires the same scheme, host, and effective port at every hop. cross-origin explicitly permits an origin change, but still blocks TLS downgrade unless allowDowngrade is true. Custom application headers and client certificate/key credentials are removed on an origin change. They are never automatically restored at a later hop.

    303 changes to GET; 301/302 change POST to GET. 307/308 preserve the method/body. Cross-origin resending of a body additionally requires redirectWithBody. A streaming upload cannot be replayed; a redirect requiring replay fails. URL-embedded credentials and non-HTTP(S) URLs are rejected at every hop.

    Certificates and portability#

    Peer verification and hostname verification are always enabled. TLS 1.2 is the minimum. The default uses the platform trust roots; caFile supplies an explicit trust bundle and pinnedPublicKey adds a public-key constraint.

    PEM client certificates and keys are supported by default. Windows also supports PKCS#12 (P12) explicitly with clientCertType, using clientKeyPassword for encrypted input. Platform trust roots are used for peer verification. Certificate formats are selected explicitly with clientCertType; unsupported inputs fail. Certificate and password inputs stay out of command-line arguments and source-generated files. Application code chooses where to obtain them.

    The built-in client exposes HTTP(S) only. HTTP/2, HTTP/3, gRPC, SMTP, and MQTT are not separate built-in protocols. Client private keys are not imported into the operating system certificate store.

    Streaming examples#

    A response stream is read-only. body.close() cancels a pending response and releases queued data. Dropping a pending task aborts its transfer; a retained stream reports that failure. Keep the task reachable while using its stream.

    Streams preserve Bytes; encode/decode text explicitly. JSON remains the one json.parse/json.stringify API. Drain streaming responses while polling, rather than waiting for the complete transfer with an unread full queue.

    Verification#

    tests/network_tests.py tests local HTTP/HTTPS, untrusted and explicit trust, redirect policies and credential stripping, decompression bounds, header/body limits, connection reuse, proxying, cancellation, separate read deadlines, request/response streaming backpressure, TCP framing, UDP, and packaged network types. All runtime scenarios run normally and with GC stress. The independent Python test servers do not contact external APIs or alter certificate stores.

    Shared networking tasks, sockets, and WebSockets#

    HTTP, TCP, UDP, and WebSocket operations use the same NetTask, CancelToken, and net.pollBlocking() scheduler. The scheduler runs on the calling SIPL thread; network transfer callbacks do not execute SIPL on background threads. DNS for outbound connections is resolved asynchronously. Pending operations are bounded at 256, open Socket objects at 128.

    Task and stream contracts#

    API and parametersReturn and failuresEffects / complexityCanonical example
    net.pollBlocking(milliseconds?: Int)Int pending count; duration must be 0..1000, default 0Moves all tasks forward; O(pending tasks + ready I/O) per iteration; may wait up to the supplied duration while work remainsnet.pollBlocking(5)
    net.cancelToken(after?: Int)CancelToken; 0..120000 ms, zero/default means no deadlineAllocation and monotonic clock; O(1)net.cancelToken(1000)
