    token.cancel()None; idempotentMarks cancellation; O(1), observed at next polltoken.cancel()
    task.cancel()None; idempotentStops the task and releases transport work; O(1) plus backend cleanuptask.cancel()
    task.waitBlocking(milliseconds?: Int)Operation result; system Fail on failure or wait timeout; 0..120000 ms, default 120000Drives the shared scheduler; O(work done while waiting), blocks explicitlytcp.connect("localhost", 9000).waitBlocking()
    net.stream(capacity?: Int)NetStream; capacity 16384..1048576 bytes, default 65536Allocates a bounded byte queue; O(capacity) spacenet.stream(65536)
    stream.write(chunk: Bytes)Bool; false means insufficient space and no bytes written; Fail on closed/read-only stream or wrong typeO(chunk bytes), no unbounded queue growthupload.write(chunk)
    stream.read(maxBytes?: Int)Bytes or none when empty; limit 1..1048576, default 16384; Fail for transfer error once queued data is drainedO(returned bytes)body.read(8192)
    stream.close()None; closes producer input, or cancels a read-only response streamSignals EOF/cancellation; O(1) plus transport cleanupupload.close()

    CancelToken.isCancelled reflects manual cancellation or its monotonic deadline. NetTask.done, .error, and .result allow polling without blocking; result is none while pending. HTTP tasks also provide .response before completion. NetStream.eof means closed and drained, .buffered reports queued bytes, and .capacity reports the queue bound. Closing a producer still lets a consumer drain its queued data. Transfer errors are observable through .waitBlocking() or stream reads; none means no data now, and .eof distinguishes completion.

    A wait timeout leaves the task pending. Cancel explicitly if the caller no longer wants it. The underlying operation's total deadline still applies. Cancellation of partially consumed framing or partially sent data can close its socket to prevent reusing a stream with an uncertain frame boundary.

    TCP and UDP#

    API and parametersReturn and failuresCanonical example
    tcp.connect(host: String, port: Int, options?: Map)NetTask yielding Socket; port 1..65535; DNS/connect/TLS failure is catchable on waittcp.connect("localhost", 9000).waitBlocking()
    tcp.listen(address: String, port: Int, options?: Map)Socket; numeric IPv4/IPv6 bind address, port 0..65535; bind failure raises Failtcp.listen("127.0.0.1", 0)
    listener.accept(options?: Map)NetTask yielding Socket; listener requiredlistener.accept().waitBlocking()
    socket.send(data: Bytes, options?: Map)NetTask yielding Int bytes sent; connected TCP requiredpeer.send(Bytes([0, 255])).waitBlocking()
    socket.read(maxBytes?: Int, options?: Map)NetTask yielding Bytes; 1..1048576 bytes, default 65536; empty Bytes means orderly EOFpeer.read(4096).waitBlocking()
    socket.readFrame(maxBytes?: Int, options?: Map)NetTask yielding complete length-prefixed Bytes; maximum 1..16 MiB, default 65536; truncated/oversized frame fails and closes socketpeer.readFrame(1048576).waitBlocking()
    socket.readLine(maxBytes?: Int, options?: Map)NetTask yielding Bytes without LF; maximum 1..16 MiB, default 65536; returns final unterminated line at EOFpeer.readLine(4096).waitBlocking()
    socket.shutdownWrite()None; half-closes connected plain TCP output; unsupported for TLSpeer.shutdownWrite()
    socket.close()None; closes transport, pending tasks fail at next pollpeer.close()
    udp.bind(address: String, port: Int, options?: Map)Socket; numeric IPv4/IPv6 address, port 0..65535udp.bind("127.0.0.1", 0)
    socket.sendTo(address: String, port: Int, body: Bytes, options?: Map)NetTask yielding Int bytes sent; numeric destination, port 1..65535, payload up to 65507 bytessender.sendTo("127.0.0.1", port, payload).waitBlocking()
    socket.receive(maxBytes?: Int, options?: Map)NetTask yielding Map with body: Bytes, numeric host: String, port: Int; 1..65507, default 65507; oversized datagram fails and is discardedreceiver.receive(65507).waitBlocking()
    framing.lengthPrefix(payload: Bytes)Bytes with 4-byte unsigned big-endian length; payload at most 16 MiB minus fourframing.lengthPrefix(Bytes([1, 2]))
    framing.line(payload: Bytes)Bytes with LF appended; rejects embedded LF or size overflowframing.line(bytes.encodeUtf8("hello"))

    TCP read limits are upper bounds, not an assumption that one send equals one read. Framing helpers make message boundaries explicit. Line reads buffer excess received bytes for the next read. A socket permits one pending read and one pending write concurrently; duplicate operations in a direction fail. UDP preserves datagram boundaries and never silently returns a truncated packet.

    Operation options are timeout (10 seconds by default), connectTimeout, readTimeout, totalTimeout, and cancel, with the same millisecond ranges as HTTP. Listener options include backlog (1..128, default 32). tcp.connect additionally accepts tls: true, caFile, client certificate/key, format/password, public-key pin, and explicit proxy options as described in HTTP. Peer/hostname verification remain enabled. Bind/UDP destination addresses are numeric so those synchronous setup calls do not perform hidden DNS.

    Socket.port is the assigned local Int port, .address is its numeric address Map, and .closed reports closure. Port zero lets the OS assign a free port. Scheduling costs O(outgoing bytes retained/copied); transfer/framing costs O(transferred bytes). Read buffers and frame allocations are bounded by their specified limits; sockets have a bounded 16 KiB read cache. Effects include DNS for connects, socket creation, network I/O, allocations, and optional TLS.

    WebSocket client and server#

    Server upgrades use the same Socket tasks:

    API and parametersReturn / failuresCanonical example
    websocket.connect(url: String, options?: Map)NetTask yielding WebSocket; ws/wss only, no embedded credentials; handshake/DNS/TLS failures are catchablewebsocket.connect(address).waitBlocking()
    websocket.accept(socket: Socket, options?: Map)NetTask yielding WebSocket; requires an idle connected TCP socket and a complete HTTP/1.1 upgrade requestwebsocket.accept(peer).waitBlocking()
    ws.sendText(text: String, options?: Map)NetTask yielding Int payload bytes sent; valid UTF-8 requiredws.sendText("café").waitBlocking()
    ws.sendBinary(payload: Bytes, options?: Map)NetTask yielding Int payload bytes sentws.sendBinary(Bytes([0, 255])).waitBlocking()
    ws.ping(payload: Bytes, options?: Map)NetTask yielding Int payload bytes sent; at most 125 bytesws.ping(Bytes([1])).waitBlocking()
    ws.receive(options?: Map)NetTask yielding Map with type (text, binary, or close), body: Bytes, code: Int; protocol violations fail and abort the transportws.receive().waitBlocking()
    ws.close(code?: Int, reason?: String, options?: Map)NetTask yielding close message after the peer reply; default 1000/empty reason; validates codes and UTF-8 reason up to 123 bytesws.close(1000, "done").waitBlocking()
    ws.abort()None; closes transport immediatelyws.abort()

    WebSocket options include the shared timeout/cancellation options, TLS/proxy client options, maxMessage (1..16 MiB, default 1 MiB), origin (up to 2048 bytes), and a single protocol token (up to 256 bytes). Upgrade headers are bounded at 64 KiB and 128 fields. Subprotocol mismatch fails. Extensions, including permessage-deflate, are not negotiated.

    The server rejects a supplied browser Origin unless it matches its explicit origin option. Clients without an Origin header are permitted. Server-side listeners currently provide plain TCP/WS; use TLS termination in front of the listener for WSS service. WSS clients verify certificates on both platforms. The server does not silently accept every browser origin or enable compression.

    Incoming ping frames automatically queue a matching pong while a receive/close task is being polled; pong frames are consumed internally. Keep a receive task pending to process control traffic. Close performs a bounded two-way handshake; timeout/cancellation aborts it. .closed, .path, and .closeCode expose status. One send and one receive may run concurrently; additional sends are rejected instead of accumulating an unbounded queue. Control output is capped at 512 bytes.

    Frames enforce role-specific masking, reserved-bit/opcode rules, canonical lengths, control-frame limits, UTF-8 text/close reasons, and a total fragmented message bound. Handshake nonces and client masks use OS secure randomness. Wire processing is O(message bytes); fragmented data plus the current frame uses O(message limit) space. Effects include sockets, TLS for WSS clients, secure random generation, handshake hashing, and bounded native allocations.

    DNS and discovery boundary#

    Outbound HTTP/TCP/WSS connections already use cancellable, timeout-bounded DNS through the shared transport. A standalone DNS query API and service discovery are optional future modules; they should return NetTask and accept CancelToken, rather than introduce a second scheduler. Multicast/device discovery should also be tested on its target network, since WSL networking mode affects those paths. Ordinary local unicast TCP/UDP/TLS tests run on WSL 2.

    Tests#

    tests/network_tests.py runs independent local HTTP/TLS/proxy/socket servers. tests/websocket_tests.py supplies a raw RFC 6455 oracle, including TLS, fragmented UTF-8, ping/pong, close, origin policy, masking and size violations. Runtime cases run normally and with GC stress. Linux/WSL and native Windows use the same tests. Test certificates are temporary and are never installed in the system trust store.

    Structured tasks and async I/O#

    async fn, await, and spawn use one runtime-owned event loop on the SIPL thread. Each task has a suspended VM stack; SIPL values never move to another OS thread. Native DNS resolvers may use threads with native data only. Tasks can share SIPL values on the event-loop thread; this does not make multi-step updates transactional.

    The runner starts an async start() automatically. Calling an async function schedules an owned Task; spawn makes this intent explicit and accepts a Task or NetTask. A function's return annotation describes its awaited result. Task itself is an annotatable handle. Async methods, nested functions, lambdas, and async test "name" { ... } use the same model. await and spawn are legal only in async functions. Synchronous callbacks cannot schedule or suspend tasks.

    Ownership and scope exit#

    The lexical block containing a task or I/O call owns it. The owner retains the operation even when its handle is discarded. At block exit, unfinished children are cancelled and joined before locals are released. This applies to normal fallthrough, return, break, continue, and failure. Cleanup can itself await I/O. Entering a failure handler waits for children of the abandoned block to finish cleanup first. An awaited task's failure is raised at the await expression; an unobserved child failure is raised in the owner and cancels its siblings.

    There is no detach or implicit ownership transfer. A handle stored outside its block refers to a completed or cancelled operation after that block closes. Loop bodies own their children for each iteration: returning a handle or adding it to an outer List does not extend that lifetime. Awaiting another owner's handle does not transfer ownership. Self-awaits, ancestor-awaits, and await cycles are rejected.

    Tasks start with their owner's lifetime rather than a hidden wall-clock limit. setDeadline() adds an optional monotonic cancellation deadline. Cancellation is cooperative: it is delivered once on resumption, at an await, or after a VM fairness slice. A slice yields at a loop backedge after approximately 10,000 instructions; ordinary expressions are not interrupted mid-instruction. Callbacks run to completion. CPU-heavy or untrusted work belongs in an isolated worker process.

    Typed cancellation and cleanup#

    Cancellation raises Cancelled, a subtype of Fail, with kind == "cancelled". It uses ordinary try / fail / next. Catching cancellation can return a result; isCancelled records the request, and .failure is none after successful recovery. next may await bounded cleanup. A deadline requests cancellation, rather than forcibly terminating SIPL code.

    I/O timeouts raise a system Fail; explicit task/token cancellation raises Cancelled. NetTask.isCancelled exposes the latter. A successful Fail value can be returned as ordinary task data and is distinct from a task that failed.

    Public task API#

    API and parametersResult and failuresEffects / complexityCanonical example
    task.current()Task in async code, none otherwiseReads current execution context; O(1)task.current().cancel()
    task.sleep(milliseconds: Int)NetTask yielding None; 0..120000 ms, cancellableMonotonic timer; O(1) scheduling and spaceawait task.sleep(20)
    task.yield()NetTask yielding None at the next event-loop turnCooperative scheduling; O(1)await task.yield()
    time.timer(delay: Duration)NetTask yielding None; nonnegative delay, cancellableMonotonic deadline; O(1) scheduling and spaceawait time.timer(time.seconds(1))
    time.at(instant: Instant)NetTask yielding the target InstantCalendar alarm following UTC wall-clock corrections; O(1) spaceawait time.at(time.now().add(time.seconds(10)))
    interval.next() / cron.next()NetTask yielding a Monotonic tick / InstantOne pending wait per schedule, cancelled at scope exitawait time.interval(time.seconds(1)).next()
    task.runBlocking(function: Function, arguments?: List)Awaited result; requires an async function and matching arguments; rethrows its failureOwns a root task and blocks this thread; O(total scheduled work)task.runBlocking(fetchTitle, [address])
    handle.cancel()None; idempotent, completed handles are unaffectedRequests cancellation; O(1) plus bounded transport cleanupchild.cancel()
    handle.setDeadline(milliseconds: Int)None; 1..120000 ms from nowSets a monotonic cancellation deadline; O(1)child.setDeadline(5000)
    await handleTask/NetTask result; rethrows original Fail or typed Cancelled; rejects cycles and non-task valuesSuspends this VM stack while other tasks run; O(1) plus bounded ownership lookuplet response = await http.get(address)

    Read-only Task properties are .done, .result, .failure, .isCancelled, and .owner. Result/failure are none while pending. Owner is the creating Task until the completed handle is released from its scope. Finished tasks release their VM stacks and captured execution state.

    At most 128 structured tasks, 256 pending native I/O operations, and 512 owned operations may exist at once. Each task has 16,384 stack slots, 256 call frames, and up to 512 nested ownership scopes. Admission fails before unlimited work is queued. Observing a completed operation releases its ownership record. Scheduler work is bounded by runnable tasks, owned operations, and ready I/O; suspended contexts and queues count toward the stated memory bounds.

    Awaitable I/O and blocking boundaries#

    HTTP, TCP, UDP, WebSockets, timers, and bounded byte streams all feed the same event loop. See HTTP and networking. HTTP responses provide text() for strict UTF-8 decoding of a completed buffered body. Requests have connect/read/total timeout policies; sockets and WebSockets have operation deadlines. Stream operations default to a 30-second total timeout.

    Synchronous callers use the explicit NetTask.waitBlocking(milliseconds?) and net.pollBlocking(milliseconds?) names. Blocking calls are rejected inside async tasks. The existing synchronous disk, database, process, stdin, UI frame, and AI ask APIs belong outside async tasks. Load configuration before entering async code. Blocking time.sleep(Duration) also belongs outside async tasks; use time.timer(Duration) for an awaitable delay. Calendar types, interval phases, cron syntax/DST behavior, and explicit locale profiles are documented in STDLIB.md.

    Worker jobs retain their process-isolated lifecycle and do not become shared-memory async tasks. Outside async code, low-level native operations belong to the program lifetime and are cancelled when that lifetime ends.

    Bounded byte-stream contract#

    net.stream(capacity?) is a binary I/O queue with capacity 16 KiB..1 MiB, default 64 KiB. Bytes are copied into the queue; a producer and consumer may hold the same stream on the SIPL thread. This is not an actor or arbitrary-value channel. Ownership applies to each scheduled operation. Only one async reader and one async writer may be pending. Polling operations cannot bypass a pending operation in the same direction; uploads already have their stream consumer.

    API and parametersResult and failuresEffects / complexityCanonical example
    stream.readAsync(maxBytes?: Int, options?: Map)NetTask yielding Bytes; empty Bytes means drained EOF; limit 1..1048576, default 16384Waits for data/EOF with a deadline; copies O(returned bytes)let chunk = await body.readAsync(8192)
    stream.writeAsync(chunk: Bytes, options?: Map)NetTask yielding Int bytes written; chunk must fit capacity; closed/read-only streams failWaits for room, writes the whole chunk atomically; O(chunk bytes)await upload.writeAsync(chunk)

    Options are timeout / totalTimeout (1..120000 ms, default 30000) and cancel (CancelToken). A full queue suspends the writer rather than growing. Closing a producer permits draining followed by EOF; closing a response stream cancels its HTTP transfer. Transfer failures propagate after queued bytes are drained. Cancellation does not retract bytes already consumed or sent.

    select, race, arbitrary-value channels, actor APIs, and shared-memory threads are not introduced by this model. The lifetime and failure tests run in isolated processes with GC stress, and the async network oracle also tests packaged code.

    SQL Tables#

    SIPL provides a lightweight Table data type for raw SQL and parameterized queries. It is not an object mapper and does not add change tracking or an ORM. SQLite is built in and needs no database server. MySQL and MariaDB use the native MariaDB Connector/C driver and a running database server. Both drivers share the Table API and bind parameters through native prepared statements.

    Creating a table#

    SQLite supports two storage lifetimes. Existing sql.memory() and sql.open(path) calls continue to use SQLite.

    PDO-style connections#

    sql.connect(dsn, username?, password?) accepts sqlite:, mysql:, and mariadb: prefixes. mysql: connects to either MySQL or MariaDB; mariadb: is an alias. MySQL options are host, port, dbname, charset, and unix_socket. Defaults are localhost, port 3306, and utf8mb4. Omitted credentials are empty strings. Unknown options, invalid ports, and NUL bytes in DSNs or credentials fail. Connection establishment has a 10 second timeout.

    For a Unix socket, use mysql:unix_socket=/run/mysqld/mysqld.sock;dbname=application. SQL dialects and schemas remain database specific; SQLite SQL is not rewritten. The API follows PDO's driver selection and binding model, with SIPL's existing query/execute result model. Parameters support positional ? placeholders with a List, or named :name placeholders with a Map. There are no user-visible reusable statement objects.

    Building the MySQL/MariaDB driver#

    Every standard build includes SQLite and MySQL/MariaDB. Pinned MariaDB Connector/C 3.4.11 source is bundled under third_party/mariadb and compiled into a static library during make, build.bat, and the Android CMake build. No separately installed Connector/C SDK, SIPL_MARIADB_ROOT, connector DLL, or connector shared library is required. TLS reuses Windows Schannel or the existing OpenSSL/LibreSSL build inputs. Authentication plugins are compiled into the client; they are not external DLLs.

    Feature-off switches such as SIPL_MYSQL=0 are rejected. A missing build prerequisite stops compilation instead of silently omitting the driver. system.buildFeatures records the compiled capabilities and connector version; standard build reports record the runtime and Toolkit sizes as well.

    The connector uses Connector/C authentication and transport support. TCP connections retain its certificate-verifying TLS defaults. Explicit Unix sockets use local transport and do not require server TLS. The DSN currently exposes no TLS configuration options; configure transport at the SDK/server level as needed. persistent describes remote database storage, not a pooled or reused PDO persistent connection.

    Transactions and inserted IDs#

    begin(), commit(), and rollback() work with both drivers. MySQL tables must use a transactional engine such as InnoDB; server rules about implicit DDL commits still apply. lastInsertId() returns a decimal String, preserving unsigned MySQL BIGINT IDs. It refers to the connection's most recent insert. No transaction or query syntax is rewritten by SIPL.

    Temporary, in-memory#

    The database exists only while the Table is open in the current process. Closing the table or ending the program destroys its contents.

    Persistent, on disk#

    SIPL writes this database to disk. It can be closed and reopened by the same program or a later SIPL process:

    SIPL creates the file when it does not already exist.

    Executing SQL#

    Use execute for statements that do not need a result grid:

    execute returns the number of rows changed by the statement.

    Parameters are safely bound. Use a List for positional ? placeholders or a Map for named :name placeholders. Both support None, Bool, Int, Float, and String values.

    Map keys may include the leading colon (":settingname") or omit it. Do not supply both forms of the same name. Names are case sensitive and use ASCII letters, digits, and underscores, beginning with a letter or underscore. Repeated markers bind the same value to each occurrence. Missing, unused, or ambiguous keys fail, and named and positional placeholders cannot be mixed with a parameter map. Markers inside quoted strings, quoted identifiers, and comments are left untouched. MySQL backslash escaping follows the connection's NO_BACKSLASH_ESCAPES status. With MySQL backslash escapes enabled, use doubled double quotes rather than backslash-escaped double quotes in named statements; the latter are rejected because ANSI_QUOTES can change their meaning. Parameters inside executable MySQL comments are not supported.

    Named markers are rewritten to native parameter slots; parameter values are never interpolated into SQL text. Both naming styles provide the same binding protection. Bind values only; identifiers such as table and column names cannot be supplied as parameters.

    Querying rows#

    query executes SQL, replaces the table's current rows and columns, and returns the same Table:

    An optional third argument caps materialized rows: table.query(statement, params, maxRows), where maxRows is 1..10000. The statement is stopped after the cap, so use this for read-only browsing queries. The default is unlimited for compatibility with existing callers.

    executeScript(script) runs a SQL script containing multiple statements and returns the number of rows changed. Scripts are limited to 16 MiB. Use this only for trusted imports or SQL entered by the user; statements already completed before an error are not automatically rolled back.

    MySQL/MariaDB integer and floating types become Int and Float. Unsigned integers above INT64_MAX stay decimal strings. DECIMAL/NUMERIC, temporal, JSON, and other nonnumeric types remain strings, preserving exact decimal precision. Binary columns become strings containing exact bytes, including NUL.

    SQLite query results use these conversions:

    SQL valueSIPL value
    NULLNone
    INTEGERInt
    REALFloat
    TEXTString
    BLOBString containing the exact bytes

    Table properties#

    PropertyTypeMeaning
    columnsListColumn names from the latest query
    rowsListRows from the latest query; every row is a List
    dataListAlias for rows, intended for consumers such as a future ui.Table
    columnCountIntNumber of columns in the current result
    rowCountIntNumber of rows in the current result
    driverStringsqlite or mysql (also for MariaDB)
    pathStringSQLite path or MySQL database name; credentials are not retained
    persistentBooltrue for a disk or remote database
    isOpenBoolWhether SQL operations can still run

    Closing#

    close is safe to call more than once. SIPL also closes an unreachable open table during garbage collection, but explicit closing releases the database immediately.

    Calling query or execute after closing raises a sql failure.

    Errors and limits#

    • Each query or execute call accepts exactly one SQL statement.

    • A placeholder count mismatch raises a sql failure.

    • Preparation, execution, constraint, and file errors raise a sql failure with a useful database message.

    • Table connections should be used by the SIPL execution context that created them.

    This intentionally remains a thin SQL layer. Application code owns its SQL, schema, transactions, and migrations.

    Verification#

    Run SQLite regression tests with build/sipl run tests/test_sql.sipl and build/sipl run tests/test_sql_named.sipl. The named-parameter suite also tests MySQL/MariaDB when SIPL_MYSQL_DSN and optional credentials are set. The opt-in MySQL/MariaDB integration test creates only a temporary table in a disposable database:

    It checks native binding, Unicode and binary round trips, numeric conversion, transactions, inserted IDs, capped results, and connection reuse after errors. Repeat with SIPL_GC_STRESS=1 to check native resources alongside collection.

    Connector implementation reference: MariaDB Connector/C prepared statements.

    Document Collections#

    SIPL's Collection and NoSqlDatabase use the same embedded BSON engine in src/nosql.c and src/nosql.h. Base opens these databases directly. SQLite provides transactional disk storage; documents are BSON bytes, not JSON text. No server is required. UnQLite and its Jx9 scripting engine have been removed; its unreleased file format and integer __id API are unsupported.

    Opening a database or collection#

    collection.open(path, name) creates the database and named collection when absent. Each call owns a separate database connection. Collection names contain 1–255 UTF-8 bytes without NUL. The parent directory must already exist.

    For multiple collections sharing one connection and transaction:

    collection.memory(name) and collection.open(path, name) own their connection: closing them closes the database immediately and rolls back an unfinished transaction. A view returned by db.collection(name) keeps the database alive through garbage collection; closing that view leaves the shared connection open. Unreachable databases release their resources and roll back unfinished writes. Closing is idempotent; reads/writes on a closed handle raise a failure.

    Named collection interface#

    OperationInterface
    Propertiesname, path, persistent, isOpen, count, lastQueryIndexed
    Readfind(filter?, options?), findOne(filter?), findById(id), countWhere(filter?)
    Insertinsert(document) returns _id; insertMany(documents) returns inserted count
    Updateupdate(filter, update, many = false, upsert = false) returns write statistics
    Replacereplace(filter, document, upsert = false) returns write statistics
    Deletedelete(filter, many = false) returns deleted count
    Clear/dropclear() returns deleted count and retains indexes; drop() removes the collection and indexes
    Indexesindexes(), createIndex(name, fieldPath, unique = false), dropIndex(name)

    TransferimportBson(path), exportBson(path, filter?) return document count

    Closeclose()

    The database interface exposes the same operations with a collection name as the first argument: db.find("notes", filter, options), db.insert("notes", doc), db.update("notes", filter, update, many, upsert), and so on. Use db.count(name, filter?) for counts. db.collections(), db.createCollection(name), db.renameCollection(name, newName), and db.dropCollection(name) manage collection names. db.begin/commit/rollback, db.backup(path) and db.close() apply to the whole connection. nosql.encode(document) and nosql.decode(bytes) convert raw BSON.

    Identity, reads and writes#

    The immutable _id field identifies each document. insert generates a BSON ObjectId when _id is absent and returns its {"$oid": "24 hex digits"} map. Explicit scalar IDs such as strings and integers are accepted. Duplicate IDs fail; replacement preserves the existing ID when omitted. There is no __id.

    find defaults to 100 documents and supports sort, descending, skip, limit (1–1000) and projection. Results are limited to 32 MiB of BSON; page through larger collections. findOne returns one document or none. lastQueryIndexed reports the latest find candidate plan. Counts may scan.

    Filters support dotted paths, scalar/array equality, $eq, $ne, $gt, $gte, $lt, $lte, $in, $nin, $exists, $type, $size, $all, $elemMatch, field $not, and top-level $and, $or, $nor. Null equality also matches missing fields. Unsupported operators are errors even with no documents.

    Updates support $set, $unset (a field map), $inc, $mul, $min, $max, $push, $addToSet, $pull, $pop, $rename, and $setOnInsert. $push/$addToSet accept {"$each": [...]}. Dotted document paths work; positional/array-index updates are unsupported. Updates return a map containing matched, modified, and upserted. Numeric aggregation returns exact Int64 integer sums or compensated floating sums; integer overflow raises an error.

    Batches, multi-document updates/deletes, and BSON imports are atomic. A failed operation rolls back its changes while preserving other operations in an explicit transaction. insertMany accepts up to 10,000 documents and 64 MiB per batch. Documents are limited to 16 MiB and nesting to 64 levels. Cyclic values, non-string map keys, unsupported SIPL objects, invalid BSON, duplicate unique keys, and unsupported operations raise catchable failures. Database/encoding failures use kind collection; argument-shape mistakes can use kind runtime.

    Indexes are ordered single-field indexes with sparse/multikey support and an optional uniqueness constraint. Compound indexes, text/geospatial/vector search, regex execution, collation, replication and network server protocols are not implemented. See src/nosql.h for exact engine limits.

    BSON values and transfer#

    BSON maps use type markers so JSON editing preserves values:

    • ObjectId: {"$oid": "507f1f77bcf86cd799439011"}.

    • Int64: {"$numberLong": "9223372036854775807"}.

    • Double: {"$numberDouble": "1"} (including NaN and infinities).

    • Date: {"$date": {"$numberLong": "1700000000000"}} (Unix milliseconds).

    • Other BSON types: {"$bson": {"type": 19, "hex": "..."}}; hex is the exact little-endian BSON value payload. Binary subtypes and Decimal128 values survive a decode/JSON edit/encode cycle without losing their original bits.

    Ordinary SIPL values encode naturally; small Int values become Int32, larger ones Int64, and Bytes become generic BSON binary. Recognized marker maps are reserved representations. This is a type-preserving BSON editing format, not a complete implementation of MongoDB Extended JSON (for example ISO date strings and $numberDecimal are not parsed). Decimal arithmetic is unsupported.

    The database is a local embedded engine, not a MongoDB server or network driver. The C header documents supported query/update operators and index limitations. BSON transfer supports ordinary uncompressed per-collection streams, not MongoDB archives, compressed dumps or live server storage directories. Export requires a new filename to avoid overwriting an open database or existing export.

    Base: tables and collections together#

    Run examples/projects/Base/base.sipl. Its sidebar has Tables followed by Collections, each with a database filename and its own create/open actions. The Databases screen opens or creates either storage type. Global Open database detects Base BSON files by their SQLite application ID and routes them to Collections; other SQLite files open in Tables. A .nsdb file is a BSON document database, while .db / .sqlite files retain the relational workflow. Both connections remain open, and switching objects preserves the other view.

    Selecting a table exposes Browse, Structure, SQL, Insert and Operations. Selecting a collection exposes Documents, Fields, Indexes, Aggregation and Collection tools:

    • Documents: JSON filter, sort, page navigation, document list, expandable typed field inspection and JSON view. Insert/Edit opens a JSON editor with validation.

    • Fields: presence/type analysis of up to 200 matching documents; this is a sample, not schema validation.

    • Indexes: inspect, create or drop single-field indexes (including unique indexes).

    • Aggregation: count, numeric count, sum, average, minimum and maximum, optionally grouped by a scalar field, using the current filter.

    • Collection tools: rename/drop, atomic JSON/BSON imports, export the current JSON page or all matching BSON documents, and Save database as for a complete persistent snapshot, including a temporary in-memory database.

    Destructive actions and discarding dirty JSON require an in-app confirmation; background controls are disabled while it is open. Failed filters leave the last successful result visible. Saving JSON preserves _id; importing duplicate IDs fails atomically.

    Checks: sipl run tests/test_nosql.sipl, sipl run examples/projects/Base/base.sipl --test, --test-ui (headless input simulation), and --test-io=NEW_PATH_PREFIX. For document screenshots use --sample --collections, optionally followed by --tab=Fields, --tab=Indexes, --tab=Aggregation or --tab=Editor.

    Mat: native linear algebra#

    mat wraps reference Netlib BLAS and LAPACK in one namespace, with two native objects: Matrix for dense numeric data and LUFactor for reusable solves. This is a CPU linear algebra foundation for simulations. It does not provide ODE/PDE integrators, sparse matrices, FFTs, probability distributions, or a complete binding to every Netlib routine.

    For an interactive desktop workbench, run sipl run examples/projects/Flux/flux.sipl. Flux combines worksheets, a command window, a matrix workspace, and figures using this API.

    Data and ownership#

    Matrices use contiguous, column-major IEEE Float64 buffers. Constructors accept ordinary row-oriented SIPL lists and convert once. mat.vector creates an n×1 matrix; vectors can also have one row. Numeric inputs must be finite. Integers are converted to Float64 and may round beyond its exact integer range.

    Calculations preserve their inputs and return independent objects. set, scaleInPlace, and functions ending in Into explicitly mutate their target. Matrices have no shared buffer views, so closing an input cannot invalidate a result. LU factors own an independent copy of the original matrix.

    Each matrix/workspace is capped at 16,777,216 elements (128 MiB). Factorizations can require several buffers; 128 MiB is a per-buffer limit, not a total process budget. Dimensions must be positive. All indexes are zero-based. close() is idempotent; unreachable buffers are also freed and counted by the GC. Closing an LU factor releases its references to the private factor buffers.

    Input validation and LAPACK INFO errors raise catchable runtime failures. Singular LU factors can be inspected (singular, zero rcond()), but cannot solve or invert. Ill-conditioned systems may produce a result with poor forward accuracy; inspect rcond() and the residual. Arithmetic may overflow to infinity or NaN; check isFinite. LAPACK solvers/decompositions reject nonfinite input.

    Construction and basic operations#

    InterfaceResult
    mat.matrix(rows)Matrix from rectangular List[List[Number]]
    mat.vector(values)Column vector from nonempty List[Number]
    mat.zeros(rows, columns = 1) / mat.ones(rows, columns = 1)Filled matrix
    mat.eye(size)Identity matrix
    mat.diag(vector)Square diagonal matrix
    m.rows, m.cols, m.size, m.dtypeShape, element count, "float64"
    m.isOpen, m.isFiniteResource and numeric state
    m.at(row, column = 0) / m.set(row, column, value)Read/write one element
    m.toList() / m.toVector()Row-oriented lists / flat vector list
    m.clone() / m.transpose()Independent copy / transpose
    m.add(other, alpha = 1)m + alpha * other (same shape)
    m.scale(alpha) / m.scaleInPlace(alpha)New scaled matrix / explicit mutation
    x.dot(y)BLAS dot product, vector lengths must match
    m.norm(kind = "fro")Frobenius, "1", "inf", or "max" norm; "2" for vectors
    m.multiply(other, options?)Same as mat.gemm(m, other, options)
    m.close()Release matrix buffer

    BLAS operations#

    InterfaceFormula
    mat.axpy(alpha, x, y)New matrix alpha*x + y; matching shapes
    mat.axpyInto(y, alpha, x)Mutate y = alpha*x + y; x == y is permitted
    mat.gemv(a, x, options?)New vector alpha*op(a)*x
    mat.gemvInto(y, a, x, options?)Mutate y = alpha*op(a)*x + beta*y
    mat.gemm(a, b, options?)New matrix alpha*op(a)*op(b)
    mat.gemmInto(c, a, b, options?)Mutate c = alpha*op(a)*op(b) + beta*c

    Options are alpha (default 1), transposeA (default false), and, for GEMM, transposeB. Only the Into variants accept beta (default 0). Output buffers must have exactly the required shape and must not alias either multiplication input. Invalid shapes, flags, and options fail before the target changes.

    Solvers and reusable LU factors#

    InterfaceAlgorithm / result
    mat.solve(a, b) / a.solve(b)DGESV, square system, one or many RHS columns
    mat.solveSPD(a, b)DPOSV, symmetric positive-definite system
    mat.solveTriangular(a, b, upper = false, unitDiagonal = false, transpose = false)DTRTRS; uses the selected triangle
    mat.solveTridiagonal(lower, diagonal, upper, b)DGTSV; off-diagonals length n−1, n≥2
    mat.leastSquares(a, b, rcond = -1)DGELSS SVD solve, including rank-deficient/underdetermined systems
    mat.inverse(a) / a.inverse()LU inverse; prefer solving when that is the actual task
    mat.factor(a) / a.factor()LUFactor with partial pivoting

    Least squares returns {"solution": Matrix, "rank": Int, "singularValues": Matrix}. Its default rcond=-1 uses machine precision; explicit thresholds are in [0,1].

    LUFactor interfaceMeaning
    size, singular, isOpenOrder and state
    solve(b, transpose = false)Reuse the factors for AX=B or AᵀX=B
    inverse()Independent inverse matrix
    rcond()Estimated reciprocal 1-norm condition number
    logDeterminant()Map with sign and logAbs; singular gives 0 and −infinity
    lower(), upper()Independent L and U matrices
    permutation()Zero-based row order p, with A[p,:] = L*U
    close()Close the factor

    Decompositions and spectral problems#

    InterfaceResult
    mat.cholesky(a) / a.cholesky()Lower L, with A=L*Lᵀ; DPOTRF
    mat.qr(a) / a.qr(){"q": Q, "r": R}, thin QR; A=Q*R
    mat.svd(a) / a.svd(){"u": U, "s": s, "vt": Vᵀ}, thin SVD; A=Udiag(s)Vᵀ
    mat.symmetricEigen(a) / a.symmetricEigen(){"values": λ, "vectors": V}; AV=Vdiag(λ)
    mat.generalizedEigen(a, b)Symmetric A and positive-definite B; AV=BV*diag(λ)
    mat.eigen(a) / a.eigen()General real square system, including complex conjugate pairs

    Symmetric routines validate symmetry with relative tolerance 1e-12, then use the lower triangle. Symmetric eigenvalues are ascending; singular values descending. Eigenvectors are columns; their signs/phases and bases in repeated eigenspaces are not unique.

    General eigen returns real, imag, vectorsReal, and vectorsImag matrices. Column j represents eigenvalue real[j] + i*imag[j] and its complex eigenvector. Real and imaginary parts are explicit because Matrix currently stores real Float64 data; arbitrary complex matrices and Float32 are not exposed yet.

    Builds, provenance, and graphics isolation#

    The pinned C distribution is Netlib LAPACK 3.12.0, as reported by mat.lapackVersion, from OpenBLAS 0.3.34's maintained translations. Reference BLAS sources from that same archive were translated with Netlib f2c 20240504. This does not link OpenBLAS's optimized kernels or threading runtime. Netlib's upstream Fortran release at integration (2026-10-16) is 3.12.1; we do not claim that the C translation is that patch release. Exact source URLs, checksums, licenses, and ABI handling are in the dependency pin.

    Ordinary builds are offline and use only the existing C compiler and CMake. A separate static archive contains the dependency closure of the public API; other upstream C routines remain vendored for future wrappers. Only referenced objects are linked into SIPL. There are no runtime BLAS/Fortran DLL requirements. Source size, archive size, and executable growth are different measurements. Measured against the previous runtime with the same build profile, the current wrapper adds 407,040 bytes (0.39 MiB) on Windows and 449,416 bytes (0.43 MiB) on Linux. The Windows imported-DLL set is unchanged. These are measurements of this binding's linked routine set, not a promise for every future Netlib binding.

    Math uses private CPU buffers and makes no graphics/GPU/compute API calls. Existing graphics backends, shader options, and type IDs are retained. Tests include numerical reconstruction/residuals, normal and GC-stress execution, packaging, existing Vulkan scenes, and math while rendering a scene.

    This backend prioritizes a portable reference implementation. Large dense simulations can benefit from optimized BLAS in a future backend; reference BLAS should not be described as the fastest implementation. Simulation timestepping, boundary conditions and stability still belong to the application.

    Generic 3D Graphics#

    SIPL exposes a generic retained graphics API. Vulkan runs on Windows and Linux (X11/XWayland); the Apple implementation uses native Metal. Backend handles, flags, synchronization objects, and prefixed constants never appear in SIPL programs.

    First Scene#

    Run it:

    Escape or the window close button exits.

    Application#

    graphics.open(title, width, height) returns a GraphicsApp. One graphics application may be open at a time.

    MemberMeaning
    app.scene()Create an empty retained scene
    app.frame()Present the previous frame, process input, and begin the next frame
    app.draw(scene, camera)Draw every visible object in a scene
    app.useCamera(camera)Apply a camera before module-level immediate drawing
    app.background(color)Set the next frame's #RRGGBB clear color
    app.close()Wait for outstanding work and release all graphics resources
    app.deltaTimeSeconds since the previous frame, capped at 0.25
    app.width, app.heightCurrent drawable size
    app.isOpenWhether the window remains open

    The module-level immediate drawing functions remain as a compatibility layer. New applications should use retained app, scene, object, and camera values.

    Scenes And Standard Primitives#

    size may be one positive number or a three-number list.

    MethodMeaning
    object.position(x, y, z)Set world position
    object.rotation(x, y, z)Set Euler rotation in radians
    object.scale(size)Set uniform size
    object.scale(x, y, z)Set non-uniform size
    object.move(x, y, z)Add to position
    object.turn(x, y, z)Add to rotation
    object.color("#RRGGBB")Set color
    object.show() / object.hide()Change visibility
    object.remove()Permanently remove the object
    object.visibleCurrent visibility

    Mutation methods return the object so calls can be chained.

    The standard primitives all use shared indexed meshes:

    Available constructors are box, plane, sphere, cylinder, cone, and capsule. Each accepts position, rotation, size, color, material, and visible.

    Custom Meshes#

    Create reusable indexed or non-indexed triangle meshes:

    positions, normals, and textureCoordinates accept nested vectors or flat number lists. Normals are optional and generated from the triangles when omitted. Invalid indices, incomplete triangles, zero normals, degenerate geometry, and mismatched attribute counts fail explicitly.

    Meshes expose vertexCount, indexCount, and remove(). A mesh cannot be removed while an object uses it. Use counterclockwise winding when looking at an outward-facing triangle. The Vulkan backend culls back faces; repeat a triangle with reversed winding when a surface must be visible from both sides.

    Materials And Textures#

    The standard material model uses glTF-compatible metallic/roughness PBR:

    Material options are:

    • color

    • texture

    • metallic from 0 to 1

    • roughness from 0 to 1

    • emissive

    • emissiveStrength

    • unlit

    object.material(material) changes an existing object. Textures decode PNG and JPEG files, upload into device-local image storage, use linear sampling, and expose width, height, and remove(). In-use materials and textures cannot be removed.

    Scene Lighting#

    Scenes retain ambient, directional, point, and spot lighting:

    The renderer uses up to four active lights per scene. A scene with no explicit lights receives a useful default sun. Lights support position, direction, and remove().

    GLB And glTF Models#

    Load a complete static model directly into a scene:

    The loader validates GLB/glTF data, buffers, indexed triangle primitives, vertex positions, normals, texture coordinates, node transforms, embedded or external images, and metallic/roughness materials. Missing normals are generated. model.remove() removes its objects and releases the imported meshes, materials, and textures.

    Toolkit GLB And glTF Preview#

    The Toolkit opens .glb and .gltf files in model tabs alongside images and video. Drag inside the viewport to orbit; use the mouse wheel to zoom and Reset view to restore the camera. The inspector offers:

    • Hierarchy: expand object branches and check or uncheck their visibility. Hiding a parent hides its descendants while preserving their own checkboxes.

    • Textures: inspect image sources, dimensions, and a thumbnail.

    • Materials: inspect base colors, texture assignments, metallic/roughness values, alpha mode, and sidedness.

    • Geometries: inspect mesh vertex, triangle, primitive, and morph counts.

    • Animations: select a named clip or return to the rest pose. The viewport also provides an animation dropdown, play/pause, a scrubber, loop, and speed.

    • Info: inspect the format, generator, and model totals.

    Small windows expose these sections through an Inspector menu. Animation pauses when leaving a model tab. Closing or reloading releases native resources.

    The preview uses native C software rendering into the Toolkit canvas without a second graphics window or Vulkan. It supports triangle geometry with base-color materials and textures, node transforms, skeletal skinning, and position morphs. Animation supports STEP, LINEAR (including quaternion interpolation), and CUBICSPLINE channels. It does not provide the graphics module's full PBR lighting. Relative local buffers and PNG/JPEG/WebP textures, embedded resources, and data URIs work in .gltf files; network resource loading is disabled. Local assets must stay beneath the selected model's directory: absolute paths, parent traversal (including URI-encoded traversal), symbolic links and Windows reparse points are rejected. Keep related buffers and textures in that directory or its subfolders. The EXT_texture_webp extension resolves WebP sources for rendering and material inspection, including files without a standard PNG/JPEG texture source. WebP texture sources up to 16 megapixels decode directly to a preview within the 4-megapixel image budget; ordinary Image decode limits stay unchanged.

    Limits include a 64 MiB input file, 256 MiB model memory budget, 4,096 nodes, 128 clips, 32 images, 1,024 primitives, and 500,000 vertices and triangles. Each software render is also limited to a one-megapixel cache and 16,777,216 triangle bounding-box pixel visits. Models that exceed the work budget produce a recoverable preview error instead of keeping the UI busy indefinitely.

    Applications can use the same UI primitive directly:

    ui.drawModel takes optional finite yaw (-1000..1000), pitch (-1.5..1.5), zoom (0.1..20), and background (#RGB, #RRGGBB, or #RRGGBBAA) values. model.pose(clipIndex, seconds) samples an animation; pose(-1, 0) restores the rest pose. Playback timing belongs to the caller. setVisible(nodeIndex, Bool) and resetVisibility() control hierarchy visibility. nodeTransform(nodeIndex) returns a column-major world matrix. texture(imageIndex) returns an independent Image that the caller closes.

    Model exposes nodes, animations, materials, textures, and geometries as lists of metadata maps, along with format, generator, nodeCount, animationCount, materialCount, textureCount, skinCount, meshCount, vertexCount, triangleCount, visibleTriangleCount, and closed. close() is idempotent. ui.modelPreviewVersion >= 2 identifies this API.

    Cameras#

    Camera methods are position, target, lookAt, up, moveForward, moveRight, and moveUp. camera.up(x, y, z) sets the view's up direction and returns the camera. It accepts a finite, nonzero vector and normalizes it. The optional up creation field defaults to [0, 1, 0]; a banked aircraft can supply its body up vector. If up is parallel to the viewing direction, the renderer uses a perpendicular fallback to keep the view valid. moveRight uses world up; moveUp moves along world Y. The type option currently accepts "perspective" and defaults to it when omitted. A camera belongs to its scene and cannot draw another scene.

    Orbit Camera#

    For model viewers, editors, and scene inspection:

    orbitControls uses left-button dragging to orbit and the mouse wheel to zoom. Pitch is clamped before the camera can flip over, and zoom keeps a safe minimum distance from the target.

    Scripted controls are also available:

    MethodMeaning
    camera.orbit(yaw, pitch, distance)Set an absolute orbit around the current target
    camera.orbitBy(yaw, pitch, zoom)Add rotation and zoom; positive zoom moves closer
    camera.zoom(amount)Positive moves closer; negative moves away
    camera.orbitControls(app)Apply default mouse orbit and wheel zoom controls

    Input#

    Input state is updated by app.frame():

    Available input:

    • app.keyDown(key) and app.keyPressed(key);

    • letters, digits, space, escape, enter, tab, arrows, shift, control, and backspace;

    • app.mouseDown(button) and app.mousePressed(button) for left, right, and middle;

    • app.mouseX, app.mouseY, app.mouseDeltaX, app.mouseDeltaY, and app.mouseWheel.

    Down means currently held. Pressed means the transition happened during the current frame.

    For native controller input, call gamepad.poll() once inside this frame loop. See gamepads for button presses/releases, sticks, triggers, and the standalone C interface.

    Conventions#

    • Positive Y is up.

    • Positions and sizes are world units.

    • Rotations are radians.

    • Colors are #RRGGBB.

    • Common creation uses named option maps.

    • Nouns create resources; short verbs change or draw them.

    • Queues, descriptors, command buffers, image views, render passes, and presentation chains are backend details and absent from SIPL.

    Ownership And Safety#

    Graphics resources are opaque typed values, not integer handles. Every resource records its owning application and slot generation. Removed resources, resources from another scene, and resources retained after close fail explicitly.

    Closing the application waits for outstanding GPU work and releases all native resources. Current bounds are 32 scenes, 4096 objects, 128 cameras, 256 meshes, 256 materials, 256 textures, 128 lights, and 64 models per application.

    Scene Inspection And Smoke Checks#

    Run tests/graphics/scene_smoke.sipl normally to inspect its scene. Drag with the left mouse button to orbit, scroll to zoom, and close the window or press Escape to exit. Add --smoke to run its resource checks and close after four frames:

    Keep calling app.frame() while a graphics window is open. A console input() pause before or inside that loop blocks window event processing and rendering. Use window input such as app.keyPressed("escape") to exit a scene viewer.

    On Windows, run the desktop resize regression with:

    It verifies rendered-frame progress across maximise/restore/minimise and closes while minimised, in normal and GC-stress modes. A test runtime linked with tests/graphics/resize_faults_win32.c can be supplied as --fault-runtime to force out-of-date swapchain creation and a temporary zero-sized surface. Resize recovery retries these transient conditions while still handling native close and restore events.

    Automatic Batching#

    Object submissions are accumulated in a dynamically sized mapped instance buffer and grouped by mesh and texture. The backend emits one indexed instanced draw per used mesh/texture pair instead of one GPU command per object. Retained draws also reject objects outside the camera frustum before submission.

    Run the stress benchmark with an optional object count and frame limit:

    The default is 200,000 independently rotating, deterministically colored objects. It reports FPS and object transforms per second. This remains a deliberately severe CPU-side test: SIPL still executes the loop and computes every object's transform each frame, while automatic batching removes the GPU-command bottleneck.

    Platform Requirements#

    Windows/Linux graphics applications require a compatible Vulkan graphics driver. Windows users do not need the Vulkan SDK. Linux desktop applications also require an X11 or XWayland session. macOS builds use Apple Metal and a Cocoa window, enabled in every standard build; no Vulkan SDK or translation library is required. Native Mac execution still needs Mac acceptance. Check graphics.available before offering an optional 3D feature; device or display failures are reported when graphics.open() is called.

    Keep the shader files distributed with SIPL beside sipl and packaged graphics executables when moving them to another folder. Programs locate these files relative to the executable rather than the working directory. This shader deployment requirement applies to Vulkan builds. The Mac executable embeds its Metal shader source and compiles it through the system Metal framework on open.

    Next Layers#

    The remaining production layers are multiple frames in flight, transparent object sorting and alpha modes, shadow maps, glTF animation and skinning, and generic shader, target, and pass APIs for advanced work.

    The high-level API remains the normal path. Advanced controls will use generic resource and pass terminology rather than exposing the backend API.

    Native audio playback#

    SIPL's native audio module provides bounded WAV, Ogg/Vorbis and MP3 decoding, portable output selection, and one-shot/loop playback. Use audio.stream(path) for music, audiobooks and long local files. It reads and decodes chunks in a C worker into a fixed one-second PCM queue. The audio callback consumes that queue without file I/O, allocation, locks, or SIPL callbacks. audio.open() and AudioApp.load/decode remain available for predecoded short effects and mixing. Native microphone recording and bounded offline synthesis/effects/mixdown are available as described below. Network audio streams are not included. Video playback is described separately in VIDEO.md.

    Opening/enumerating hardware and reading/decoding files are synchronous control work. AudioApp.load predecodes a clip before an interactive/async playback loop; audio.stream provides chunked file playback. Playback itself runs independently of SIPL execution. No sound is played until play() is requested. Closing the application stops all owned sounds.

    Streaming music and long files#

    The sleep above keeps the console program alive. It does not feed the decoder: playback and native looping continue even when SIPL is busy. GUI applications use the same controls from their ordinary event loop. Prism is a complete single-file music/video player using this API.

    audio.stream(path: String, options?) -> AudioStream opens a local, Unicode-aware regular file, validates its format and duration, primes a small block and starts a native decoder worker. Playback starts paused. Options accept headless: Bool, with the same SIPL_AUDIO default as audio.open. Hardware uses the system default device; custom backend/device selection is currently available through AudioApp only. Initialization and seeks are synchronous control operations; ongoing chunk reads and decoding run in C, never in a SIPL refill loop.

    Supported formats are RIFF/WAVE, MP3 and Ogg/Vorbis. A file may contain up to 2 GiB and 24 hours of audio. These streaming limits are independent of the 16 MiB encoded / 64 MiB PCM clip limits. PCM queue and decode-block storage are always 416,768 bytes (about 407 KiB), with up to 32 MiB of separate decoder scratch, plus device/native bookkeeping. Encoded input is read from disk in chunks. At most eight streams may remain open. audio.info() exposes streaming, openStreams, maxStreams, maxStreamFileBytes, maxStreamSeconds and streamPCMBytes alongside the clip/mixer limits.

    Streams expose play, pause, stop, seek(Duration) and idempotent close, with the same control meanings as sounds below. loop, volume (0..4), and pan (-1..1) are writable. Looping refills across the boundary in C; disabling it flushes any prefetched next-cycle audio. Read-only properties are playing, closed, headless, position, duration, frames, sampleRate (48000), channels (2), and pcmBytes (zero after close). Duration may be refined by a few frames at EOF because of resampler rounding. Positions represent consumed PCM, so buffering does not advance the playback clock. Seeking to the end stops; play() at the end restarts the track. A stopped/failed device reports a catchable error rather than silently switching output.

    Explicit headless streams provide render(frames) and advance(Duration) for deterministic tests, using the same native decoder and PCM consumer. Their output format, request bounds and fractional-frame carry match the corresponding AudioApp APIs below. In headless mode, these explicit operations advance time; sleeping does not. Decoder errors can surface during a later control/property query or render, since streaming does not validate the entire file upfront.

    Close joins the decoder worker and output device before freeing memory. Native state is cleaned up on GC and ordinary process exit. The full decoder budget is reserved in GC pressure on the control thread; workers never access the VM. Closing is recommended when changing tracks rather than waiting for collection.

    Output and discovery#

    • audio.info() -> Map: compiled codecs/backends, canonical PCM format and hard resource limits. Compiled support does not imply an installed output device.

    • audio.devices(options?) -> List[Map]: enumerate outputs on the selected backend; each entry has id, name, backend and isDefault.

    • audio.open(options?) -> AudioApp: start a stereo output app. Options are headless: Bool, sampleRate: Int (8000..192000, default 48000), maxSounds: Int (1..64, default 32), maxPCMBytes: Int (8..256 MiB, default 64 MiB), backend: String (default "auto") and device: String.

    Device enumeration accepts only headless and backend. Select a returned ID with the same backend:

    IDs are opaque and backend/session-specific, not persistent identifiers. Refresh enumeration after device changes. auto uses the platform's default output; an unavailable backend/device fails catchably and never becomes headless silently. Output stop/interruption notifications cause playback/position queries and controls to fail catchably instead of waiting forever on a lost callback; check the device and reopen the app. Automatic device recovery is not a beta feature. The null backend is not compiled. Hardware unplug/recovery, latency qualification, and device interoperability need testing on the actual release targets.

    The compiled output backends are WASAPI and WinMM on Windows; ALSA and PulseAudio on Linux; Core Audio on macOS. Linux loads installed backend libraries at runtime. Headless mode needs no device libraries. Windows and Linux are the beta build/test targets; the Core Audio path is present but not hardware-qualified in this workspace.

    SIPL_AUDIO=headless explicitly requests headless defaults; SIPL_AUDIO=device requests ordinary defaults. A supplied headless option overrides the environment. Any other nonempty environment value fails. Headless apps cannot also select a hardware backend/device. Enumeration in explicitly headless mode returns one synthetic PCM output.

    Sound loading and controls#

    app.load(path: String, options?) -> AudioSound uses the bounded, Unicode-aware binary filesystem reader. app.decode(data: Bytes, options?) -> AudioSound decodes immutable bytes without retaining the encoded input. Both accept maxSeconds: Int (1..600, default 120) and maxPCMBytes: Int (8..64 MiB, default 64 MiB). The duration, PCM, app and global limits are all enforced; increasing one does not bypass the others. Decoding converts to the app sample rate and interleaved float32 stereo off the real-time thread.

    Sound operation/propertyMeaning
    play()Resume; restart at frame zero if positioned at the end.
    pause()Pause without changing position.
    stop()Stop and reset position to zero.
    seek(position: Duration)Nonnegative position through duration, rounded to the nearest frame; seeking to the end stops playback.
    close()Idempotently retire the sound and release its decoded PCM safely.
    volume: NumberMutable finite gain 0..4, default 1.
    pan: NumberMutable finite stereo balance -1..1, default 0; attenuates the opposite channel, not equal-power panning.
    loop: BoolMutable looping, default false; exact end wraps to frame zero.
    playing, closedRead-only playback/lifecycle flags.
    duration, positionRead-only Duration, quantized to sample frames.
    frames, sampleRate, channelsRead-only decoded frame count, app sample rate and 2 channels.

    Mixing sums voices then clamps output to [-1,1]. Hardware control commands apply in order on an output callback; playback position snapshots can lag by one callback. playing reflects queued play/pause/stop requests immediately until the callback acknowledges them, then reflects actual completion. Control setters report the requested value immediately. A full 256-command queue fails catchably instead of growing or blocking the callback; retry after an output callback. Closing a sound does not require a queue slot.

    App read-only properties are closed, headless, sampleRate, channels, backend, device, framesRendered, elapsed: Duration, soundCount and pcmBytes. app.close() is idempotent. Playback/decode/render/control calls on a closed owner fail; sound closed becomes true even if its own close() was not called. Immutable sound metadata remains readable after close; playing becomes false and position reads zero.

    Deterministic headless PCM#

    Headless is a real decoder/mixer with no hardware thread, not a playback stub. render(frames: Int) -> Bytes advances the mixer and returns canonical little-endian IEEE-754 float32 stereo samples. Each request accepts 0..2097152 frames, at most 16 MiB. advance(duration: Duration) -> Int advances without allocating PCM output, accepting 0..60 seconds per call. Fractional frames carry across advance calls so splitting a duration does not discard time. render adds whole frames without discarding that fractional carry. Both calls are headless-only. Controls apply immediately in headless mode.

    elapsed and sound position use rendered sample counts, not a wall clock. Sleeping, async timers or test.advanceTime() do not automatically advance a headless app. This makes tests repeatable even when the wall clock is changed.

    Bounds, codecs and lifetime#

    For predecoded clips there may be at most 8 open apps, 64 loaded sounds per app, 16 MiB encoded input, 64 MiB decoded PCM per sound, 256 MiB PCM per app and 512 MiB decoded PCM across apps. Decoder scratch heap allocations are capped at 32 MiB. Decode temporarily holds the bounded encoded input, scratch and PCM allocation; render can use a bounded 16 MiB native buffer plus its 16 MiB returned Bytes. These are intentional predecode limits. Use audio.stream for long music playback.

    Supported containers are ordinary little-endian RIFF/WAVE; one complete, CRC-validated Ogg/Vorbis logical stream (1..8 channels); and complete standard MPEG-1/2/2.5 Layer III MP3 frames, CBR or VBR, with ID3v2/ID3v1/APE metadata. RF64/RIFX, Ogg/Opus, chained/multiplexed Ogg, legacy Vorbis floor-0 files and free-format MP3 are not beta codecs. RIFF chunk boundaries, Ogg page sequence, checksums/EOS and MP3 frame/tag bounds are checked before decoding. Malformed, truncated, empty, oversized and non-finite-PCM inputs fail catchably. File access failures keep the normal filesystem failure kind; decoder/control failures use the runtime failure kind. Unknown option keys fail, including embedded NULs.

    The callback owns mixer state; all callback-visible atomics must be lock-free. It does no allocation/free, locks, file I/O, user callbacks or SIPL/GC access. Immutable native PCM is published through a bounded single-producer/consumer command queue. Closing/GC requests generation-tagged retirement; only the control thread frees/reuses PCM after callback acknowledgement. Native refcounts retain owner state independently of GC sweep order. Closing an app or normal process exit stops/joins hardware callbacks before reclaiming PCM. Explicit close remains recommended: real-device retirement may wait for the next output callback, and GC is not an immediate resource-management policy. Persistent backend/PCM storage is charged to GC pressure without reallocating callback-visible pointers; accounting changes and reclamation stay on the control thread. Closing an app immediately releases heavy backend storage even when a closed wrapper or sound metadata is retained.

    Tests and dependencies#

    Run sipl test tests/test_audio_stream.sipl --jobs 2, python3 tests/audio_stream_tests.py build/sipl, sipl test tests/test_audio.sipl --jobs 2 and python3 tests/audio_tests.py build/sipl (use build/sipl.exe on Windows). Tests cover real WAV/OGG/MP3 PCM, an independent WAV numeric oracle, sine-wave spectral checks, malformed/truncated containers, bounds, controls, mock-clock independence, normal/GC ownership, slot reuse, recipes and standalone packaging. The Python driver also builds native concurrent callback/control/retirement stress tests if a C compiler is available.

    On supported Unix hosts, SIPL_AUDIO_SANITIZE=1 enables ASan/UBSan for the native stress driver. Under ptrace-based tool sandboxes, LeakSanitizer may be unavailable; ASAN_OPTIONS=detect_leaks=0 preserves address/undefined-behavior checks, not a claim of leak-sanitizer coverage. Physical output has not been verified by these headless tests.

    The runtime vendors miniaudio 0.11.25 and stb_vorbis 1.22, with upstream revision, source hashes and licenses in third_party/miniaudio/README.md and third_party/stb/README_AUDIO.md. File audio uses those native decoders; no codec subprocess is required. Video uses its separate static FFmpeg backend. Original regression fixture generation is documented in tests/fixtures/audio/README.md. See also sipl api audio --json, sipl api AudioApp --json, sipl api AudioSound --json, sipl api AudioStream --json, and examples/recipes/audio.sipl.

    Native recording and offline production#

    audio.record(path, options?) -> AudioRecording creates a new PCM16 WAV without overwriting an existing file and starts capture from the system default microphone. Options: sampleRate 8000–192000 (default 44100), channels 1–2 (default 1), maxSeconds 1–600 (default 120), and explicit headless (default false). Microphone capture does not inherit a headless playback environment. Two captures may be open concurrently. No input device selection API is provided in this first implementation; use system input settings.

    Read active, closed, headless, sampleRate, channels, frames, position: Duration, and peak (latest captured block, 0–1). stop() / close() join the device and writer and finalize the WAV header. Duration limits stop capture automatically; call stop/close to finalize and release resources. GC and ordinary process exit also finalize captures. Abrupt process termination cannot guarantee a finalized header. Disk/input failures report an error at stop; a partial WAV is retained. Physical device timing and recovery need hardware qualification on each platform.

    The capture callback copies finite/clamped PCM into a fixed 65,536-frame ring; only the writer thread performs WAV I/O. Producer overruns fail explicitly. Headless captures expose write(Bytes) for deterministic tests: interleaved float32 little-endian input, frame-aligned, at most 2 MiB per call. This method is unavailable on hardware captures. A record error is never replaced by silence or a synthetic input device.

    audio.importFile(source, target) -> Map decodes a WAV/MP3/Ogg-Vorbis local file, at most 120 seconds, into a new stereo PCM16 WAV at 48 kHz. It returns file, seconds, peaks (128 amplitude maxima), peak and tracks (empty for imports). It uses the existing bounded file decoder. WAV input formats retain the decoder's existing supported format rules; malformed inputs fail.

    audio.renderSession(session, target) -> Map creates a new stereo PCM16 WAV at 48 kHz. The synchronous API is intended for CLI jobs or a SIPL worker process, not an audio callback. Limits are 12 tracks, 16 bars, 40–240 BPM, 120 seconds, 32 clips per track, and 128 metering bins. Buffers are bounded to three stereo float32 session arrays (about 132 MiB at 120 seconds), plus existing decoder scratch. Native synth/mixer rendering does not open a hardware device.

    A session Map has tempo, whole bars, master (dB, -48..6) and tracks. Each track has a unique positive Int id, an instrument kind from audio.instruments() or audio, gain (-48..12 dB), pan (-1..1 balance), mute, solo, note (MIDI 0..127), steps (16 velocities, 0..1), fx, and clips. Effects are low, mid, high (-18..18 dB) and compress, drive, delay, reverb (0..1). Missing numeric controls take their native defaults; required track/clip collections must still be supplied. A clip supplies a file path, start, source offset and length, measured in beats. Files are decoded only when rendering an audible audio track. Synth patterns repeat for every bar.

    Tracks optionally supply mode (steps or notes, default steps) and notes (at most 512 Maps). Each note has start (0..64 beats), length (.0625..16 beats), whole MIDI pitch (0..127), and velocity (0..1). In notes mode the renderer plays the note list instead of the repeating steps. Notes may overlap for chords; releases can extend past the gate and are cropped at the session end. Notes outside the current arrangement are retained but not rendered. A track may accumulate at most 600 seconds of audible note gates plus a conservative 1.1 seconds of release per note, bounding offline voice work. Invalid pitches, velocities, modes and excess note counts fail before writing output.

    audio.instruments() -> List[Map] enumerates 64 native presets with stable id, display name and category. These are additive/FM/noise synthesis definitions, not sample files. The original kick, snare, hat, bass and chord pad remain available. Acoustic names describe synthesized approximations. Definitions are in src/audio_instruments.def; voices are in src/audio_synth.inc.

    audio.synthesize(kind, pitch, options?) -> Bytes produces a new in-memory stereo PCM16 WAV at 48 kHz. kind is a catalog ID; pitch is a whole MIDI 0..127. Options are seconds (.03..4 gate seconds, default .35) and velocity (0..1, default .8). The preset's release follows the gate, up to 1.1 additional seconds. Decode these Bytes with an AudioApp to audition them without disk files:

    Keep the app/sound alive while playing; close them after use. Synthesis is synchronous and bounded to less than 4 MiB of temporary native buffers. It does not open a device, and silent velocity produces silence. The per-note audition has no channel effects. audio.info().instrumentVersion is 2 for this API set.

    EQ uses the bundled miniaudio low shelf at 220 Hz, peak at 1100 Hz (Q .7), and high shelf at 4 kHz. Compression blends a -18 dB / 4:1 envelope compressor (5 ms attack, 80 ms release); drive is tanh saturation. Delay adds four decaying eighth-note taps; room reverb adds seven short stereo diffusion taps. Effects are applied before per-track gain/pan and summing. The returned master peak is measured before [-1,1] output clamping; peaks and tracks contain actual rendered amplitude bins (track bins are after track gain/pan).

    Output Maps include file, seconds, peak, peaks and a tracks Map keyed by decimal track ID. Render/import never overwrite an existing target. Render to a temporary file, then publish it after success when an application needs replacement semantics. File write failures may leave an identifiable partial target. No audio effect callbacks enter SIPL or the GC.

    Copperline Studio demonstrates these APIs without Python or an external audio processor. It is an initial workstation, with rendered effects and unqualified hardware overdub timing, not a VST host or sample-accurate production DAW.

    Gamepads#

    SIPL's gamepad module reads controllers in native C, independently of UI, graphics, Vulkan, and SDL. Windows uses XInput plus native WinMM input for DualShock 4 controllers; Linux uses nonblocking evdev. Other platforms report gamepad.info()["supported"] == false and return empty input state. No new build dependencies or link libraries are required.

    Call gamepad.poll() once per game tick, then read any controls you need:

    app.frame() does not poll controllers automatically. The module also works with ui.frame() loops and programs without a window. Polling never waits for input. It uses fixed native storage; reading buttons and axes allocates no SIPL collections.

    FunctionResult
    gamepad.poll()Refresh all slots and reset the previous tick's edges
    gamepad.connected(index)Whether the slot has a controller
    gamepad.justConnected(index)Whether it connected during this poll
    gamepad.justDisconnected(index)Whether it disconnected during this poll
    gamepad.name(index)Device name; empty when disconnected
    gamepad.buttonDown(index, button)Whether the button is held
    gamepad.buttonPressed(index, button)Whether the button went down during this poll
    gamepad.buttonReleased(index, button)Whether the button went up during this poll
    gamepad.axis(index, axis, deadzone?)Normalized axis value, with a default deadzone of 0.15
    gamepad.info()Map with backend, supported, and maxGamepads
    gamepad.close()Release handles and clear state; safe to call repeatedly

    Indices are 0..3. Unknown controls and invalid indices raise catchable errors. State starts empty until the first poll. Edges remain available through repeated reads until the next poll. A controller connected with a held button reports that button as pressed. Disconnecting releases all held buttons and zeros all axes. Calling another input function after close() creates fresh empty state; native handles are also released at process exit.

    Buttons use Xbox-style names for their physical positions:

    NamesControls
    a, b, x, ySouth, east, west, north face buttons
    leftShoulder, rightShoulderShoulder buttons
    leftStick, rightStickPressing each stick
    back, startSelect/menu buttons
    up, down, left, rightD-pad directions

    Axes are leftX, leftY, rightX, rightY, leftTrigger, and rightTrigger. Sticks range from -1 to 1, positive right/down on both platforms. Triggers range from 0 to 1. Deadzones must be finite numbers greater than or equal to 0 and less than 1. Values inside the deadzone become zero; the remaining range is rescaled to reach 1 at full deflection. Pass 0 for raw normalized values. Deadzones are applied per axis; games can read raw axes to implement a circular stick deadzone.

    Windows supports XInput-compatible controllers in the four XInput player slots. DualShock 4 controllers that report Sony's USB/Bluetooth v1, v2, or wireless adapter IDs (054c:05c4, 054c:09cc, 054c:0ba0) use the native WinMM joystick API and occupy available slots. This includes compatible PS4 controllers that report those IDs. No controller emulation software is required. Windows loads the system XInput and WinMM DLLs dynamically; backend is xinput+winmm. Other DirectInput layouts and rumble are not currently supported. Both Windows paths provide snapshots, so transitions entirely between polls cannot be observed. Poll at your game rate. PS4 connections are scanned once per second.

    On PS4 controllers, a is Cross, b is Circle, x is Square, y is Triangle, back is Share, and start is Options. Shoulders are L1/R1, stick buttons are L3/R3, and trigger axes are L2/R2. The D-pad includes diagonal directions. If an XInput player reconnects into a PS4's slot, the old slot publishes a disconnect before replacement, and the PS4 moves to a free slot when available. Games should select a connected slot and reselect after a disconnection.

    Linux discovers standard gamepads among /dev/input/event0 through event63, scanning for connections at most once per second. Slots stay assigned while a controller remains connected and may be reused after disconnection. The user running SIPL must have read access to the controller's evdev node; devices absent from the environment, including those not forwarded into WSL, cannot be read. The backend follows the Linux gamepad mapping, including digital or hat D-pads, standard stick axes, analog triggers on ABS_Z/ABS_RZ or ABS_HAT2Y/ABS_HAT2X, and digital trigger fallbacks. Legacy devices with nonstandard mappings need driver configuration. Linux preserves button edges from multiple input packets within a poll, limits reads to 1024 kernel events per slot per poll, and resynchronizes after queue overflow.

    The macOS implementation uses Apple's system GameController framework for controllers with an extended gamepad profile. Up to four slots retain their assignments until disconnect; a retired slot publishes a disconnect before reuse. Buttons and axes use the same SIPL names and ranges. Call poll() at the game's update rate; transitions entirely between snapshots are not retained. Native device acceptance is described in MACOS.md.

    For deterministic runs without hardware access, set SIPL_GAMEPAD=headless. The default is device. info().supported describes the compiled platform, not the presence of a controller or the current user's device permissions.

    Native C interface#

    src/gamepad_backend.h exposes the backend without depending on SIPL's VM:
