    Call this interface on one thread. States are owned by the context and valid until it is closed. Native axis values have no deadzone; the SIPL binding applies the requested deadzone. sipl_gamepad_open(false) disables hardware access.

    Run make test-gamepad for native input fixtures, SIPL validation, GC stress, packaging, and API discovery checks. Physical hardware qualification is separate.

    Native video playback#

    SIPL uses a statically linked, decoder-only FFmpeg 9.0.2 build with dav1d 1.5.3 for AV1. Windows and Linux use the same player and decoder allowlist. No FFmpeg executable, FFmpeg DLL, system codec pack, Vulkan device, or network access is needed for playback. Miniaudio remains the audio device backend: FFmpeg decodes and resamples audio; miniaudio sends stereo PCM to the operating system.

    The Toolkit opens .mp4, .webm, and .mkv files, including uppercase suffixes, in reusable, read-only media tabs with controls enabled. Leaving a video tab pauses it. Reload and close release its decoder and audio device. SIPL chooses the tab from the extension; C inspects the bytes and selects the actual container and codecs. Renaming a WebM file to .mp4 does not change its decoder.

    Supported content#

    LayerIncluded
    ContainersMP4; WebM; Matroska/MKV
    Video decodersH.264/AVC; HEVC/H.265; VP9; AV1 through dav1d
    Audio decodersAAC; Opus; video without audio
    OutputSDR RGBA software frames; stereo float audio at 48 kHz

    A container can hold codecs outside this list. For example, an MKV containing MPEG-4 Part 2, Vorbis, MP3, AC-3, or DTS is rejected with an unsupported-codec error. A present but unsupported audio track is an error, rather than silently discarded audio. FFmpeg's MOV/MP4 demuxer also contains QuickTime parsing internally; the Toolkit's accepted extensions remain exactly MP4, WebM, and MKV.

    Encoding, muxing, CLI tools, networking, capture devices, filters, and hardware decoders are disabled. The player supports square/non-square pixels and 90-degree display rotation. HDR PQ/HLG and changing resolution are rejected. Subtitles, track selection, arbitrary display transforms, color-managed/HDR output, streaming, recording, and video editing are outside this initial playback implementation.

    API#

    video.open(path, options?) and ui.loadVideo(path, options?) are equivalent. Loading decodes the first frame and leaves playback paused. Options are Bool:

    OptionDefaultMeaning
    controlsfalseShow native play/pause, seek, time, and mute controls
    autoplayfalseBegin playback after loading
    loopfalseRestart when an observed playback snapshot reaches the end
    mutedfalseStart with silent output
    headlessSIPL_UI=headlessAdvance the audio clock without opening a device

    ui.drawVideo(x, y, width, height, clip) draws in the active frame, preserves the display aspect ratio, and letterboxes in black. Coordinates and dimensions are Int logical pixels; coordinates must be within ±16,384 and sizes within 0..16,384. Controls occupy 40 pixels at the bottom. Small rectangles hide controls that do not fit: all controls below 100×64, mute below width 280, seek/time below width 360. Controls use the UI's clipping, DPI scaling, and pointer input. An optional sixth argument, {"enabled": false}, disables control input while keeping the controls visible. The Toolkit uses it behind menus and dialogs.

    Video methods:

    • play(), pause(), stop(); stop pauses and seeks to zero.

    • seek(position: Duration); requires 0 <= position <= duration. Seeking is synchronous and decodes forward from a preceding keyframe. The first displayed frame is at or after the target, within the video's frame cadence.

    • frame() -> Image; copies the current RGBA frame. It follows the Image limit of 4,194,304 pixels; larger videos can be drawn directly but cannot be copied into an Image through this method.

    • close(); idempotent, stops and joins the decoder worker and audio callback.

    Read-only properties: width, height (display dimensions), duration, position (Duration), playing, ended, hasAudio, and closed. Mutable properties: controls, muted, loop (Bool), and volume (finite Number from 0 to 1). video.info() reports the backend/version, decoder names, limits, and open count. Garbage collection and process exit also release players; explicitly close unused players to release devices and stay within the open-player limit.

    Ownership and limits#

    Only local, nonempty regular files are accepted. Limits are 2 GiB per file, 24 hours, 32 streams, 16,384 per display dimension, 8,294,400 display pixels shared across open players, and four open players. Individual decode contexts also cap decoded pixels. Initial open/probe and seek have a 10-second interrupt deadline; this is cooperative and cannot interrupt an individual codec instruction.

    A worker owns the FFmpeg contexts, reads bounded frame queues, and performs decode/conversion. The UI consumes three queued RGBA frames and keeps one display frame. Rotation requires one additional scratch frame. Audio uses a one-second stereo ring and one bounded conversion block. The device callback performs no allocation, VM work, file I/O, or mutex locking. PCM consumption drives the video clock; underflow buffers playback, delayed audio tracks insert streamed silence, and decoder/resampler tails are drained. Pause and seek synchronize the worker and device before buffers are reset or released.

    Persistent frame/PCM buffers contribute to GC pressure. FFmpeg/dav1d internal scratch allocations are additional memory and do not have a separate aggregate allocator cap; these bounds are not a sandbox for hostile files. Decode errors, unsupported media, and audio-device failures are reported as SIPL errors. Normal audio output does not silently switch to headless mode if a device cannot open.

    Building#

    Source pins and archive hashes are in third_party/ffmpeg/SIPL_PIN.md and third_party/dav1d/SIPL_PIN.md. Complete upstream sources are retained unchanged; only the selected features are compiled. The common allowlist is scripts/ffmpeg_video_options.txt. Dependency builds do not download anything. SIMD and CPU dispatch remain enabled for playback performance.

    Linux development requirements: a C/C++ toolchain, GNU Make, pkg-config, Python 3, Meson, Ninja, and NASM. Install them with the host's development package manager, then run make (plus the project's existing network/X11 build dependencies). scripts/build_video_deps.sh supports MESON, SIPL_BUILD_JOBS, and SIPL_VIDEO_BUILD_DIR; the Makefile's corresponding directory is VIDEO_DIR.

    macOS uses the same pinned codec sources and allowlist, Apple's C/C++ toolchain, CMake, pkg-config, Python 3, Meson and Ninja (plus NASM for Intel assembly). The build script supports the system Bash 3.2 and writes to build/video-macos by default. Core Audio/device playback requires native Mac acceptance.

    Windows development requirements: x64 MSVC, Git Bash, Python 3/Meson, Ninja, NASM, and MSYS GNU Make. Native Windows GNU Make has incompatible shell quoting for FFmpeg's dependency rules. Run build.bat; the dependency script shares its initialized MSVC environment. SIPL_VIDEO_PYTHON, SIPL_VIDEO_BASH, SIPL_VIDEO_MAKE, and SIPL_BUILD_JOBS can select tools. Ninja bundled with Visual Studio is detected. Local tools under build/video-tools are recognized when present; they are development tools, not runtime dependencies.

    Video is required in every desktop build. SIPL_VIDEO=0 is rejected; missing video build tools fail compilation. video.info()["available"] reports compiled support, and system.buildFeatures records it for build validation.

    Distribution#

    Packaged applications contain the selected decoder libraries in their executable. Ship the media files they open as application assets. The client still needs the ordinary operating-system UI/audio services; Vulkan is only needed by separate SIPL features that use it.

    The enabled FFmpeg profile is LGPL 2.1-or-later, with GPL/nonfree options disabled; dav1d is BSD 2-Clause. Static linkage does not remove license obligations. Include FFmpeg/dav1d notices and license texts and provide corresponding source and a usable rebuild/relink route for the distributed executable, following the included upstream licenses. This repository contains the pinned library sources, SIPL source, and build scripts for rebuilding the runtime. A binary-only toolkit download by itself is not a complete release compliance bundle. Preserve the application's SIPL source or other relink material as needed for packaged apps; the sipl build command does not assemble that release bundle automatically.

    Validation#

    tests/test_video.sipl, test_ui_video.sipl, and test_toolkit_videos.sipl cover native decoding, content detection, seeking, lifecycle/limits, controls and tab routing in normal and GC-stress modes. tests/video_backend_tests.c exercises threaded playback, seek/restart/close, all selected decoders, and the compiled decoder/demuxer/protocol allowlist. Test media and regeneration commands are in tests/fixtures/video. Headless tests establish decoded pixels, timing, and resource behavior; audible quality and real desktop/device behavior still need release-target qualification.

    Run python3 tests/video_tests.py build/sipl for the portable integration/package checks. On Linux, add --video-prefix build/video-linux/install --sanitize to compile the native player/profile and concurrent audio-callback tests with AddressSanitizer and UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer. These instrument SIPL's wrapper and audio code, not the prebuilt FFmpeg/dav1d archives. LeakSanitizer is disabled by the runner for hosts that execute tests under ptrace.

    PDF generation and viewing#

    The native pdf module creates PDF files on Windows, Linux and macOS without a browser or external process. It uses the vendored PDFGen C library, which is public domain. pdf.open() reads and renders pages through the pinned PDFium runtime installed beside SIPL by the build on Windows/Linux. The Mac implementation uses the system Core Graphics PDF engine instead. Toolkit opens a .pdf file in a read-only preview tab when selected, with page controls. Editing existing PDF files is outside this API.

    Coordinates and dimensions use PDF points (72 per inch). The origin is at the bottom left; text() positions the baseline. pdf.create(width, height, options?) sets the default page size. The optional Map accepts title, author, subject, and creator strings. addPage() appends a default-sized page; addPage(width, height) uses a custom size. Pages are numbered from 1, and selectPage(number) switches the target for later drawing. Drawing requires at least one page. width and height report the default size, and pageCount, currentPage, and closed report document state.

    setFont(name) selects a built-in PDF font such as Helvetica, Times-Roman, or Courier; setFontFile(path) embeds and selects a TrueType (.ttf) font. text(value, x, y, size, color?) adds one line. wrapText(value, x, y, size, width, align?, color?) returns the height it used; align is left, center, right, or justify. Colors are #RGB or #RRGGBB; omitted text color is black. For shapes, line(x1, y1, x2, y2, width, color), rect(x, y, width, height, color, filled?, borderWidth?), and circle(x, y, radius, color, filled?, borderWidth?) use the same point system.

    image(encodedBytes, x, y, width, height) embeds PNG or JPEG bytes. For an existing file, use fs.readBytes("photo.jpg"). For an Image value, encode RGB pixels first:

    PNG alpha is not supported by PDFGen; convert to RGB if transparency is present. save(path) writes a PDF file and overwrites an existing path. toBytes() returns the complete PDF as Bytes for APIs that accept bytes. Both require at least one page. close() releases the native document and is idempotent; the garbage collector also releases documents that are no longer reachable.

    Inputs are bounded: page dimensions are 1–14,400 points; documents may have up to 256 pages and 20,000 drawing calls. text() accepts 64 KiB per call, wrapText() accepts 511 bytes per call (PDFGen's fixed line buffer), and total text is limited to 4 MiB per document. Each encoded image is at most 8 MiB and 4 million pixels, with 16 MiB of encoded image data per document. Each TTF file is at most 8 MiB, with up to eight fonts and 16 MiB of font data per document. toBytes() follows the Bytes size limit of 16 MiB. Invalid arguments and PDFGen failures raise SIPL errors; check sipl api pdf and sipl api PdfDocument for exact signatures.

    Run the PDF recipe with an output path to generate a complete sample.

    Viewing PDFs#

    pdf.open(path) returns an owned PdfFile for an existing PDF. Pages use 1-based numbers. pageCount reports the number of pages; pageWidth(number) and pageHeight(number) return the page dimensions in points. render(number, width, height) rasterizes a page at the requested pixel size and returns an independent Image suitable for ui.drawImage() or saving. Close each rendered image and then PdfFile when finished:

    pdf.open() reads at most 64 MiB and supports 1–4,096 pages. A rendered image may have at most 4,194,304 pixels and follows the Image dimension limits. Password-protected, invalid, or unsupported PDFs raise a SIPL error, which Toolkit shows in the preview tab. On Windows/Linux, rendering uses PDFium's C API; the DLL or shared library must remain beside SIPL and Toolkit. Mac page-content rendering needs no adjacent library; interactive PDF forms and annotation overlays are not implemented on that path. See Mac acceptance and PDFium dependency notes for the pinned runtime and redistributable notices.

    AI in SIPL#

    Toolkit OpenAI agent#

    Toolkit has an expandable AI rail on its right edge. Open it by clicking the rail or choosing View → AI Agent. Configure the key and model in Tools → Settings → API keys, then write a message and press Ctrl+Enter or Send. Enter inserts a newline. Missing configuration offers Open Settings and keeps the current draft.

    The default model is gpt-6-astra. The model field is editable for accounts with different model access.

    The OpenAI and Google key fields are masked and can be remembered in an encrypted user or project config.enc file. Project settings override user defaults. The OpenAI field supplies the coding agent; the Google field supplies programs launched with Run through GEMINI_API_KEY and GOOGLE_API_KEY. Keys stay out of source files and command lines. See encrypted settings for locations and API contracts. When encrypted storage is unavailable, Settings offers Use for session.

    An empty OpenAI field can use an existing OPENAI_API_KEY environment value. The agent can create and edit files under the opened project. Attach active buffer is off by default; enable it to include that buffer with a request. See the agent workflow.

    Requests use the OpenAI Responses API with store: false. Escape cancels an active request. Request and response sizes are bounded, temporary key data is cleared after use, and captured output never includes the key.

    Conversation API#

    SIPL exposes a provider-neutral Ai conversation object:

    ai.google(model, options?) and ai.load(provider, model, options?) create the same Ai value. Google options are apiKey, endpoint, system, temperature, maxOutputTokens, and timeout. The API key is read from GEMINI_API_KEY, then GOOGLE_API_KEY, unless explicitly supplied. Keep keys out of source control; cloud requests send prompts to the selected provider and may incur charges.

    Conversations retain successful user and model turns. Call .reset() to clear that history. The endpoint option supports compatible gateways and local test servers.

    Chat window example#

    Set your Google key in the current shell and run the included chat example:

    The key is read from the environment and is not stored in the source file. The chat waits for each response before accepting the next message.

    Background Worker Jobs#

    The worker module runs one isolated tool or program job at a time while a SIPL interface remains responsive. Jobs report their combined output, exit code, cancellation state, and output-limit state through worker.result().

    API#

    • worker.start(executable?) creates the single background supervisor thread. By default child jobs use the current executable. A packaged development tool can provide a SIPL runtime path so its Run, Scan, Build, and Format jobs do not relaunch the packaged application. It is safe to call repeatedly; later calls are no-ops.

    • worker.scan(path) runs sipl check path: parse, load modules, and compile without running top-level initializers or start().

    • worker.pageCheck(path) runs sipl page-check path for one .sipl.html file or an entire private page directory.

    • worker.run(path, apiKeyEnvironment?) runs the program in a child SIPL process. Sources with top-level named tests or use test use sipl test (normal plus GC-stress supervision), so Toolkit Run handles test files correctly. Ordinary programs retain their normal output and arguments. Optional overrides are limited to OPENAI_API_KEY, GEMINI_API_KEY, and GOOGLE_API_KEY and apply only to that Run job. They are not command-line arguments or changes to the parent environment. See encrypted Toolkit settings for validation and examples.

    • worker.runPython(script, workingDirectory) runs a .py file with Python 3, captures standard output and standard error, reports the process exit code, and supports cancellation like other process jobs. It launches Python directly rather than through cmd, PowerShell, or a POSIX shell. Set SIPL_PYTHON to an explicit interpreter when needed. Otherwise Windows searches for py.exe, python3.exe, then python.exe; Linux and macOS search for python3, then python. Toolkit asks for confirmation before every Python run because the script has the user's normal OS permissions.

    • worker.build(path, output, pages?) runs sipl build in a child process. Give the optional private Pages folder to compile templates into the output.

    • worker.git(root, action, value?) runs a shell-free Git job in root. Supported actions are setup (initialize and add/update origin), status, pull (fast-forward only), commit (stage all and commit), push (publishes HEAD to origin and establishes its upstream), remote, publishPrivate, and publishPublic. The publish actions initialize and commit the project, then use the official GitHub CLI to create and push a new repository. Actions that need a URL, commit message, or repository name take value. Git credentials remain with Git Credential Manager, the SSH agent, or GitHub CLI; SIPL does not collect or store passwords or access tokens. The source-control sidebar also uses inspect, fetch, stage, unstage, stageAll, unstageAll, commitStaged, diff, diffStaged, and show. File actions require a literal repository-relative path; show requires a full commit hash. commitStaged commits the existing index without staging working-tree changes. inspect returns NUL-separated repository root and origin URL, then git status --porcelain=v1 --branch -z records, an empty record, and six fields per commit: full hash, short hash, full parent hashes, subject, author, and refs. History includes up to 100 commits from all refs. Missing origin and an unborn HEAD are valid empty fields.

    • worker.openai(apiKey, requestBody) performs a fixed OpenAI Responses API request. An empty key reads OPENAI_API_KEY. The key is never passed through a process command line or temporary file and is cleared when the request finishes. This operation currently supports HTTPS on Windows. Request JSON is capped at 4 MiB.

    • worker.format(path) runs sipl fmt path. Formatting mutates the file and

    is deliberately not cancellable.

    • Only one job may be pending or running. Submit another after the first job

    completes. This bounded design avoids unbounded process/thread creation.

    • worker.done() is a nonblocking completion check. worker.wait(milliseconds)

    blocks the caller and is intended for command-line programs and tests, not UI frame loops.

    • worker.result() requires a completed job and returns Result[Map]. The Map

    contains exitCode, output, cancelled, and outputTruncated. The output capture is capped at 8 MiB. A child exit with nonzero status is still an Ok result; inspect exitCode. Worker setup/runtime failures raise a catchable Fail.

    • worker.cancel() requests cancellation of the active scan, run, build, or Git job.

    On Unix it terminates the child process group; on Windows it terminates the child Job Object when the OS permits assignment. A pending job is cancelled before launch. Cancellation is cooperative only at the process boundary; it does not interrupt worker.format().

    • worker.stop() shuts down the supervisor, cancelling a pending/running scan

    or run and waiting for it to exit. A queued format may be discarded before it starts; an in-progress format is allowed to finish and is never killed. It is called automatically at process exit.

    • worker.isStarted and worker.isBusy are read-only status properties.

    UI Pattern#

    Never call worker.wait() from a window's frame loop. Submit once, keep rendering, and poll done() from the main thread as shown in the API example.

    toolkit/main.sipl uses this pattern for Run, Build, Scan, Format, and AI requests: input and redrawing continue while a job works, and output appears after completion.

    The toolkit's multi-step coding-agent loop and its separate project-confined workspace filesystem module are documented in AGENT.md.

    Scope#

    This is an asynchronous process-job API, not parallel execution of arbitrary SIPL functions. General-purpose worker.submit(fn, value) is not implemented. No async syntax is needed: worker.scan, run, runPython, build, format, and openai submit work, while done() and result() expose completion to normal SIPL code.

    Toolkit Codex process bridge#

    worker.codexInfo() -> Map reports available, the resolved native executable path, and setup error. It checks SIPL_CODEX, PATH and the Windows VS Code Codex extension. It does not start a model request.

    worker.codex(root: String, prompt: String, options?: Map) starts a background Codex turn. Call worker.start first. Options are model: String, session: String (an explicit UUID, default new session), apiKey: String, network: Bool (default false), and timeoutSeconds: Int (1..3600, default 900). The key falls back to CODEX_API_KEY / OPENAI_API_KEY, then existing Codex login. It never enters argv. Prompt input is bounded to 512 KiB and supplied through a private temporary stdin handle removed on close. Project, model, session and key values are validated before a job is submitted.

    worker.readOutput() -> String drains complete JSONL records while a Codex job runs; an incomplete UTF-8/JSON record stays buffered until its newline or job completion. It returns empty when no complete record is ready. worker.result contains any undrained tail and the normal exit/cancellation/truncation fields. Only Codex jobs support live draining. Keep polling to avoid the 8 MiB pending queue cap; after done, drain until empty before classifying completion.

    Cancel and shutdown terminate the owned process group/job, including children. Windows creates the broker suspended and assigns its job before starting it; failure to establish process-tree ownership prevents launch. The broker passes workspace-write, no additional writable roots, and explicit command network and approval policies to Codex. Commands inherit no provider-key variables from the Toolkit-selected credential. See the agent reference for UI, security boundaries, engine installation, budgets and offline tests.

    SIPL projects and packages#

    SIPL's project commands use sipl.toml, a committed sipl.lock, and a local content-addressed cache. File-oriented commands continue to work for scripts outside a project. Inside a project, all compilation validates the lock and cached package contents first. Compilation never downloads dependencies.

    Commit sipl.toml, sipl.lock, source, tests and your license. Keep .sipl/ and build/ out of version control. init creates both configuration files, source, a smoke test, .gitignore, and .gitattributes; it refuses to overwrite existing source, tests or license files. The generated attributes preserve LF text bytes across checkouts so lock checksums survive platform changes. The initial license is LicenseRef-Proprietary with “All rights reserved.” Choose your actual license and replace LICENSE before distributing a package. Use sipl init my_library --lib to create src/lib.sipl without start(). sipl check validates libraries as well as applications.

    A complete path-dependency example, including both lockfiles, is in the locked path dependency example. Its initial fetch works offline and restores the exact library snapshot from the repository.

    Manifest and layout#

    Package names match [a-z][a-z0-9_]{0,63} and exclude language keywords, so they can be imported without new language syntax. Versions are stable MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH semantic versions. Requirements support exact versions (with optional =), caret and tilde: ^1.2.3 permits compatible 1.x versions, ^0.2.3 permits 0.2.x, ^0.0.3 is exact, and ~1.2.3 permits 1.2.x. All ranges exclude older versions. Prereleases, build metadata, wildcards and compound ranges are rejected in format version 1.

    entry must point to a .sipl file under src/. sipl is the minimum runtime version. license declares an SPDX identifier/expression or your LicenseRef identifier, and license-file names a nonempty root-level file. The parser validates the identifier's shape; it does not resolve licensing terms. api = "public" uses the language's existing convention: module members are public except names starting with _. Packages expose their entry module. Consumers cannot import internal files through the cache.

    The standard archive includes sipl.toml, the license file, optional README.md, and regular files beneath src/, tests/, docs/, pages/ and public/. It excludes .git/, .sipl/, build/ and the library's own lockfile. Paths, filenames, total bytes, file count and directory depth are bounded; absolute paths, traversal entries, symlinks and reparse points are rejected. Archives contain at most 4,096 files and 64 MiB. The graph contains at most 128 packages with one version/source per package name.

    The supported TOML subset includes comments, basic/literal strings, string arrays, tables, inline dependency tables and integer format versions. Arrays may span lines and use trailing commas. Inline dependency tables occupy one line. Duplicate keys/tables, unknown fields, hooks and unsupported syntax fail with a diagnostic instead of being ignored.

    Dependencies and lockfiles#

    A declared dependency name resolves to the cached package's entry module. Local use folder/module and use ../module declarations must stay inside that package's src/, tests/ or pages/ layout. A package can import only its direct dependencies; a transitive dependency must be declared explicitly. Dependency and import cycles fail.

    Resolution chooses the alphabetically first unresolved name, tries stable versions newest first, and backtracks against all transitive requirements. The result does not depend on index ordering. Unsatisfiable versions or source conflicts leave the existing manifest and lock unchanged. Add/remove operations resolve the updated graph before committing either file.

    sipl add geometry chooses a caret requirement for the newest registry release; an explicit requirement is preferable for review. sipl add helpers --path ../helpers reads the local package version and creates a checksummed snapshot. Path dependencies always need a version in the manifest. Nested path packages are independently snapshotted. Builds read those cached snapshots, even when the original directories change or disappear. Git dependencies are rejected.

    The lock records format/runtime versions, the exact manifest SHA-256, exact package versions/sources, archive SHA-256, provenance/signatures and dependency edges in stable order. Review and commit it. The lock is a trusted project input: modifications to it are code changes and need the same review as source.

    CommandBehavior
    sipl fetchReuse a current lock; resolve if the manifest changed or there is no lock
    sipl fetch --lockedFetch exact locked bytes; fail if the lock is absent/stale
    sipl fetch --updateResolve against the current registry or original path contents
    sipl fetch --offlineUse local snapshots and the cached registry index/packages only
    sipl fetch --locked --offlineVerify/fill the cache without network access or lock changes

    A missing locked registry archive is fetched by its checksum without consulting the current index. A missing path snapshot can be reconstructed from its original path only if its bytes still match the lock. Changed bytes fail; use --update deliberately to accept a new snapshot. Checksum failures in existing cache entries fail closed; remove the affected .sipl/cache/<checksum> entry and fetch again to restore it. To provision disconnected builds, copy the verified .sipl/cache directory from a machine that has fetched the same lock.

    build, check, run, test and doc require the lock and complete cache. Their dependency handling ignores registry/network settings and never invokes a downloader or signature tool. With identical source, pages, lock, SIPL runtime binary and host target, executable output is byte-identical. SIPL's source-free executable contains a copy of the runtime, so changing the runtime binary or platform changes its output. The lock pins the SIPL version, not the host compiler/linker used to produce that runtime.

    Capability requests and package limits#

    Allowed capability names are filesystem, network, process, environment, ui, graphics and ai. Every dependency request must be explicitly present in the root project's requests, including requests from transitive packages. A new request stops resolution/building until the manifest declares it.

    These declarations make dependency effects reviewable. They do not sandbox SIPL execution or dynamically restrict built-in APIs; runtime capability enforcement is a separate roadmap item. Tests and program execution run the project's SIPL code with the existing runtime permissions.

    Only kind = "sipl" is accepted. Packages cannot load binary extensions or run build scripts, install scripts, or arbitrary package commands.

    targets accepts host, windows-x64, linux-x64, linux-arm64, macos-x64 and macos-arm64. Builds select the current host and fail if the manifest does not allow it. Cross-compilation and additional runtime profiles are not implemented.

    Tests and documentation#

    sipl test discovers named test "name" { ... } blocks recursively under tests/. Legacy test_*.sipl and smoke.sipl programs with start() remain supported. Each case runs in fresh normal and GC-stress processes. Filtering, parallel jobs, deterministic seeds, snapshots, property and fuzz hooks, JSON/JUnit reports, and line coverage are built in. Production modules cannot import test sources or use test. See TESTING.md.

    sipl doc checks the package entry and writes build/doc/api.md with public signatures and methods, source comments, canonical examples, package metadata, and dependency licenses. Each public contract states parameters, return type, failures, effects, complexity, and one example. Missing contracts fail creation without replacing the existing output. Use sipl doc --check to lint contracts or sipl doc -o docs/api.md to choose a destination.

    The source debugger and structured crash reports are described in DEBUGGING.md.

    Single official registry and publishing#

    Format version 1 supports one logical official registry. Its HTTPS endpoint and trusted RSA public key must be provisioned by the operator:

    SIPL_REGISTRY can instead name a trusted local mirror directory. No hosted registry or production signing key is created by this implementation. SIPL does not silently select an unprovisioned endpoint. There are no per-dependency registries. Mirrors must serve packages attested by the provisioned key. Distribute the key through a trusted channel separate from downloads. Never use the deliberately public test key in tests/fixtures/registry in production.

    The endpoint/mirror contains:

    index.toml starts with registry-version = 1 and contains [[package]] records with name, version, checksum, provenance and signature. Versions are immutable. signature is a 256-byte RSA PKCS#1 v1.5 SHA-256 signature, encoded as 512 lowercase hexadecimal characters, over this exact UTF-8 record, including the final newline:

    The trusted key file contains the 2048-bit RSA public modulus as 512 lowercase hexadecimal characters, with optional trailing whitespace; the exponent is

    1. Windows verifies with CNG. POSIX uses the OpenSSL CLI for signature

    verification and curl for HTTPS downloads; local mirrors need no curl. These tools are required only for fetching/attestation, not locked builds or deployed executables. HTTPS verifies normal TLS certificates, rejects redirects, and has bounded downloads/timeouts.

    .sipkg is a canonical uncompressed source archive: SIPLSRC1, a little-endian u32 file count, then sorted records containing u32 UTF-8 path length, u32 content length, path bytes and content bytes. There are no timestamps or mode fields. The complete archive checksum and signature are checked before extraction; the extracted file tree is rehashed on every compilation. Cached source bytes are checked again immediately before parsing, so a concurrent cache edit cannot replace a verified module during the build.

    sipl publish checks the package and prepares a deterministic archive, release.toml and provenance.txt under build/publish/. Use --output dir to choose a fresh directory. Submit these artifacts to the registry operator, who reviews the source/provenance, signs the attestation and installs the archive at its checksum path. Path dependencies must first become registry dependencies; publishing rejects local snapshots. The command performs no remote upload and needs no registry credentials.

    An operator-signed release can be verified while preparing the submission:

    The archive's source files and manifest must remain unchanged between obtaining the signature and this command. Output directories are never overwritten.

    Run the integration checks with python tests/project_tests.py build/sipl.exe on Windows or python3 tests/project_tests.py build/sipl on POSIX. Fixtures cover signed local-registry packages, deterministic resolution/backtracking, snapshot paths, cache corruption, stale locks, capability declarations, offline/identical builds, publication and failing test aggregation.

    Packaged applications#

    sipl build creates a directly executable SIPL application without copying the application's .sipl files into the output.

    On Windows, sipl build selects the executable subsystem automatically. A program that directly calls ui.open(), ui.openFixed(), or graphics.open() in its controller or any compiled module is emitted with IMAGE_SUBSYSTEM_WINDOWS_GUI, so launching it from File Explorer does not create a console window. Other programs retain IMAGE_SUBSYSTEM_WINDOWS_CUI and behave as command-line applications.

    Override detection when an application opens its window indirectly through a stored function or another dynamic call:

    --subsystem windows|console changes only the Windows PE subsystem. It does not replace the process entry point, alter system.args, change application exit codes, or hide a console after startup. For debugging a GUI application, build the same source with --subsystem console; stdout and stderr then remain available in the terminal and can be redirected to a log file normally.

    Arguments passed to the packaged executable are available in system.args. A packaged executable runs its application directly; it does not expose the run, check, or other compiler commands.

    Toolkit embeds its UI modules and the compiler/runtime in build/toolkit (build/toolkit.exe on Windows), so that executable can Run, Scan, Format, and Build when copied without a neighboring sipl executable. Updating source files or rebuilding only sipl does not update an older packaged application. make and build.bat now rebuild both artifacts; make package-toolkit refreshes Toolkit without launching it. The Linux toolkit.sh launcher checks the runtime's API/security revision, then refreshes the packaged Toolkit using that runtime before opening the app. Save and close existing windows, then reopen them to load a rebuilt version.

    Toolkit uses toolkit/sipl.ico as its icon on Windows and Linux. The build extracts its largest PNG frame into toolkit/sipl.png and embeds the same image in Toolkit for its native window icon. Linux builds also create build/toolkit.desktop, a desktop launcher with the matching icon. Replacing sipl.ico and rebuilding updates all generated icon assets.

    On Windows, package another application with its own executable icon using sipl build app.sipl -o app.exe --icon app.ico. The ICO's image sizes are preserved in Windows resources before the compiled application is appended.

    PDF previews use the pinned PDFium shared library installed beside sipl and Toolkit by the build (pdfium.dll on Windows, libpdfium.so on x64 Linux). Carry that library and its notices when copying either executable to another folder. PDF creation with pdf.create() remains self-contained in the runtime. See PDF generation and viewing and the PDFium dependency notes.

    macOS builds use the system Core Graphics PDF engine and native Metal, so neither PDFium nor Vulkan is deployed there. make also assembles build/SIPLToolkit.app. Signed Mach-O packaging, the Apple build tools, current coverage and native acceptance requirements are documented in MACOS.md.

    In toolkit, open the .sipl controller and click Build, or choose Run → Build Executable…. The build runs in the background and reports its output in the existing Output panel. When the controller contains web.pages() and the workspace has a pages/ folder, toolkit embeds that folder automatically.

    SIPL Pages#

    Compile private .sipl.html pages into the executable with --pages:

    The package contains each page's compiled bytecode, literal HTML chunks, and include graph. It does not contain the page source or build-machine paths. A packaged application's existing web.pages("pages") call selects the embedded registry, so the pages directory is not needed in production. Development reload: true is automatically disabled because packaged pages are immutable; the controller does not need a production-only code path.

    Static public files are deliberately separate. Deploy the directory passed to web.serve() beside the executable, or place those files in your normal static asset service.

    What the package protects#

    The output is a copy of the SIPL runtime with a versioned bytecode image. At startup SIPL:

    1. verifies the image's SHA-256 digest before parsing it;

    2. checks that its built-in ABI matches the runtime;

    3. bounds-checks every record and object reference;

    4. verifies every function's opcodes, operands, branches, stack depths, and exception-handler state;

    5. runs the verified bytecode, with the JIT enabled normally.

    Original source, comments, imported module files, page expressions, and absolute source paths are not stored. Values required by the program still exist: string literals, type/field/method names, and function names can be recovered by someone analyzing the executable. Machine code and bytecode can also be reverse engineered. Packaging raises the cost of copying the program; it is not a perfect secrecy boundary.

    Keep API keys, database passwords, signing credentials, and uniquely valuable logic on a server or in an operating-system secret store. Do not treat an embedded key or bytecode encryption key as secret.

    Bytecode checks and the embedded SHA-256 digest do not authenticate a publisher or restrict the program's host permissions. Only run applications you trust.

    Preparing a SIPL beta release#

    Use release.bat on Windows or make release on Linux to build the runtime and packaged Toolkit, run the release checks, and generate build/release-windows.json or build/release-linux.json with adjacent .SHA256SUMS files. These commands prepare files locally; they do not publish them. Build prerequisites and enabled features must be available for the selected platform.

    The manifests record source/dependency content, component provenance and notices, the actual runtime/Toolkit/PDFium artifacts, static libraries, platform imports or system-library hashes, build features, and validation evidence. The gate rejects changed inputs and checks that the shipped PDFium library matches its pinned archive. After changing release inputs, prepare a new release manifest.

    On Linux, use python3 and build/release-linux.json. Verification checks local content consistency. Authenticate published artifacts through a trusted release channel or set SIPL_RELEASE_SIGNING_KEY to your own provisioned GPG key before the release command to sign the manifest. Supply both --signature and the expected --signer fingerprint when verifying a detached signature. Signing a manifest and Windows executable signing are separate steps. See the repository's release instructions for the complete commands.

    Signing a Windows release#

    Sign only after sipl build, because packaging and subsystem selection change the executable:

    Use a certificate from the Windows certificate store or a managed CI signing service. Do not commit a .pfx password or signing key. Signing authenticates the publisher and detects later modification; it does not hide the program.

    Windows packages use the platform's stack protection, control-flow protection, ASLR, DEP, and high-entropy 64-bit ASLR features.

    Compatibility and deployment#

    A package is tied to the exact SIPL runtime ABI that created it. Rebuild the application after upgrading SIPL. The executable has no runtime dependency on the compiler source files or application modules.

    Included networking#

    HTTP, TCP/UDP, and WebSocket runtime support is included in packaged programs. HttpResponse, HttpClient, NetTask, CancelToken, NetStream, Socket, and WebSocket annotations survive packaging. Packages use the same shared task and cancellation API; there is no separate networking task runtime to deploy.

    Netlib numerical library#

    Normal Windows and Makefile builds compile the pinned Netlib C sources into a separate static archive using CMake. No Fortran compiler, downloaded dependency, BLAS DLL, or graphics backend change is required. The mat namespace, supported algorithms, memory bounds and exact versions are documented in MAT.md. The source pin is third_party/netlib/SIPL_PIN.md.

    Windows candidate builds can set SIPL_OUTPUT and SIPL_TOOLKIT_OUTPUT to new filenames, preserving working runtime/Toolkit binaries while testing changes.

    Compiled features and binary sizes#

    Standard builds include every feature supported by the selected platform. Missing prerequisites and feature-off switches fail the build. MySQL/MariaDB is built from bundled Connector/C source and linked statically; it requires no separate connector SDK, DLL or shared library.

    system.buildFeatures exposes the actual compiled capability inventory. build/build-report.json records compiledFeatures and exact artifactSizes; direct Make builds also write build/sipl.capabilities.json and build/toolkit.capabilities.json, with sizeBytes. Both runtime and packaged Toolkit are validated. Runtime headless settings retain compiled support. See full build policy and platform boundaries.

    macOS implementation and acceptance#

    The Apple implementation targets macOS 11 or later on Intel x64 and Apple Silicon ARM64. Build each architecture natively. It adds a Cocoa host for SIPL's existing software canvas and widgets, and a Metal backend for the shared graphics scene API. Windows continues to use Win32/Vulkan and Linux continues to use X11/Vulkan. No widget or application rewrite is required.

    Release status: the Apple-specific Objective-C and GPU paths still require a native Mac build and the acceptance checks below. Source review or Windows/Linux regression results do not qualify a Mac release. The minimum OS version is a deployment target, not a claim that every Mac/driver combination has been tested.

    Build and launch#

    Install Apple's Xcode Command Line Tools and the existing project's build tools: CMake, Python 3, pkg-config, Meson and Ninja. Intel video assembly also needs NASM. SIPL does not install these tools or download dependencies during a build.

    make builds build/sipl, the packaged build/toolkit, and build/SIPLToolkit.app. The app contains its compiler/runtime and license notices. It needs no neighboring source tree or third-party dynamic libraries. make macos-app rebuilds the bundle alone after the executables are available.

    The deployment target defaults to MACOSX_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET=11.0. The compiler and dependency builds inherit it. Apple-only sources are compiled as Objective-C with ARC; the shared runtime and UI engine remain C. Build separate native artifacts on Intel and Apple Silicon; combining packaged executables with lipo is not supported by the current bytecode-footer format.

    Standard builds include Cocoa, Metal, video, WebP and MySQL/MariaDB. Feature-off switches are rejected. SIPL_UI=headless, SIPL_AUDIO=headless and SIPL_GAMEPAD=headless select runtime behavior while retaining every compiled capability. Opening a graphics window still requires a Metal-capable device.

    Platform coverage#

    AreaApple implementation
    Language, compiler, verified bytecode and GCShared C runtime; interpreter execution on both CPU architectures
    UI and ToolkitSIPL widgets/layout/fonts on a Cocoa window; resize/maximize, focus, keyboard/Unicode input, mouse, wheel, Retina scaling, clipboard, file/folder/save panels and Dock icon
    Keyboard shortcutsCommand-letter and Control-letter are delivered through SIPL's existing ctrl+ key names; Command-Q requests application windows to close
    3D graphicsNative Metal, indexed meshes, instanced batches, textures, depth, materials and scene lighting; shared glTF loading, resources and camera logic
    PDFExisting PDFGen creation; system Core Graphics rendering for pdf.open() and Toolkit previews, with the existing input/page/pixel limits
    Audio/videoExisting Core Audio backend and pinned portable codecs; device playback needs native hardware qualification
    ControllersSystem GameController framework, four stable controller slots, standard buttons/sticks/triggers and disconnect edges
    Files, networking and HTTPSShared POSIX operations; existing pinned LibreSSL/zlib and curl sources; Apple SecTrust for the system certificate store
    PackagingNative Mach-O executables with sealed bytecode and local ad-hoc signatures; Finder-launchable Toolkit bundle

    Apple system frameworks used are AppKit, Foundation/Core Foundation, Core Graphics, Metal, QuartzCore, Core Audio/AudioToolbox, GameController, Security, CoreServices and SystemConfiguration. These ship with the OS/SDK. No new third-party library, MoltenVK, SDL, GTK or Qt is introduced. TLS, image, media, font and numerical dependencies reuse the repository's existing pinned sources.

    Native CPU JIT compilation and automatic List.map GPU offloading remain qualified for Windows/Linux x64 only. Mac programs preserve language behavior through the interpreter. The Metal implementation is the graphics backend; a Darwin JIT allocator/ABI and a Metal compute offloader are separate future work. Toolkit's encrypted settings retain the existing Windows DPAPI limitation; Mac keys can be supplied for the session. A per-control macOS accessibility provider and on-screen IME preedit drawing are not part of this first host. Committed Unicode/IME text is delivered through NSTextInputClient.

    Core Graphics renders PDF page content. Interactive PDF forms and annotation overlays are not implemented on the Apple path. PDFium remains the pinned renderer for Windows/Linux and is not redistributed in the Mac app.

    Native acceptance#

    Run from a Mac desktop login session:

    make macos-check checks executable discovery, signed packaging/repackaging, portable worker/gamepad/audio behavior, and Core Graphics PDF rendering. Its native smoke program opens a Cocoa window, checks key/Unicode event delivery, and submits indexed, textured Metal frames before and after resizing with Metal validation enabled. It requires a Metal-capable GPU. These checks have been added for execution on Mac hardware; they cannot run in the Windows/WSL workspace.

    Before advertising support, also exercise Toolkit editing, Command shortcuts, clipboard exchange, file panels, Retina monitor changes, maximize/minimize, text input methods, audio/video devices, controllers, model textures and scene lighting on the native release architectures. Existing Windows/Linux desktop and Vulkan checks remain separate acceptance gates.

    Signing and release#

    sipl build stages a Mach-O executable privately, replaces the old package image/signature, includes the bytecode in __LINKEDIT, and uses Apple's /usr/bin/codesign to create and verify a local ad-hoc signature before committing the result. It uses direct process arguments and directory capabilities; neither output filenames nor signing commands pass through a shell. Existing outputs remain in place when packaging/signing fails.

    An ad-hoc signature is for local execution. A public Mac release needs the maintainer's Developer ID signing identity and Apple notarization. Sign nested executables first and the app bundle last, after packaging, then notarize and staple using Apple's tools. Do not append more data after signing. See Apple's distribution guide and code-signature storage.

    make release produces build/release-macos.json and adjacent checksums after the build/test gate. The manifest includes the app, static input archives and system-framework imports, and rejects accidental Homebrew/local dylib links. It does not sign with a publisher identity or submit anything to Apple.

    Tests and API documentation#

    Named tests#

    Test files can declare named blocks without a start() function:

    Names must be nonempty literal Strings and unique within a file. Test blocks are top-level declarations. Their functions take no arguments. A returned value does not determine success: a test passes when execution completes without an uncaught failure. Use assertions to check its behavior.

    Discovery, filtering, and isolated execution#

    Without a path, the runner uses the project's tests/ directory, or tests/ in the current directory when no manifest is present. It discovers named tests recursively in .sipl files, skipping hidden directories, build output, and links. Existing test_*.sipl and smoke.sipl programs with start() remain supported as one legacy case per file. An explicit file can use either form.

    --filter matches a substring of the file path or test name. --list lists matching cases without executing them. Finding no matching tests is an error. Discovery and report ordering are deterministic.

    Every case runs in a fresh process, then runs again in another fresh process with SIPL_GC_STRESS=1. The stress run begins after its normal counterpart finishes. Globals, VM state, environment changes, and random state are isolated between cases. --jobs controls concurrent processes, from 1 to 64; the default is 1. Filesystem effects remain visible to other processes, so parallel tests must use separate paths for resources they mutate.

    --timeout is a per-process timeout in milliseconds, default 30000 and maximum

    1. Timed-out processes and their descendant processes are terminated.

    Logs are capped at 8 MiB per process. --gc-stress remains accepted for compatibility; both execution modes always run.

    Project tests validate their lockfile and dependency cache. Testing does not fetch dependencies. The child process's system.args is empty, preserving the contract of legacy test programs.

    Test and production imports#

    use test exposes test helpers inside test sources. Ordinary run and build commands reject named test declarations and the test-only module. Production modules cannot import a test source, even when a test process is compiling the production module. Test sources can import production modules.

    Keep production code under src/ and test helpers under tests/ or test_support/. Files named test_*.sipl or *.test.sipl are also test sources. An explicitly selected test file is a test entry regardless of its name. Each test source that accesses test helpers declares its own use test. check, JSON diagnostics, and the language service can validate conventional test sources without executing them.

    Assertions#

    The three assertion functions are available as unqualified names and as members of test. They return None on success and raise a catchable Fail on a failed assertion. Their equality rule is SIPL's ordinary == rule.

    APIParametersReturnFailuresEffectsComplexity
    assertEqual(actual, expected, message?)Two values; optional String explanationNoneValues are unequal; invalid message typeMay invoke a user-defined equals methodScalar O(1); structural values proportional to compared contents
    assertNotEqual(actual, expected, message?)Two values; optional String explanationNoneValues are equal; invalid message typeMay invoke a user-defined equals methodSame as assertEqual
    assertThrows(callback, contains?)Zero-argument Function; optional String message fragmentNoneCallback succeeds, fragment is absent, or arguments are invalidExecutes the callback and catches its failureCost of the callback

    Canonical examples:

    Add use test at the top of the file containing these examples.

    Deterministic seeds and property tests#

    --seed accepts an integer from 0 to 9223372036854775807 and defaults to 1. Each case and its GC-stress replay start with the same seed. The runner seeds both the ordinary random/randomInt functions and the test module's random generator. Scheduling does not change a case's input sequence. Reproduce a failure using its reported seed and the same test code.

    APIParametersReturnFailuresEffectsComplexity
    test.seedNoneInt: the case's initial seedNoneRead onlyO(1)
    test.nameNoneString: the current test name, or start for legacy casesNoneRead onlyO(name length) when returning the String
    test.randomInt(min, max)Int bounds, lower inclusive and upper exclusiveIntInvalid bounds or non-Int inputsAdvances deterministic random stateExpected O(1), constant space
    test.property(generator, predicate, iterations?)Zero-argument Function; one-argument Function; optional Int from 1 to 100000NoneGenerator fails; predicate returns false or fails; invalid argumentsRepeatedly executes both callbacks and advances their random stateO(iterations × callback cost); one generated value live per iteration

    Canonical example for a property and its generator:

    A predicate may return Bool or none after making assertions. Failure output includes the seed, zero-based iteration, input, and callback's failure reason. The runner reports the original failing input; it does not shrink inputs. --iterations sets the default property and fuzz iteration count, normally 100. An explicit callback API argument overrides that default.

    Canonical seed and name inspection:

    Deterministic clock fixtures#

    These helpers are available only while executing a test. They never change the OS clock. Each isolated case starts with real clocks; a fixture freezes the runtime's wall and monotonic providers, including async deadlines.

    APIContract
    test.clock(instant, monotonicNanoseconds?)Freeze wall time at an Instant and monotonic time at a nonnegative Int nanosecond value (default 0)
    test.advanceTime(duration)Advance both providers by a nonnegative Duration; overflow fails atomically
    test.setWallClock(instant)Change only wall time; monotonic elapsed time is unaffected
    test.resetClock()Return to real providers

    All return None, mutate only the test process's clock fixture, and take O(1) time/space. Advancing/changing time without configuring a fixture fails. Create timer/interval/cron waits, explicitly advance time, then await the result:

    Time does not advance automatically. Awaiting a future frozen deadline without advancing it reaches the test supervisor's timeout. Configure/reset before creating waits; switching providers while waits exist changes their clock domain. Use seeded PRNGs and local HTTP/socket fixtures alongside these clocks for deterministic tests. See sipl api --task clock_tests --json.

    Fuzz hooks#

    test.fuzz(callback, iterations?, maxBytes?) invokes a one-argument Function with deterministic arbitrary Bytes values. They can contain zero bytes and invalid UTF-8. Binary parsers accept Bytes directly; validate and explicitly decode before calling a text parser.

    Parameters are a Function, optional Int iterations from 1 to 100000, and optional Int maximum length from 0 to 1048576; maximum length defaults to 256. The API returns None. It raises Fail when the callback returns false or fails, and a runtime failure for invalid arguments or callback return types. It executes user code and advances deterministic random state. Complexity is O(iterations × (maxBytes + callback cost)) time and O(maxBytes) generation space, plus memory retained by the callback.

    Canonical example:

    Snapshots#

    test.snapshot(name, value) compares the readable, quoted SIPL representation of a value with a checked-in snapshot. name is a String of 1 to 80 ASCII letters, digits, underscores, or hyphens. value can be any printable SIPL value. The return is None. Missing or changed snapshots raise Fail; invalid names raise a runtime failure; failed writes raise a file failure.

    Normal execution reads snapshots. --update-snapshots explicitly permits creating or replacing them. Files live beside the test source under .snapshots/<source filename>/<test-name hash>-<snapshot name>.snap. Updates use an atomic per-process temporary file. Snapshots should be reviewed and committed with their tests. Map insertion order is preserved in snapshots. Printing custom values may call their toString methods.

    Complexity is proportional to the formatted value and stored snapshot size, with the formatted representation retained while comparing or writing.

    Canonical example:

    JSON, JUnit, and coverage#

    The runner returns zero when all selected executions pass and all requested reports can be written. It returns nonzero for failed, crashed, or timed-out tests, no matches, or report-writing failures.

    JSON uses schema version 1 and includes a summary, seed, and one record per normal/stress execution: path, name, status, GC mode, duration, exit code, timeout state, log truncation state, output, and structured failure. JUnit is an XML testsuites document with cases, failure details, captured output, and a seed property. XML metacharacters are escaped.

    Coverage is line coverage, not branch coverage. It records executable source lines, including zero-hit lines in uncalled functions, and merges hits from all selected processes and both GC modes. Its JSON report has schema version 1, kind: "line", covered/executable totals, and per-file line/hit records. Collection uses the interpreter with JIT execution disabled so native execution cannot bypass instrumentation. Ordinary test runs retain the JIT.

    Public API contracts and sipl doc#

    For a project, documentation covers public declarations under src/, their public methods, package metadata, and dependencies. For an explicit source file it renders that module. The source is checked without running it. --check validates contracts without writing an output file.

    Names beginning with _ and the executable start entry are omitted. Every documented public API must provide an adjacent /// comment with a summary, each parameter's type and description, its return type and description, failures, effects, complexity, and exactly one canonical example. Constructor fields are parameters of a public type. Enum payload parameters use qualified names such as @param Some.value Int Payload description.. A declared parameter or return type must match its documented type. Private helpers do not need a public contract.

    Incomplete contracts fail generation before replacing an existing document. The generated Markdown contains signatures, comments, and fenced examples. Examples are rendered; documentation generation does not execute example code.

    Source debugging and crash reports#

    Start a debugger session#

    The debugger compiles the program, stops at its first executable source location, and accepts commands on standard input. --commands reads commands from a file for a reproducible session. All debugger events are JSON lines on standard output. SIPL print output becomes an output event, preserving the event stream. A command file keeps debugger commands separate from a program that reads standard input.

    Debug execution uses the interpreter. JIT execution is disabled during the session so breakpoints, locals, and stepping use the source's actual execution order. Ordinary execution keeps the JIT enabled.

    Commands#

    CommandBehavior
    break 12Set a breakpoint in the current source file
    break path/to/module.sipl:12Set a breakpoint in another loaded source file
    clearDisable all breakpoints
    continue or cRun until a breakpoint, uncaught failure, or program exit
    step or stepInStop at the next distinct source location, entering callees
    next or stepOverAdvance at the current depth, stepping over calls
    finish or stepOutRun until the current function returns
    stackInspect source locations and locals of live stack frames
    localsInspect the current frame's live local and captured bindings
    locals 1Inspect the caller; frame zero is the top of the stack
    helpPrint the supported command forms
    quitEnd the session with exit code 130

    Breakpoints are verified against loaded executable lines. A requested blank or comment line resolves to the next executable line in that source file; a request with no executable line at or after it is rejected. Loops can stop at the same source line on later iterations. Calls, recursion, and returns remain observable while stepping. Up to 1024 breakpoints are supported.

    Breakpoints in deeper calls remain active while stepping over or out. An exhausted command file resumes execution. The debugger displays an uncaught exception before the process exits; it supports inspection there, but cannot resume an operation that has already failed.

    Structured command and event format#

    Commands may also be JSON objects:

    Commands use command and optional path, line, and frame fields. Lines are one-based. Frame IDs begin at zero for the current function. Commands are bounded to 8191 bytes and malformed commands produce an error event without terminating the program.

    Events include stopped, breakpoint, stack, locals, output, error, help, breakpoints, and terminated. A stop identifies its reason as entry, breakpoint, step, or exception and includes source stack frames. The final event states the exit code.

    Inspection reports source names, current types, lexical scope, mutability, and primitive values. Captured closure bindings are identified separately. Out-of-scope bindings and uninitialized slots are omitted. Lists, maps, instances, enum payloads, and Results show bounded previews: up to eight entries or fields at each of two levels. Deeper values use summaries. Inspection never invokes user formatting methods. Strings are limited to a 4096-byte preview, and at most 64 stack frames are reported. Invalid byte sequences are escaped in JSON.

    Structured crash reports#

    --crash-report writes a JSON report for an uncaught runtime error or Fail in a debugger session. To capture one during an ordinary run, set SIPL_CRASH_REPORT to the desired file path before starting the process:

    Reports contain schemaVersion: 1, the SIPL runtime version, failure kind and message, and source stack/local records captured before unwinding. Report writing is atomic. Catching an expected failure with try does not create a crash report. Enabling source crash inspection also disables JIT execution for that process so reported locals remain reliable.

    The built-in test runner includes the same structured failure information in its JSON report. Its parent supervisor also reports process exits and timeouts when a child cannot produce a language-level report.

    These are language runtime reports. Source compile errors retain the sipl check --json diagnostic format. Native operating-system faults are reported by a supervising test process's exit status rather than being recovered inside the virtual machine.

    Editor service and structured diagnostics#

    sipl lsp runs the native language server over standard input/output. It uses the SIPL parser, compiler name resolution, type checker, import/package loader, runtime method tables and official formatter. Editor source buffers are passed to an isolated compiler process; no program, initializer or package hook is run. The server does not fetch dependencies or change source files.

    The service implements diagnostics, definition, references, hover, completion, signature help, prepare/rename, document/workspace symbols, formatting and quick fixes. Open documents accept incremental UTF-16 edits and increasing versions. Editing an imported buffer also rechecks its open importers. Closed files are refreshed through workspace/didChangeWatchedFiles; repaired imported files clear their previous diagnostics.

    Toolkit#

    Toolkit's shared editor also opens JavaScript (.js, .mjs, .cjs) and CSS files. Its built-in completion popup offers JavaScript keywords, local functions, variables, parameters and common browser APIs, plus CSS properties, property values and custom properties. Suggestions appear while typing or with Ctrl+Space and use the existing Tab/Enter acceptance and undo flow. HTML and SIPL Pages use these language profiles inside <script> and <style> blocks; multiline comments, strings and opening tags retain their state when scrolling. These offline suggestions do not require Node or a separate language server. The native sipl lsp service described here continues to analyze SIPL programs.

    VS Code#

    The extension is in editors/vscode. Install build/sipl-language-0.2.0.vsix through VS Code's Install from VSIX… command for syntax highlighting, comment/bracket support and snippets. Highlighting works without a SIPL executable, including .sipl.html Pages.

    Its optional compiler adapter uses Microsoft's language-client SDK and requires VS Code 1.91 or newer. The dependency graph is locked and the adapter has no compilation step:

    Launch a development extension host with that directory:

    In the extension host's user settings, point to the compiled runtime:

    Reload the VS Code window after changing these settings. The compiler adapter is disabled by default and runs only in trusted workspaces; it analyzes .sipl programs. On POSIX use /path/to/sipl/build/sipl, or put sipl on PATH. The executable setting is machine-scoped so a repository's settings cannot substitute a different executable. sipl.trace.server enables protocol logging in the SIPL output channel. The adapter starts a separate server for each workspace folder and uses the containing directory for a standalone file. This source adapter is available locally; no Marketplace extension is published by the build.

    For a manifest project, run sipl fetch --locked before opening it. A missing or stale lock/cache is reported as a project diagnostic. Unsaved edits can override project source files; immutable cached dependencies retain their checksum verification and cannot be overridden or renamed.

    Other editors#

    Configure an LSP client with:

    SettingValue
    Commandsipl
    Argumentslsp
    Transportstdio
    File typesipl
    Workspace rootproject directory, preferably containing sipl.toml
    Position encodingUTF-16
    File notifications**/*.sipl, sipl.toml, sipl.lock

    The wire protocol follows the Language Server Protocol. Messages use Content-Length headers and UTF-8 JSON. Standard output contains only framed protocol messages; ordinary compiler output is suppressed in analysis workers. The server implements initialize/shutdown/exit and returns JSON-RPC errors for invalid requests, positions and unsupported methods.

    Each server owns one workspace. It indexes at most 512 source files, accepts at most 128 open buffers, bounds individual source buffers at 4 MiB, and bounds protocol messages and analysis results at 16 MiB. Compiler processes have a 10-second time limit. Exceeding a worker limit produces SIPL4001 instead of terminating the editor server. Checks run in an isolated background worker and are cached per document; only changed files, known importers and previously failing documents are rechecked. New edits cancel stale workers, and only current generation results are published. Requests waiting for compiler facts are bounded to 128 requests/16 MiB and support $/cancelRequest (-32800). Input framing remains responsive even across fragmented messages. The full compiler still validates each invalidated document/import graph; there is no second incremental type checker or persistent command-line cache. Rename is disabled when the workspace file/depth limit is reached, so a partial index cannot produce an incomplete refactor. Open a smaller project folder in that case.

    Compiler diagnostic contract#

    The last form selects the current project's entry. A successful command exits 0; a compiler/project error exits 1. Standard output is one JSON object with no terminal prose. A library does not need start() for checking; building and running an executable still require the normal entry function.

    Ranges use zero-based lines and UTF-16 character offsets, including for non-BMP characters in source. The end is exclusive. Codes identify stable diagnostic categories independently of message wording. message describes the immediate error, detail explains the rule, and help gives repair guidance. A suggested fix contains a title and edits with path, range and newText. Fixes are offered only when the parser can supply a safe concrete edit, currently canonical and/or spellings and missing closing delimiters. Other errors retain guidance without inventing an edit.

    CodeCategory
    SIPL1000Syntax rule
    SIPL1001Invalid token/canonical spelling
    SIPL1002Missing closing delimiter
    SIPL2000Other semantic rule
    SIPL2001Unknown name
    SIPL2002Unknown type
    SIPL2003Duplicate declaration
    SIPL2004Type/operation mismatch
    SIPL2005Argument count/name rule
    SIPL2006Private module member
    SIPL2007Immutable assignment
    SIPL2008Missing return path
    SIPL2009Missing module
    SIPL2010Import cycle
    SIPL3000Tool/compiler infrastructure failure
    SIPL3001Manifest, lock or cache validation
    SIPL3002Unreadable source
    SIPL4001Failed/timed-out editor analysis worker
    SIPL4002Semantic index limit

    Normal command-line checks preserve the existing first-error behavior. Editor analysis additionally retains complete declarations/statements preceding an unfinished statement. Parser failures carry the same structured diagnostic; partial semantic facts remain useful for completion, hover and navigation.

    LSP diagnostics carry standard range/code/severity/message fields, with the complete compiler diagnostic in Diagnostic.data. An agent can therefore use the same schema through either the CLI or the editor protocol. Published open document diagnostics include the document version.

    Semantic features and refactoring#

    Symbol identities derive from the defining file, declaration span and resolved namespace. They distinguish shadowed locals, parameters, captures, imported members, fields and methods. References use those compiler binding identities, including named argument labels and type annotations. Comments and literal text are not renamed; names inside interpolated expressions are resolved by the parser/compiler and can be referenced.

    Hover exposes the compiler's annotation/inferred type, including generic and nominal types, plus declared function/method signatures. Any remains Any where the compiler does not prove a concrete type. Completion and signatures use the shared API contracts for core/std-library/network/ calendar/test names, parameter/property types, and awaited results. Domain APIs not yet in the inventory retain registered runtime names/arity and argN: Any. The service does not invent types or duplicate the toolkit's heuristic resolver.

    Rename produces an editor-applied WorkspaceEdit. It requires valid relevant source, an editable declaration, a valid identifier, and no detected namespace or capture collisions. Native symbols, cached packages and files outside the workspace are read-only. Type/enum names retain their uppercase convention; renaming an imported public member to a private name is rejected. Supported clients receive versioned documentChanges; other clients receive changes. Conservative collision checks can reject a refactor rather than risk changing its bindings. Incomplete code can still be navigated; repair it before rename.

    Formatting returns edits from the same self-verifying formatter used by sipl fmt, with SIPL's single official style. It does not write the file. Code actions return proposed quick fixes; the editor decides whether to apply them. Document symbols support both standard flat locations and document symbol ranges, according to the client's advertised capabilities.

    Run the protocol/diagnostic tests with:

    On POSIX use python3 tests/lsp_tests.py build/sipl. The tests drive a real stdio client, unsaved and incomplete buffers, imported file updates, exact types, UTF-16 positions, references/rename, formatting, quick fixes and structured lockfile errors. The VS Code adapter can be syntax-checked with node --check editors/vscode/extension.js; its dependencies install with the committed lock via npm ci --ignore-scripts.

    Toolkit AI Agent#

    The toolkit's right sidebar offers Codex with native sandboxed command execution and API with the original direct OpenAI Responses file tools. Codex is selected automatically when installed. Both work on the folder opened as the Toolkit project, including creating new projects beneath that folder.

    Start it#

    1. Launch toolkit.bat with the folder you want the agent to work in.

    2. Open Tools → Settings…, choose the model, and enter the OpenAI key (or use an existing Codex CLI login with the Codex engine). The key and model are remembered in encrypted user or project settings. Select User for defaults across projects or Project for this folder's overrides. Enter a Google key in the separate field for programs launched with Run. An empty OpenAI field can use OPENAI_API_KEY. Save, then close the modal and expand AI. See encrypted settings.

    3. Describe the result you want. For example: Create a reusable adventure engine under examples/projects/adventure-engine, with a runnable demo and usage docs. A name is helpful but optional: the agent is instructed to choose a descriptive unused folder when you request a new project.

    The message composer wraps and grows upward from two to eight visible lines, subject to available panel space, then scrolls. Enter inserts a newline; Ctrl+Enter or Send submits. Pasting preserves line breaks. Selection, clipboard shortcuts, and navigation work across wrapped lines.

    Attach active buffer is off by default. Turn it on when that file is relevant. It attaches up to 16000 bytes of reference text; the instructions explicitly distinguish an attached buffer from a destination for a new project. The tutorial projects under examples/packages/locked-path-dependency are not a suggested destination.

    The API key is not placed on a child-process command line or in a temporary file. Native request copies are cleared after use.

    Codex sandbox and command tools#

    The Codex engine uses the same installed native engine that powers the VS Code Codex extension. Toolkit discovers codex on PATH; on Windows it also finds the newest Codex extension in .vscode/extensions or .vscode-insiders/extensions. SIPL_CODEX can specify a native Codex executable explicitly. The engine is not bundled with SIPL and no Node/Python bridge is needed. A missing or invalid engine produces a setup message.

    When an engine is available, Codex is selected automatically. The AI panel has a Codex / API engine button. Its selection is saved in the encrypted user store as agentEngine; Other JSON can specify "codex", "api", or "auto". New conversations and folder changes reset the corresponding Codex session identity. Subsequent messages and Continue target that explicit session UUID, never the most recent unrelated CLI session.

    Codex can inspect, search, edit, run commands, compile, test and fix failures with the installed development tools. Toolkit supplies its SIPL executable path and language guidance so the agent can query actual APIs and verify generated programs. An OS-enforced workspace-write sandbox permits project and temp writes while protecting locations outside those writable roots. Extra writable roots are cleared for this invocation. Command requests that require more access fail inside the sandbox; Toolkit never invokes a bypass/full-access flag. The broker runs outside the command sandbox to contact OpenAI and manage its own session, as in Codex's normal architecture. This is a workspace-write boundary, not a VM that hides every readable file on the computer.

    On Windows, Toolkit explicitly enables the unelevated sandbox implementation. Selecting workspace-write alone does not enable Windows command sandboxing; without an implementation, unattended runs can reject even basic read commands. This implementation uses a restricted Windows token and filesystem boundaries without administrator setup. Its network isolation is weaker than the elevated implementation: offline controls use environment settings rather than dedicated firewall rules. See the Windows sandbox documentation.

    Net: Off is the default and requests offline command execution, subject to the platform implementation described above. Net: On allows network access for package installs or network-dependent tests. It does not control the Codex broker's connection to OpenAI. 15m limits a run's elapsed time; click to choose 30m or 5m. The API mode request budget does not govern Codex's internal model requests. The panel shows completed-turn usage when the engine reports it; Cancel and the time limit bound running work.
