A time limit is not a token or dollar spending cap.

    A configured Toolkit OpenAI key is passed only to the trusted Codex broker as CODEX_API_KEY, never in its command line, model prompt, or diagnostic request JSON. Inherited provider-key variables are removed from that broker's launch environment before selecting the intended credential. Codex command environment policy excludes names matching *KEY*, *TOKEN*, *SECRET*, and *PASSWORD*. Toolkit leaves Codex's authentication selection unrestricted; it does not set forced_login_method. With no supplied/environment API key, the engine can use its existing CLI login; expired logins require signing in again. Both new turns and resumes use --ignore-user-config, keeping personal Codex model defaults and unrelated MCP connectors out of Toolkit runs. Project instructions, execution-policy rules and managed requirements still apply. Automatic plugin marketplace setup/downloads are disabled for this embedded client; native shell, editing and search tools remain available. Toolkit's overrides apply to this invocation; saved model, connector and login settings are preserved. Codex may record its own project-trust metadata.

    Live JSONL events show commands, exit codes, multiline output, file changes, agent messages and failures. Completed writes refresh clean open buffers and the explorer. Save unsaved files before starting a Codex turn; if you edit a buffer during a run, refresh preserves that unsaved buffer. Closing a dirty buffer or saving over disk changes follows the editor's usual behavior. Cancel / Escape stops the owned process tree, including child commands; partial edits are retained. Continue resumes the saved session. Failed or incomplete runs cannot be reported as successful merely because the process exited without an error code.

    Copy Log retains displayed conversation and tool output. Individual command output is displayed up to 24,000 bytes; View Last AI Response retains the most recent 2 MiB of raw event data and marks shortened history. The native pending output queue is capped at 8 MiB and detects overflow. API keys are omitted from View Last AI Request. Codex stores its session history according to its own configuration; Toolkit itself does not persist its sidebar transcript.

    The native broker is in src/codex_process.c, worker scheduling/cancellation in src/worker.c, and event presentation in toolkit/codex_agent.sipl. tests/test_codex_agent.sipl tests protocol handling offline. python tests/codex_agent_tests.py build/sipl.exe (use build/sipl on Linux) builds a native fixture that actually creates a broken SIPL file, observes a compiler failure, repairs it, checks/runs it, then verifies live UTF-8 output, explicit resume, process-tree cancellation, editor integration and packaging. Use a C compiler developer shell on Windows. These checks make no paid model requests; model response quality still depends on the selected model and task. With SIPL_CODEX_REAL set on Windows, the same driver additionally forwards the actual bridge arguments to the real engine against a local mock Responses server. It verifies exec and explicit session resume, real command execution, SIPL check/run, credential filtering, denied outside writes and config isolation. This regression reproduces the original policy failure when the Windows sandbox selection is removed; it makes no paid model requests.

    The integration follows the official Codex non-interactive interface and sandbox configuration.

    Direct API mode: inspection and editing#

    Each turn starts with a compact local overview: root entries, relevant common folder entries when present, root AGENTS.md, and a heading/line index for docs/LANGUAGE.md when available. This needs no additional model request. The agent is instructed to read relevant ranges together, avoid repeated reads, and begin implementing after one or two consolidated inspection rounds when it has enough information.

    Preferred tools:

    • inspect_project(paths) lists up to 12 folders together, with applicable AGENTS.md instructions. It finds instruction filenames directly rather than searching every file's contents for the string AGENTS.md.

    • read_files(files) reads up to 12 focused file ranges together. Each range is bounded to 500 lines; combined content is bounded to 48000 bytes.

    • apply_changes(changes) applies up to 12 ordered directory, write, or exact replacement operations together. Missing parent directories are created inside the opened project. Every operation states operation, path, content, old_text, and new_text; unused text fields are empty strings.

    • search_files(query, path) searches relevant supported text files, with bounded traversal, file count, match count, and a short UI time budget. A truncated result can be narrowed to a smaller folder.

    Single-file list_files, read_file, write_file, replace_in_file, and make_directory tools remain supported. Independent function calls may share one model response. Local operations execute in their returned order so writes and directory creation have predictable dependencies.

    Repeated unchanged listings, searches, and read ranges return a reference to already supplied context instead of sending the same content again. Reads still inspect current disk or editor text, so changed files produce fresh results. The transcript names each successfully saved file.

    Before editing, a batch checks all paths and unsaved-buffer conflicts. If it finds applicable instructions not yet supplied, it returns them without writing and asks the model to review them before retrying. Batches are not filesystem transactions: later operation failures retain earlier successful writes and report the exact successes and errors. An editor reload failure is reported separately from a successful write.

    Direct API mode: budget, progress, and Continue#

    Budget cycles through 12, 24, and 48 model requests. The default remains 12; it counts API requests, including the final summary, rather than individual file operations. One request can perform many reads or writes through the batch tools. Selecting a larger budget permits more requests; it does not change the model or promise a particular price.

    The last permitted request disables tools and asks for an honest summary of successful changes, blockers, and remaining work. Earlier requests receive progress guidance to finish useful edits before the limit. Two consecutive tool batches that return no new information or successful operations trigger an early summary instead of continuing a repeated-read loop.

    The panel displays requests, saved-file count, and tokens reported by returned API responses. Its closing transcript also distinguishes input, cached input, and output tokens. These are usage counts, not a dollar billing estimate. The editor remains usable while an API request or retry is pending. File tools run one per UI frame, and writes still check for unsaved editor changes. Copy Log copies the full conversation, including multiline errors and tool results. The visible transcript also supports selecting text across lines. Tools → Copy Last AI Error copies just the latest complete error message. Use Tools → View Last AI Request JSON or View Last AI Response to inspect the most recent payload and status; Copy Raw in that preview copies the complete unmodified body, even when the on-screen preview is shortened.

    When a turn pauses, is cancelled, fails, or returns incomplete output, the Continue button resumes the same task with its existing conversation and successful edits. It grants a fresh selected request budget. Errors do not throw away completed tool calls and force another repository tour. New explicitly clears the conversation. Conversations remain in this toolkit process's memory; restarting the app clears them.

    Empty or malformed API responses, connection failures, timeouts, rate limits, and server errors are retried up to twice with a short backoff while the request budget allows. The panel shows the cause and countdown; Escape cancels the retry. API key, quota, and other request errors stop immediately. A server-requested delay longer than one minute also stops automatic retries, so Continue can be used later. Retries count toward the selected request budget.

    Incomplete responses never execute partial function arguments. Continue after an output-token limit allows a larger per-response output cap, up to 32768 (including reasoning). There is no automatic paid retry for that condition. Intermediate assistant commentary is displayed while the agent continues; reasoning items and assistant message phases are preserved for subsequent requests. Requests retain store: false and disable silent context truncation.

    Direct API mode: filesystem boundary and verification#

    The native workspace module enforces the opened-project boundary. Absolute paths, traversal, alternate data streams, and targets outside the project are rejected. Operations keep the selected root open and resolve child paths relative to retained directory handles. Symbolic links and Windows reparse points are rejected while traversing children, and writes reject hard-linked targets. Creation uses the retained parent rather than reopening a checked pathname. Batched tools use the same native operations:

    Native reads and writes are capped at 2 MiB; agent whole-file writes are limited to 200000 bytes. Search skips generated and dependency folders. Reads can use current editor buffers; writes cannot overwrite unsaved changes. Successful writes reload clean open buffers and refresh the explorer.

    The direct API engine has file tools only. It must state which verification remains for the user; file creation alone is not a test result. Select Codex to give the bot sandboxed command execution and a compile/run/repair loop, or use the Toolkit Scan/Run controls yourself. Working directories alone do not confine arbitrary shell programs to the project.

    The agent policy, Responses handling, and filesystem batches live in toolkit/agent.sipl. tests/test_agent.sipl exercises a mocked multi-call read → create-project → finish workflow, caching, dirty buffers, instruction handoff, partial writes, budgets, continuation, and incomplete responses. The repository runner executes it normally and under GC stress, without paid API calls.

    Network and privacy#

    Codex supplies selected project contents, command results and conversation context to its configured provider. Direct API mode sends user messages, the compact local overview, optionally attached reference text and file-tool results to OpenAI. The agent uses current local files; it does not require a vector store. Its integration follows the official function-calling and reasoning-state protocols.

    Encrypted Toolkit settings#

    Open Tools → Settings… to manage encrypted settings. Select User or Project, edit the masked OpenAI/Google fields under API keys, or edit additional key/value pairs under Other JSON. Save or Ctrl+S validates and encrypts only the selected scope. Cancel, Escape, or X discards unsaved modal drafts; changes already saved remain saved. Switching scopes keeps each scope's draft until the modal closes. Invalid JSON, reserved provider properties in Other JSON, and invalid keys leave the existing file untouched.

    Provider fields live only in Settings. When the coding agent lacks a model or OpenAI key, its pullout offers Open Settings; sending a message also opens Settings and preserves the message without starting a request. A configured OPENAI_API_KEY environment fallback counts as an available key. Saved keys reload when Toolkit starts. Saving or loading makes no API request.

    User and project scopes#

    The Settings dialog has User and Project tabs. Editing or saving changes only the selected scope.

    ScopeWindows locationApplies to
    User%LOCALAPPDATA%\.sipl-toolkit\config.encThe current Windows user, across Toolkit installations and projects
    Project<opened-project>/.sipl-toolkit/config.encThat opened project

    Project provider values override user values. An empty project OpenAI key, Google key, or model inherits the corresponding user value. Clearing a user key removes it from user storage. With no saved effective key, the existing provider environment fallback still applies. Changing the opened folder loads that folder's project store and resets the coding-agent project context. The user store stays the same. Unsaved project changes are saved before switching; a failed save keeps the existing project open.

    Both scopes encrypt for the same Windows user. Project scope controls configuration selection; it is not a separate cryptographic identity or an access boundary between programs running as that user. Each user's user store is separate. A project file created by another Windows account normally cannot be decrypted by this account.

    A folder is created on its first save. The project folder is excluded from Git by .gitignore. The explorer hides .sipl-toolkit, and the coding agent's filesystem tools reject these paths and omit them from directory listings.

    JSON key/value pairs#

    Each file contains an encrypted JSON object, rather than editable plaintext JSON. Toolkit's fields create and update its provider properties in memory. You can also store arbitrary JSON properties with the explicit secrets API; Toolkit preserves those properties when it saves its provider fields.

    For example, a program can create encrypted project configuration:

    Choose the user file with secrets.userPath(). Reading both scopes explicitly uses the existing JSON configuration API:

    config.merge performs a shallow merge, with project properties taking precedence, including empty values. Toolkit's three provider fields additionally use the empty-project-field inheritance rule described above. Programs choose which properties they read; Run does not automatically export every secret as an environment variable.

    Unlike ASP.NET Core's usual User Secrets file, this file is encrypted at rest. See Microsoft's User Secrets documentation.

    Encryption and failure handling#

    Windows DPAPI encrypts the complete settings record using the current Windows account's credentials. No application master password or encryption key is stored beside the file. Decryption normally requires the same Windows account and computer; this is a local credential store, rather than a portable encrypted configuration. See Microsoft's DPAPI documentation.

    The on-disk format has an eight-byte SIPLSEC version header followed by the DPAPI-protected blob. Updates write encrypted bytes to a randomly named sibling file, flush it, and atomically replace the previous configuration. Temporary files contain ciphertext. Native DPAPI plaintext buffers and native worker key copies are cleared after use. Values needed by the running Toolkit remain in process memory.

    Missing configuration starts with empty keys and the default model. A damaged, unreadable, or undecryptable record is preserved and disables saving. Settings offers Use for session instead: it validates and applies the selected scope in memory without writing any file. Ctrl+S performs the same action. Move the existing config.enc aside, then restart Toolkit to create a fresh record. Save failures are reported in Settings; there is no plaintext fallback. Encrypted persistence currently requires Windows; other platforms can use session/environment keys.

    Which key is used where#

    The OpenAI field supplies the Toolkit coding agent (the direct API transport or the trusted native Codex broker). It is not placed in the agent prompt or automatically exported to programs launched with Run. An empty field retains the existing OPENAI_API_KEY environment fallback.

    The Google field supplies Run programs through a dedicated child-process environment containing GEMINI_API_KEY and GOOGLE_API_KEY. It does not change the Toolkit's environment, the system environment, or source files. Scan, Format, Build, Git, and tool-catalog operations do not receive this saved key.

    The standard ai.google(...) provider already reads these environment names, so examples/ai_chat.sipl needs no key embedded in its options. An explicitly provided options.apiKey takes precedence. If the Google field is empty, Run inherits any existing environment configuration. Run programs are trusted code and can read their supplied credential. Standalone runs outside Toolkit use explicit options or environment variables, without automatically searching Toolkit settings.

    Native APIs#

    secrets.userPath() -> String returns the current Windows user's %LOCALAPPDATA%\.sipl-toolkit\config.enc path using the OS profile lookup. It creates no directory or file. It raises Fail if the profile lookup or Unicode conversion fails, or on unsupported platforms. Effects: OS profile lookup and String allocation. Complexity: O(path length). Canonical example: secrets.load(secrets.userPath()).

    secrets.load(path: String) -> Map reads an explicitly named encrypted file. A missing file returns an empty Map. It raises Fail for invalid UTF-8/NUL paths, unsupported format, reparse-point/nonregular files, files larger than 128 KiB, decryption failures, or decrypted data that is not a JSON object. Effects: filesystem read, DPAPI decryption, and allocations. Time and space are O(file bytes + parsed JSON), subject to the existing JSON parser's limits. Canonical example: secrets.load(".sipl-toolkit/config.enc").

    secrets.save(path: String, values: Map) -> None serializes with the existing JSON API, encrypts with DPAPI, and atomically writes the file. The parent folder must exist. It raises Fail for invalid paths, unsupported JSON values, plaintext larger than 64 KiB, encryption/randomness failure, or filesystem failure. Effects: JSON allocation, OS cryptography, encrypted file creation/replacement. Time and space are O(serialized bytes). Canonical example: secrets.save(".sipl-toolkit/config.enc", {"model": "my-model"}).

    worker.run(path: String, apiKeyEnvironment?: Map) -> None accepts explicit String overrides for OPENAI_API_KEY, GEMINI_API_KEY, and GOOGLE_API_KEY. No other override names are accepted. Values are printable ASCII without whitespace, at most 512 bytes; empty Strings explicitly override an inherited value with an empty value. The Map is copied for the job. Keys are absent from the child command line. The environment applies only to that Run job and does not change subsequent jobs or the parent. Invalid inputs, missing supervisor, or a busy supervisor raise Fail. Complexity is O(inherited environment bytes + override bytes), plus the launched program's work. Canonical example: worker.run("app.sipl", {"GEMINI_API_KEY": suppliedKey}).

    Verification#

    The tests use synthetic keys only. Normal and GC-stress checks cover encrypted round trips, ciphertext containing neither key, replacements, damaged-file handling, clearing/reloading keys, user/project precedence and isolation, arbitrary JSON properties, storage locations, agent exclusions, child environment delivery, and unchanged parent environment. No live OpenAI or Google request is needed to verify persistence.

    SIPL Tools Store Format#

    This document defines version 1 of the package and server contract used by the toolkit Tools view.

    The canonical catalog is:

    Field names are case-sensitive. JSON files use UTF-8 without a byte-order mark. Versions use semantic versioning (MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH).

    Server Layout#

    The server is a static HTTPS origin with this layout:

    Required routes:

    RouteContent typePurpose
    GET /index.jsonapplication/json; charset=utf-8Complete current catalog
    GET /packages/<id>/<version>/<file>.zipapplication/zipImmutable package bytes
    GET /media/<id>/<version>/<file>Correct image typeScreenshots and icons

    The origin should also return the catalog from GET / while the store is being brought online, but /index.json is the stable client contract.

    Package and media URLs are immutable. Publishing a changed package requires a new version. index.json may use ETag and Last-Modified; publishing should replace it atomically only after every referenced file is available.

    Catalog#

    index.json is an array of tool records:

    Required catalog fields#

    FieldTypeRule
    schemaVersionIntMust be 1
    idStringStable lowercase package identifier
    nameStringHuman-readable name
    versionStringSemantic version
    typeStringOne of the types below
    shortdescStringOne sentence, at most 120 characters
    longdescStringPlain-text description, at most 2,000 characters
    authorStringPerson or organization
    licenseStringSPDX identifier or Proprietary
    downloadStringHTTPS URL or root-relative package URL
    sha256StringSHA-256 of the exact ZIP bytes, 64 hexadecimal digits
    sizeIntZIP size in bytes
    minSiplStringOldest supported SIPL version
    minToolkitStringOldest supported toolkit version

    Optional fields are homepage, repository, downloads, screenshots, and icon. downloads is server-owned metadata and must not be copied from the package manifest.

    The catalog contains only the newest non-yanked version of each tool. A future version-history API may expose older releases; installers must not infer version URLs.

    Tool types#

    TypeMeaning
    ToolA command or workflow launched by toolkit
    UIA toolkit-integrated panel or visual utility
    LibrarySIPL modules imported by programs
    TemplateFiles copied into a project
    ThemeToolkit colors and presentation data

    Type values describe installation and presentation. They do not grant permissions.

    Package ZIP#

    A package is a ZIP with tool.json at its root. It must not add an extra top-level directory.

    README.md and the license file are required. Source, assets, and screenshots are optional according to the tool type. Version 1 packages may not contain native executables, dynamic libraries, device files, symlinks, or absolute paths.

    tool.json#

    Required manifest fields are schemaVersion, id, name, version, type, description, author, license, minSipl, minToolkit, and permissions. Tool and UI packages also require entrypoint.

    The manifest id, version, type, author, and compatibility fields must exactly match the catalog. Catalog descriptions may be shortened for display.

    Identifiers#

    An id:

    • is 3 through 64 characters;

    • begins with a lowercase ASCII letter;

    • contains only lowercase letters, digits, and single hyphens;

    • does not end in a hyphen;

    • never changes after the first release.

    Command identifiers begin with the package ID followed by a dot. Paths in a manifest are relative POSIX-style paths, even when installed on Windows.

    Permissions#

    Packages have no implicit privileges. Version 1 permission names are:

    PermissionCapability
    workspace:readRead files under the open workspace
    workspace:writeCreate or change files under the open workspace
    networkMake HTTP requests
    process:runStart child processes
    clipboardRead or change the system clipboard
    dialogsOpen native file or folder dialogs

    The installer shows permissions before installation and again when an update adds permissions. Unknown permissions make the package incompatible rather than being silently ignored.

    The initial toolkit catalog is read-only. Package installation and runtime permission enforcement must be implemented before packages are executed.

    Installation#

    The user-level Windows location is:

    Other platforms use the operating system's user-local application-data directory. The installer maintains an installed.json file beside the tool directories to select one active version per ID. Installation follows this transaction:

    1. Download to a temporary file.

    2. Verify the byte count against size.

    3. Verify SHA-256 against sha256.

    4. Inspect and validate every ZIP entry.

    5. Extract into a new temporary directory.

    6. Validate tool.json against the catalog.

    7. Rename the directory atomically into <id>/<version>.

    8. Atomically update installed.json.

    Failure before the final rename leaves the active version unchanged. Uninstalling removes only the exact resolved package directory.

    Validation And Security#

    The publisher and installer both enforce:

    • HTTPS only, except an explicitly enabled loopback development server;

    • a catalog no larger than 1 MiB;

    • a package no larger than 16 MiB, matching the current native HTTP limit;

    • at most 10,000 ZIP entries and 64 MiB uncompressed total;

    • no empty, absolute, drive-prefixed, .., backslash, or NUL-containing paths;

    • no duplicate paths after case-insensitive Windows normalization;

    • no symlinks, hard links, device files, executables, or dynamic libraries;

    • no extraction outside the temporary package directory;

    • exact manifest/catalog identity and version matching;

    • exact size and SHA-256 verification before extraction;

    • explicit user approval for requested permissions.

    Clients fail closed on unknown schema versions, malformed semantic versions, invalid hashes, duplicate IDs, unsupported types, or incompatible SIPL/toolkit versions. They never replace a validation error with an empty or success-looking catalog.

    Package signing may be added in a later schema. SHA-256 provides integrity against the trusted HTTPS catalog but is not a substitute for publisher identity.

    Publishing Checklist#

    1. Validate tool.json.

    2. Run the package's tests with its declared minimum SIPL version.

    3. Create a reproducible ZIP with sorted paths and fixed timestamps.

    4. Compute its byte size and SHA-256.

    5. Upload the immutable ZIP and media.

    6. Fetch the uploaded ZIP and verify its hash again.

    7. Add or replace the tool's catalog record.

    8. Validate the complete catalog for unique IDs and URLs.

    9. Atomically publish index.json.

    Changing package contents, permissions, dependencies, or entrypoints requires a new version.

    Troubleshooting Discovery#

    The toolkit discovers tools only from /index.json. It never scans /packages/, because directory listing is not a safe or complete source of package metadata.

    If the Tools view says Connected but lists no tools:

    1. Fetch https://tools.superintuitive.net/index.json.

    2. If the response is [], the catalog is connected but empty.

    3. Add the package's catalog record and atomically replace index.json.

    4. Press Refresh in the Tools view. Refresh sends Cache-Control: no-cache.

    The validated test-tool package currently published at /packages/test-tool/1.0.0/test-tool-1.0.0.zip has size 981 and SHA-256:

    Its catalog record is:

    The ZIP existing with HTTP 200 proves package delivery works; it does not by itself publish the package in the catalog.

    JIT and execution#

    SIPL verifies bytecode before execution. Eligible code can be compiled automatically on Windows x64 and Linux x86-64; unsupported code continues in the interpreter with the same language behavior.

    The Apple implementation currently runs through the interpreter on Intel and Apple Silicon. Its Metal renderer does not enable the native CPU JIT or automatic GPU List.map offloading. See Mac coverage and acceptance.

    Large pure integer List.map operations can also use GPU compute on supported Windows and Linux systems. SIPL checks availability, memory limits, and the measured cost before selecting the GPU. Unsupported or unprofitable work stays on the CPU.

    Eligible code#

    The CPU JIT supports a growing subset that includes typed numeric operations, comparisons, branches, instance fields, positional calls, while loops, for loops, returns, common collection access, and Range iteration. Functions with unsupported operations remain valid and run in the interpreter.

    GPU map execution currently requires a pure closure-free integer callback with no observable side effects. Float operations, captures, arbitrary loops, and effectful callbacks stay on the CPU.

    All paths preserve SIPL's checked 64-bit integer behavior, failures, collection bounds, field mutability, and declared types. If an optimized assumption does not hold, execution resumes safely without repeating completed effects.

    Status and diagnostics#

    Functions expose these read-only properties:

    • .jitStatus: "uncompiled", "ready", or "unsupported"

    • .nativeCallCount

    • .callCount

    • .loopCount

    GPU maps additionally report .gpuStatus, .gpuCallCount, .gpuElementCount, .gpuTileCount, .gpuLastMilliseconds, and .gpuDevice. Counters advance only after a complete result is committed.

    Use the command-line diagnostics when investigating execution choices:

    jit-explain reports why reachable functions are eligible or unsupported. profile records interpreter telemetry and call/loop activity.

    Controls#

    • SIPL_DISABLE_JIT=1 forces interpreter execution for differential tests.

    • SIPL_JIT_CPU=auto|off controls automatic CPU compilation.

    • SIPL_JIT_GPU=auto|off controls automatic GPU map execution.

    Disabling optimization does not change program results or public APIs. Unsupported operating systems run SIPL programs through the interpreter.

    Safety and limits#

    Generated execution is bounded and never bypasses bytecode verification. Compilation failure is not a program failure; SIPL falls back to verified bytecode. CPU code is limited to 256 KiB per function and 32 MiB per session. GPU work uses private result storage and commits only after the complete map succeeds. Cancellation, allocation failure, device loss, or validation failure discards that private result and preserves the original list.
